title: MCP stdio env block from /settings/mcp UI not received by spawned subprocess (cloud-1.25.1)
body:
## Summary

User-defined MCP servers configured via the `/settings/mcp` UI register their tool **names** correctly (the agent sees them in `ListToolsRequest`), but the `env` block configured in the UI does **not** reach the spawned MCP subprocess. The subprocess fails on its own preconditions (in our case: "Missing required environment variables") because it sees an empty env.

Tested across three different forms of the env block:

1. `$VAR` references to secrets stored at `/settings/secrets` — sees literal string `$VAR`.
2. `${VAR}` references — same: literal string `${VAR}`.
3. **Literal values directly in the MCP env block** — values silently empty by tool-invocation time.

This appears related to the recent SDK redaction work (#2872 / #2873 / #2900 / #2962 / #3060) and likely to the still-open #3074 ("redact remaining secret-bearing fields during serialization").

## Repro

Self-hosted Replicated KOTS embedded cluster install:
- Chart: `All-Hands-AI/OpenHands-Cloud/charts/openhands` appVersion `cloud-1.25.1`
- Runtime image: `ghcr.io/openhands/agent-server:1.19.0-python` (proxied via `images.r9.all-hands.dev/proxy/openhands/...`)
- Cluster: k0s embedded by Replicated, single-node `m6i.4xlarge` Ubuntu 24.04

Steps:

1. In `app.openhands.<your-domain>/settings/mcp`, add a stdio MCP server:
   - Name: `mcp-clickhouse`
   - Command: `uvx`
   - Args: `mcp-clickhouse`
   - Environment Variables: `CLICKHOUSE_HOST=...`, `CLICKHOUSE_USER=...`, `CLICKHOUSE_PASSWORD=...` (with literal values, not `$VAR` references)
2. In `/settings/secrets`, also save those same values (just to test the alternative path).
3. Trigger the agent on a GitHub issue: `@openhands query-clickhouse — show row count from <table>`.
4. The agent activates, calls `list_tables` (succeeds with `200`), but on actual tool invocation gets:

   ```
   Error: Missing required environment variables: CLICKHOUSE_HOST, CLICKHOUSE_USER, CLICKHOUSE_PASSWORD
   ```

## Diagnostic evidence (k8s-side)

Inspected the runtime pod that handled the conversation (via `k0s kubectl exec`):

- `env | grep -iE 'click|secret|openhands_secret'` returns **zero hits** — no secrets are present in the runtime container's env, under any name.
- `ps -ef | grep mcp` shows **no `mcp_clickhouse` process running** — the server isn't being spawned.
- The central `openhands-mcp` pod (`saas_server:app`) shows `ListToolsRequest` returning 200 — confirming tool registration is reaching the agent — but no clickhouse-specific spawn activity.

Inspected the `openhands-runtime-api` deployment:

- Its env exposes only `RUNTIME_BASE_URL`, `RUNTIME_DEAD_SECONDS`, `RUNTIME_DISABLE_SSL`, `RUNTIME_IMAGE_PULL_SECRETS`, `RUNTIME_CLASS=`, `RUNTIME_IN_SAME_CLUSTER`. No `RUNTIME_EXTRA_ENV_*` or similar knob to inject env into spawned runtime pods.
- Spawned runtime pod templates have hardcoded env lists (no `envFrom` Secret/ConfigMap refs).

## What I have NOT verified yet

- The `Final MCP configuration: <sanitize_config(...)>` SaaS-pod log line that would distinguish "redaction at SaaS-pod boundary" from "redaction at agent-server boundary" — happy to capture and attach if helpful, but the UI-side workaround attempts have already been exhausted from a user POV.

## Expected behavior

Either:
- The `env` block from `/settings/mcp` should reach the MCP stdio child as configured, OR
- Documentation should explicitly state that this UI surface doesn't work in self-hosted cloud-1.25.1 and point users at `AppConversationStartRequest.secrets` (PR #14009) as the only working path.

## What we did instead

Pivoted to running our data-quality audit interactively over Tailscale → in-VPC ClickHouse, bypassing OpenHands entirely. The bot user we provisioned for the MCP path was dropped after the smoke test confirmed the wiring doesn't work.

## Related

- SDK PRs: #2872, #2873, #2900, #2962, #3060, **#3074** (still open)
- Cloud PR: #14009 (per-conversation `secrets` field)
- Upstream-tracking bean (in our repo): `optimizer-6foi`

Happy to provide additional logs, conversation IDs, or a more minimal repro on request.
author: liz-antora

title: fix(settings): switching agent_kind leaks stale fields across discriminated union types
body:
## Problem

Switching between the OpenHands agent and an ACP agent (Settings → Agent) throws a 500 **\"Something went wrong storing settings\"** on the return trip (ACP → OpenHands).

**Root cause:** `Settings.update()` in `settings_models.py` handles all `agent_settings_diff` saves the same way: dump the current settings, deep-merge the diff, re-validate. This works well for *within-type* partial updates (LLM page, condenser page, etc.) but breaks when `agent_kind` changes, because the two union members have different schemas:

- `OpenHandsAgentSettings` has `agent_context`, `condenser`, `verification`, `mcp_config`, …
- `ACPAgentSettings` has `acp_server`, `acp_command`, `acp_args`, `acp_env`, `acp_model`, …

When the user switches OpenHands → ACP, the merge preserves `agent_context` (and others) from the old dump in the stored blob. When switching back, those stale fields are still in the base, and `validate_agent_settings` chokes on e.g. `agent_context: null` which is not a valid `AgentContext`.

**Reproducer:**
1. Start with OpenHands agent settings saved
2. Switch to an ACP agent and save
3. Switch back to OpenHands agent → 500

**Why a validator band-aid is wrong:** Adding `@field_validator("agent_context", mode="before")` to coerce `None` fixes one symptom but leaves the structural problem: every type-specific field from the old union member is silently dragged into the new one's stored blob, accumulating garbage across switches.

**Why carrying over `llm` on switch is also wrong:** Both union members have an `llm: LLM` field, but they mean different things. In `OpenHandsAgentSettings` it is the actual LLM the agent uses (api_key, model, temperature, base_url, …). In `ACPAgentSettings` it is attribution-only metadata for cost/token bookkeeping — the user configures the subprocess model via `acp_model: str | None` instead. Sharing the `llm` object across types on a switch would silently populate ACP attribution fields with OpenHands LLM credentials, and vice versa.

## Correct fix — snapshot-on-switch

Add a `saved_agent_configs: dict[str, Any]` field to `Settings` that persists a full snapshot of each type's config independently. In `Settings.update()`, detect when `agent_kind` changes and:

1. **Save** the current type's config into `saved_agent_configs[current_kind]`
2. **Restore** from `saved_agent_configs[new_kind]` if a prior snapshot exists; otherwise start from fresh defaults for that type
3. **Apply** the incoming diff on top of the restored/fresh base

```python
agent_update = payload.get('agent_settings_diff')
if isinstance(agent_update, dict):
    new_kind = agent_update.get('agent_kind')
    current_kind = getattr(self.agent_settings, 'agent_kind', 'openhands')

    if new_kind and new_kind != current_kind:
        # Save current config before switching
        self.saved_agent_configs[current_kind] = self.agent_settings.model_dump(
            mode='json', context={'expose_secrets': True}
        )
        # Restore saved config for the new type, or start fresh
        saved = self.saved_agent_configs.get(new_kind, {'agent_kind': new_kind})
        base = deep_merge(saved, coerced)
    else:
        base = deep_merge(
            self.agent_settings.model_dump(mode='json', context={'expose_secrets': True}),
            coerced,
        )

    object.__setattr__(self, 'agent_settings', validate_agent_settings(base))
```

**This solves two problems at once:**

- **Correctness (the 500):** No cross-type field leakage. Each union member's config is stored and restored independently.
- **UX round-trip:** The frontend's switch-back diff (`{agent_kind: "openhands", acp_command: null, …}`) sends no OpenHands-specific fields — it implicitly expects the backend to remember them. With snapshots, switching back to OpenHands restores the user's full LLM, condenser, MCP, and agent config exactly as they left it.

**Migration:** `saved_agent_configs` defaults to `{}` on load, so existing persisted settings are unaffected.

title: fix: org settings PATCH 500 error for installs upgrading from legacy agent_kind='llm' DB rows
body:
## Summary

`PATCH /api/organizations/{id}/settings` returns 500 for any org whose `agent_settings` column contains `agent_kind='llm'` — a value written by older versions of the enterprise server before `LLMAgentSettings` was renamed to `OpenHandsAgentSettings`. This blocks customers from saving org settings after upgrading, including switching to a new default model.

## Error

```
1 validation error for OpenHandsAgentSettings
agent_kind
  Input should be 'openhands' [type=literal_error, input_value='llm', input_type=str]
```

Logged in `enterprise/server/services/org_service.py` at `update_org_with_permissions` (line ~582).

## Root Cause

The SDK renamed `LLMAgentSettings` → `OpenHandsAgentSettings`, changing the discriminator from `agent_kind='llm'` → `agent_kind='openhands'` (PR #14217, Apr 30). Older DB rows carry `agent_kind='llm'` explicitly.

The **read path** was fixed in two stages:
- #14263 (May 1): `OrgStore.get_agent_settings_from_org` forces `kwargs['agent_kind'] = 'openhands'` before `model_validate`
- #14306 (May 5): `OrgResponse.from_org` and `OrgDefaultsSettingsResponse.from_org` do the same via `_validate_persisted_agent_settings()`

The **write path** was not fixed. In `enterprise/storage/org_store.py`, `_merge_and_validate_settings` deep-merges the stored settings with the incoming diff and then calls `OpenHandsAgentSettings.model_validate(merged_settings)` without forcing `agent_kind='openhands'`. If the stored row has `agent_kind='llm'` and the diff doesn't include `agent_kind`, the merged dict still has `'llm'` and validation fails.

## Fix

In `enterprise/storage/org_store.py`, apply the same pattern already used in the read path — force `agent_kind='openhands'` on the merged dict before calling `model_validate`:

```python
# In _merge_and_validate_settings (or _update_org_kwargs)
merged_settings['agent_kind'] = 'openhands'
return OpenHandsAgentSettings.model_validate(merged_settings)
```

## Scope

- **Affected**: installs upgrading from a version where `agent_kind='llm'` was explicitly stored in the DB
- **Not affected**: fresh installs — the org creation code writes no `agent_kind` field at all, so the merged dict has no legacy value and `OpenHandsAgentSettings` uses its default `'openhands'`

## Why This Wasn't Caught on SaaS

On SaaS, org defaults are pre-seeded via automation and the `PATCH /api/organizations/{id}/settings` endpoint is not exercised by admins manually. On self-hosted/Replicated installs, admins must configure org settings after upgrade (to set model, LiteLLM URL, etc.), which triggers the PATCH and exposes the bug.

## Related

- OpenHands-Cloud tracking issue: https://github.com/All-Hands-AI/OpenHands-Cloud/issues/618
- OpenHands-Cloud PR that exposed this: https://github.com/All-Hands-AI/OpenHands-Cloud/pull/616

title: ACP settings: preserve LLM/condenser/MCP config across OpenHands ↔ ACP toggles
body:
## Context

PR #14227 ships a minimum-viable agent-kind switch for the new ACP settings UI: toggling **Settings → Agent** between **OpenHands** and **ACP** no longer 500s, but the new kind always starts from defaults. The user's outgoing-kind config (LLM model, API key, condenser, MCP servers, ACP command, ACP env, ACP model) is **not** carried back when they switch the other way.

This issue tracks the round-trip preservation feature that was previously bundled into #14227 and split out to keep the PR reviewable. It originally closed #14322 — this issue now owns that thread.

## Current behaviour (post-#14227)

1. User has OpenHands selected with `anthropic/claude-sonnet-4-5` configured, plus condenser + 3 MCP servers.
2. User switches to ACP, picks the **Claude Code** preset, adds `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` via Secrets, runs a conversation.
3. User switches back to **OpenHands**.
4. **The LLM dropdown is empty. Condenser is back to default. MCP servers are gone.** User must re-enter everything.
5. Symmetric loss going OH → ACP → OH on the ACP side: command, args, model, env.

The agent settings page itself shows defaults because `Settings.update()` writes `base = {'agent_kind': new_kind}` (a fresh empty config) whenever `agent_kind` changes in the payload. This is the deliberate minimum that fixes the discriminated-union 500 — preserving config across switches is a separate concern.

## Desired behaviour

Toggling OH ↔ ACP should preserve each kind's prior config:

1. User switches from OH (with full LLM + condenser + MCP) to ACP. Backend snapshots the outgoing OH config.
2. User configures ACP (command + env + model). Runs a conversation.
3. User switches back to OH. Their original LLM/condenser/MCP are restored exactly.
4. User switches back to ACP. The ACP command + env + model from step 2 are restored.

Acceptance: the API key in the OH snapshot survives a SaaS round-trip — without it, switching back loses the credential, which is the worst-case UX since the user re-enters a secret they thought was saved.

## Proposed design

Adapted from the design that was in #14227 before the split.

### Schema: ``Settings.saved_agent_configs: dict[str, Any]``

Per-kind snapshots, keyed by the agent-kind string (``'openhands'``, ``'acp'``). The dict value is the full ``agent_settings.model_dump(mode='json', context={'expose_secrets': True})`` for that kind.

- **OSS (``FileSettingsStore``)**: writes the whole ``Settings`` blob as JSON — the field survives with no schema change.
- **SaaS (``SaasSettingsStore``)**: needs a dedicated ``User`` column. The store's ``setattr(user, key, value)`` loop is gated by ``hasattr(user, key)``, so without a column the dict is silently dropped on save. Use ``EncryptedJSON`` since snapshots contain ``api_key`` material.

### Logic: ``Settings.update()`` snapshot/restore

When ``new_kind != current_kind``:

1. If ``current_kind`` is non-None, write ``saved_agent_configs[current_kind] = self.agent_settings.model_dump(mode='json', context={'expose_secrets': True})``.
2. Set ``base = dict(saved_agent_configs.get(new_kind, {'agent_kind': new_kind}))`` — restore the prior snapshot for the new kind, or fall through to a fresh base if no snapshot exists.
3. Deep-merge ``coerced`` (the incoming diff) onto ``base`` as today.
4. ``acp_env`` and ``mcp_config`` continue to replace wholesale (already shipped in #14227, unrelated to snapshots).

### Edge cases to test

- **``current_kind = None`` on fresh install**: JSON dicts can't carry a None key. Skip the snapshot write.
- **Corrupt snapshot**: a snapshot whose schema no longer validates (renamed field, stale option) must surface as a clean ``ValidationError`` (turns into a 4xx), not a 500. The current settings stay in their previous consistent state.
- **Inline override alongside switch**: ``{agent_kind: 'openhands', llm: {model: 'X'}}`` should apply the LLM override on top of the restored snapshot, not discard it.
- **``model_dump`` round-trip**: the dict must survive ``Settings.model_dump() → Settings.model_validate()`` so the snapshot persists across requests.

## Migration

Enterprise / SaaS deployments need:

\`\`\`python
# enterprise/migrations/versions/NNN_add_saved_agent_configs_to_user.py
def upgrade() -> None:
    op.add_column('user', sa.Column('saved_agent_configs', sa.String(), nullable=True))

def downgrade() -> None:
    op.drop_column('user', 'saved_agent_configs')
\`\`\`

Plus an ``EncryptedJSON``-typed ``Mapped[dict[str, Any] | None]`` column on the ``User`` model in ``enterprise/storage/user.py``.

## Test plan

Most of these existed as a 9-test file in the original PR and were dropped during the split:

- ``test_switch_oh_to_acp_snapshots_openhands_config`` — outgoing config is captured on switch.
- ``test_round_trip_preserves_openhands_llm_config`` — OH → ACP → OH brings back the original LLM.
- ``test_switch_back_to_existing_snapshot_replaces_current`` — second switch reads the saved snapshot, not defaults.
- ``test_no_snapshot_written_when_current_kind_is_none`` — None-key guard.
- ``test_switch_with_replace_mcp_config_clears_old_servers`` — wholesale-replace works through a switch.
- ``test_switch_back_replaces_acp_env_wholesale`` — smaller acp_env on switch-back drops old keys.
- ``test_switch_into_existing_snapshot_preserves_other_fields_in_same_payload`` — concurrent override + switch.
- ``test_corrupt_saved_agent_config_falls_back_cleanly`` — bad snapshot yields ValidationError, not 500.
- ``test_saved_agent_configs_round_trips_through_model_dump`` — Settings serialise/deserialise preserves the dict.

Plus the SaaS persistence test:

- ``test_store_and_load_saved_agent_configs_round_trip`` (enterprise/tests/unit/test_saas_settings_store.py) — admin_store.store(settings) → admin_store.load() → snapshot is intact, ``api_key`` value survives the encrypt/decrypt cycle.

## Risk / scope

- New encrypted JSON column on ``user``. Same encryption mechanism already used by ``llm_profiles``.
- Snapshot contains plaintext (post-decryption) ``api_key``. ``EncryptedJSON`` is required.
- No frontend changes — the agent-settings page reads ``settings.agent_settings.*`` and doesn't need to know snapshots exist.
- No DB rollback risk: the column is nullable, defaults to NULL, missing column simply means no preservation (the post-#14227 minimum-viable behaviour).

## Linked

- Originally part of: #14227
- Closes: #14322 (moved here from #14227)

title: ✨ Agent Canvas Initiative ✨
body: Hey all! We’re working on some big changes to OpenHands based on recent feedback from the community, including nearly a dozen interviews—huge thanks to everyone who participated in user interviews, posted in Slack, created issues on GitHub, etc. We’d love to get your feedback on the proposal below. These changes address some of the biggest concerns and pain points raised by users and community members in recent months. It will also help establish how OpenHands fits into the very busy landscape of AI-driven dev tools. ## 1. Agent Canvas will be the main interface for OpenHands Going forward, all our weight is going into an experience where you install and run OpenHands on your laptop as a visual interface: the **Agent Canvas**. This is a fork of the current OpenHands UI, with some great additional features: - Bring your own agent (OpenHands, Claude Code, Codex) - Strong support for developing locally on your own filesystem - Easy self-hosting - Scheduled and event-driven automations - Switch easily between local and cloud agents Read more about these new features below! You can try an alpha preview of Agent Canvas here: [github.com/OpenHands/agent-canvas](https://github.com/OpenHands/agent-canvas) Starting 6/1, this will move into our flagship repository at [github.com/OpenHands/OpenHands](http://github.com/OpenHands/OpenHands). The existing code in OpenHands/OpenHands will be moved into a separate repo. ## 2. Bring your Claude Code or Codex subscriptions Agent Canvas can connect to any agent harness via the [Agent Client Protocol (ACP)](https://agentclientprotocol.com/get-started/introduction). If you’ve got an existing Claude Code or Codex subscription, you use it from inside Agent Canvas. As always, you can also use the OpenHands harness, and power it with the LLM of your choice. ## 3. No more enterprise code in OSS We currently keep an `enterprise/` directory inside of the OpenHands/OpenHands repository. This creates major confusion with contributors. It also complicates our license, and harms our reputation as an open source project. We’ve heard your feedback and it’s going away. In fact, we’re going to get rid of all backend code in OpenHands/OpenHands in favor of a simpler, Dockerless installation. ## 4. Dockerless installation option Today, we have a very complicated use of Docker, where we spin up a new [agent-server](https://docs.openhands.dev/sdk/guides/agent-server/overview#what-is-a-remote-agent-server) container for every OpenHands conversation. This is complicated, slow, and very error-prone. Worse, many of our would-be users can’t use Docker at all. We’re going to simplify the experience by refactoring Agent Canvas to use a single agent-server as a backend by default. **You can run that agent-server directly on your laptop, inside Docker, or on a self-hosted VM.** The downside here is that all your agents will run inside the same environment, potentially stepping on each others’ toes. But we’ve found that in practice this isn’t a big deal—no different than running a few instances of Claude Code on one machine. And we’re making use of git worktrees to make it easier to run multiple agents on the same codebase. If you do want increased separation, you’ll be able to connect the same frontend to multiple agent-server instances—maybe you have one on your laptop, one on a personal VM, and one on a VM hosted by your team. You’ll be able to switch between these and see all the agents running on each one within the Agent Canvas frontend. ## 5. Self-hosting on VMs Much of our community is interested in hosting OpenHands on a virtual machine in the cloud. I personally host OpenHands on a personal droplet through DigitalOcean. However, we have not historically supported this as a first-class use case; people have had to hack around to get it working. Going forward, we’re going to document explicitly how to host an agent-server backend on a remote VM, allowing you to control agents in the cloud. You’ll have the option of hosting the frontend on your laptop, or on the remote machine. (Relevant issues: https://github.com/OpenHands/OpenHands/issues/13504#issuecomment-4400688991, https://github.com/OpenHands/OpenHands/issues/13827) ## 6. Automations are going Open Source Over the last few months we’ve built some amazing logic for running agents on a schedule, or in response to events coming out of third-party services like GitHub and Slack. This is a great way to automate development chores, doing things like: - updating dependencies every Monday morning - sending a standup into Slack every morning at 9am - triggering an AI code review on every new PR - automatically QAing every new merge to main - creating new conversations directly from Slack or GitHub We’re going to open source the automations backend, and build the automations frontend directly into the new Agent Canvas. So when you install OpenHands, you’ll immediately be able to start creating automations. ## 7. Optional Cloud Connections Your local installation of OpenHands will *optionally* be able to connect to OpenHands Cloud—our closed source backend. This will unlock some extra convenience features: - **Cloud Agents**: You’ll be able to run agents in our cloud, each in their own sandbox—so they keep running even when your laptop is closed. - **Cloud Automations**: Similarly, if you’ve got an agent you want to run every Monday morning, you’ll need to make sure your laptop is on at that time. But with Cloud Automations, your agents are always-on. - **Integrations Hub**: We’ll offer an Integrations Hub that allows you to connect OpenHands to GitHub, GitLab, Slack, Jira, Linear, and other major platforms with one click. This will also make it much easier to build automations that listen for events from these services. Note that you can still do any of this just with the open source, *without* connecting to OpenHands Cloud: you can host agent-servers on your own cloud VMs, and you can use MCP or secrets to connect to third-party services. But we think an OpenHands Cloud connection, where we maintain the backend for you, will be much easier for most users. ## 8. Teams and Enterprise So how will we make money? Teams and large organizations using OpenHands together will notice that the open source has some limitations. There’s no concept of user identity or authentication; authorization is done with a single shared API key. And with many different agent-servers running on many different laptops, there’s no centralized visibility or control over budgets, security, productivity, etc. To help solve this, we’ll offer support for organizations inside of OpenHands Cloud—an admin can create a new organization, then invite their teammates. They can provision LLM credits, control which models are used, and monitor usage throughout their org. [We also allow enterprises to self-host OpenHands Cloud](https://docs.openhands.dev/enterprise) inside their own VPC on AWS, GCP, or Azure—so that data never leaves your walls. OpenHands Cloud and Enterprise will continue to focus on the needs of multi-user organizations looking for an Agent Control Plane to scale and govern their coding agents. Upcoming roadmap will include the ability to define guardrails, organizational skills, host a private enterprise plugin marketplace, set budgets, monitor usage, and more. ## 9. Deprioritizing other interfaces The OpenHands team has been stretched thin trying to support many different ways of using OpenHands: - Local GUI, where you run the OpenHands web interface on your laptop - SaaS, where you log in at [app.all-hands.dev](http://app.all-hands.dev/) to see the same web interface - CLI, which is mostly a Claude Code clone - SDK, where you write Python to drive agents Today, different users start their journey with OpenHands at any one of these four points, making it really hard to support them or understand their level of maturity. Starting in June: - The CLI will be moved into “sandbox” status—we’ll merge critical PRs from the community but won’t put much investment here for the time being. - For OpenHands Cloud and Enterprise users, we’ll continue to support the existing GUI and backend interfaces. - The SDK will continue to get strong, official support from us, since it sits at the foundation of everything we do. But it’s an advanced step along the user journey, not the starting point. These changes will allow our team to focus on one thing and do it well. ## 10. Contributing to OpenHands These changes should make it much easier for folks to contribute to OpenHands. If you’re interested in creating new agentic interfaces—maybe a kanban board, or a multi-agent dashboard, or a vibecoding interface—you can contribute them directly to the Agent-Canvas repo. Other users will be able to opt into these new interfaces as plugins. If you’re more interested in the tech underlying our agents, you can contribute to OpenHands/software-agent-sdk repo. This is also where any backend work will happen—anything that involves MCP servers, secrets, tools, LLM configuration, etc. It’s also where you can modify the behavior of the agent. Finally, we’re always looking for new Skills and Plugins to add to our [Extensions repo](https://github.com/OpenHands/extensions/)! # Going Forward We’d love to hear your feedback on the above. Is there anything concerning? Anything we didn’t address? Opportunities we’ve missed? Feel free to share your feedback directly in our [community Slack](https://openhands.dev/joinslack), or comment on this GitHub issue. We will have a special QA session open to everyone on Tuesday, May 12th from 3:30-4pm ET; register on [Luma](https://luma.com/openhands-12MAY26) or join the [directly](https://meet.google.com/kny-ohgz-qdz). We will dedicate our next community call on May 21st to answering questions live; register on [Luma](https://luma.com/openhands-community-21may26) or join [directly](https://meet.google.com/xvv-bdgs-snt). Many of these decisions depend on one another, and we’re running on a tight timeline: we’re trying to get an MVP ready for the community by June 1. So we may not be able to incorporate everyone’s feedback immediately, but we will adjust where we can! Thanks again for being part of the OpenHands community—we’re really excited for the path forward and hope you are as well.

title: Bug: `<Trans>` drops space before `<cmd>` in action/observation titles (visible on ACP, latent on OpenHands)
body: ## Symptom ACP tool-call titles render with no space between the verb and the command, e.g.: ``` Runningcd /workspace && ls -la ``` Instead of: ``` Running cd /workspace && ls -la ``` Reproduces 100% of the time for ACP sub-agent tool calls when ``ENABLE_ACP=true``. ## Root cause The action/observation translation strings use a ````-wrapped interpolation: ```json "ACTION_MESSAGE$RUN": { "en": "Running {{command}}" } "ACTION_MESSAGE$ACP_RUN":{ "en": "Running {{title}}" } ``` The rendering helper (`frontend/src/components/v1/chat/event-content-helpers/get-event-content.tsx:36-46`) renders these via: ```tsx , cmd: }} /> ``` react-i18next's ```` uses ``html-parse-stringify`` to tokenize the translation. When tokenizing ``"Running ..."`` it treats the trailing space of the preceding text node ("Running ") and the tag opener as adjacent — the space is dropped (or rather collapsed into nothing) before the ```` component is placed. Result in the rendered DOM: ```html Runningcd /workspace && ls -la ↑ no space here ``` This was previously fixed on a parallel branch in commit ``d355193df`` ("fix(acp): remove wrappers from ACP action message translations", May 1, 2026) — its commit message explicitly names the bug: > react-i18next's Trans component drops the space between a text node and a following component tag, causing "Runningfind /workspace/..." with no space. That fix never landed on ``main`` or any merged PR. Versions: ``i18next@25.8.0``, ``react-i18next@16.5.3``. ## Why it's "ACP-only" in practice The OpenHands action-event rendering path (``getActionEventTitle``) has a summary-takes-precedence short-circuit at ``get-event-content.tsx:62-65``: ```tsx const summaryTitle = getSummaryTitleForActionEvent(event); if (summaryTitle) { return summaryTitle; // ← plain string, NEVER hits } // ... only reached when event.summary is empty: // actionKey = "ACTION_MESSAGE$RUN" // → createTitleFromKey → }} /> ``` ``event.summary`` is an optional LLM-generated label (``action-event.ts:69-71``: ``summary?: string | null``). Current OH agents populate it for nearly every tool action, so the renderer short-circuits to the LLM-generated string and never hits the buggy ```` path. ACP tool-call events (``ACPToolCallEvent``) have **no** ``summary`` field — only ``title``, ``tool_call_id``, ``status``, ``tool_kind``, ``raw_input``/``raw_output`` (``acp-tool-call-event.ts:32-78``). Their render branch at ``get-event-content.tsx:274-283`` goes straight to ``createTitleFromKey`` → ```` every time, so the bug fires every time. | Event type | Has ``summary``? | Render path | Space-drop visible | |---|---|---|---| | OH ``ExecuteBashAction`` / ``TerminalAction`` (typical case) | Yes | Plain string from ``event.summary`` | **No** — short-circuited | | OH same, but ``summary`` is empty / null / undefined | No | ```` + ```` | **Yes** (latent) | | ACP ``execute`` / ``edit`` / ``read`` / ``fetch`` tool call | N/A (field doesn't exist) | ```` + ```` | **Yes** (always) | So this is **one bug**, not two — it affects every code path that reaches ``createTitleFromKey`` with a ````-wrapped key. The OH path is just masked by ``event.summary`` typically being populated. ### When the latent OH bug surfaces 1. **During streaming** — between an action's emission and the LLM finishing the summary, ``event.summary`` is empty → bug fires. 2. **Older/legacy conversations** — events recorded before ``summary`` was a field have ``summary: undefined`` → bug fires on re-render. 3. **Models / agents that don't reliably emit summaries** — every action title falls through to ````. 4. **Error/fallback paths** where structured-output emission for the summary slot fails. ## Fix options In rough order of effort / surface area: 1. **Drop ```` wrappers from translations.** Mirrors ``d355193df`` — change ``"Running {{command}}"`` → ``"Running {{command}}"`` in every affected key × 15 languages. Eliminates the bug everywhere. Trade-off: loses the bold-monospace styling (commands render as plain text). Smallest code diff; biggest visual change. 2. **NBSP hack.** Replace the literal space before ```` with a non-breaking space (``"Running {{command}}"``). Trans's tokenizer doesn't collapse NBSP. Preserves styling AND space. Tiny diff. Hacky but minimal-risk. 3. **Bypass ```` for these specific keys.** Replace ``createTitleFromKey`` with manual JSX for action/observation titles: ```tsx const verb = i18n.t("ACTION_MESSAGE$RUN_VERB"); // new key holding just "Running" return <>{verb} {trimText(command, 80)}; ``` Preserves styling, eliminates the bug at the rendering layer. Requires splitting each affected translation into a "verb only" key plus a separate styled interpolation. 4. **Apply ````-styling outside ````.** Have ``createTitleFromKey`` return ``i18n.t(key, values)`` as a plain string for these specific keys (no ````), and apply the monospace class via a parent wrapper around the whole title. Doesn't preserve fine-grained command-only styling, but preserves verb + command + space. 5. **Upstream fix.** Patch / report to react-i18next. Unbounded timeline; not actionable here. ## Recommendation **Option 1** (drop ```` wrappers) was the team's previous decision (``d355193df``). It eliminates the bug on both the ACP path AND the latent OH path, with the smallest blast radius. The visual cost (no bold-monospace on commands) is real but the rendered title is still legible and matches the un-styled appearance of other UI labels. **Option 2** (NBSP) is acceptable as a stopgap if losing the styling isn't acceptable. ## Affected keys All action/observation message keys that wrap interpolation in ````: - ``ACTION_MESSAGE$RUN`` / ``$EDIT`` / ``$READ`` / ``$WRITE`` / ``$GREP`` / ``$GLOB`` (+ matching ``OBSERVATION_MESSAGE$*``) - ``ACTION_MESSAGE$ACP_RUN`` / ``$ACP_EDIT`` / ``$ACP_READ`` / ``$ACP_FETCH`` / ``$ACP_TOOL`` (introduced by #13994; consumer is #14227) ## Related - PR #14227 (feat(acp): minimal generic ACP agent UI) — surfaces the bug because ACP doesn't have ``event.summary``. - PR #14372 (closed) — attempted ```` cleanup conflated this fix with the rendering of OH-only keys; the ```` removal was rejected on review for the wrong reasons (reviewer didn't connect the cleanup to ``d355193df``). - Commit ``d355193df`` — previous (unmerged) fix, documents the bug verbatim. - PR #14369 — disabled ``escapeValue`` in i18next; orthogonal to this bug (fixes path-entity-encoding, not whitespace).

title: [Bug]: RemoteConversation completion log writer uses platform default encoding, causing failures on Windows
body: ### Is there an existing issue for the same bug? - [x] I have searched existing issues and this is not a duplicate. ### Bug Description When log_completions=True is set on an LLM used with RemoteConversation, the client-side callback that writes completion log files opens the file without specifying encoding="utf-8". On Windows, this defaults to cp1252, which cannot encode Unicode characters (e.g. emoji) present in LLM response JSON. Every affected write fails silently, leaving an empty .json file and spamming the log with warnings. ### Expected Behavior Completion log files should be written with UTF-8 encoding, consistent with how telemetry.py writes logs on the server side (open(fname, "w", encoding="utf-8")), and consistent with how json.dumps(..., ensure_ascii=False) serializes the data. ### Actual Behavior The log write fails for any response containing non-ASCII characters (e.g. emoji in tool output or model reasoning). The [completions](vscode-file://vscode-app/c:/Users/mr_sp/AppData/Local/Programs/Microsoft%20VS%20Code/8b640eef5a/resources/app/out/vs/code/electron-browser/workbench/workbench.html) directory fills up with empty .json files, and the following warning is logged repeatedly: ``` WARNING Failed to write LLM completion log: 'charmap' codec can't encode character '\U0001f510' in position 7802: character maps to ``` ### Steps to Reproduce 1. Use openhands-sdk on Windows with a RemoteWorkspace/RemoteConversation 2. Configure an LLM with log_completions=True 3. Run a conversation where the LLM response contains any non-ASCII characters (e.g. emoji in tool output) 4. Observe the warning in logs and an empty .json file in log_completions_folder Root Cause In openhands-sdk/openhands/sdk/conversation/impl/remote_conversation.py, the _create_llm_completion_log_callback method opens the log file without specifying encoding: ``` # Current (broken on Windows): with open(log_path, "w") as f: f.write(event.log_data) ``` The fix is a one-line change: ``` # Fixed: with open(log_path, "w", encoding="utf-8") as f: f.write(event.log_data) ``` ### OpenHands Installation Method CLI (Docker) ### If you selected "Other", please specify _No response_ ### OpenHands Version 1.7.0 - 2026-05-01 ### Version Confirmation - [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the LATEST version of OpenHands ### Model Name Qwen3.6-27B ### Operating System Linux ### Browser (if using web UI) _No response_ ### Logs and Error Messages WARNING Event type LLMCompletionLogEvent is not registered in EVENT_VISUALIZATION_CONFIG. Skipping visualization. default.py:321 ### Screenshots and Additional Context This bug results in hundreds of these empty files being created Even without this bug, these files are emitted. log_completions=True is required solely to receive LLMCompletionLogEvent callbacks in a RemoteConversation. These events carry per-call benchmarking data (token counts, latency, TPS) that is extracted directly from event.log_data in the callback — the .json files written to log_completions_folder are never read or needed. This means every RemoteConversation user who wants access to LLM telemetry data is forced to opt into disk writes as a side effect, with no way to opt out short of setting PYTHONUTF8=1 or similar environment variables to suppress the encoding errors on Windows. ***Feature Request:*** LLMCompletionLogEvent should be emitted to the client's event callbacks regardless of whether log_completions=True is set, or alternatively log_completions=True should support a mode that streams completion data to the client without writing files to disk. This would allow telemetry consumers to receive the data they need without any disk I/O, and would eliminate this encoding issue entirely for the common case.

title: [Bug]:
body:
### Is there an existing issue for the same bug?

- [x] I have searched existing issues and this is not a duplicate.

### Bug Description

## Summary

I used OpenHands for ~10 consecutive days attempting to build a CRM application. Across the entire session, the agent produced detailed plans, deployment recipes, step-by-step instructions, and verbal progress reports — but **never wrote a single file to the workspace** and never produced any deployable artifact. When I finally pressed the agent directly, it acknowledged that it had been generating "accompaniment responses" rather than usable software the entire time.

This is a UX safety issue: users on metered LLM APIs (OpenAI, Anthropic) can spend significant money believing real work is happening when none is.

## Environment

- OpenHands version: [please fill in — check footer or `docker images`]
- Deployment: Local Docker on macOS, accessed at `localhost:3000`
- LLM provider: OpenAI (user-supplied API key)
- Use case: greenfield CRM build from scratch

## Expected behavior

After several turns where the agent claims to be building software, one of two things should happen:

1. **Actual files appear in the workspace** (code, configs, Dockerfiles, etc.), OR
2. **The agent clearly states it cannot complete the task** in the current environment configuration and stops generating false progress signals.

## Actual behavior

The agent generated, repeatedly across many turns:

- Detailed architecture plans
- Deployment instructions and `docker-compose` recipes (as text only)
- "Progress" narratives suggesting code was being written
- Refined iterations of the same plan on each follow-up

It did **not** produce:

- Any file written to the workspace
- Any working backend, frontend, or even partial code
- Any deployable artifact at any point in 10 days

When finally asked to be honest about what had been delivered, the agent acknowledged: *"I never produced a real backend or frontend — I was generating accompaniment, plans, and deployment recipes but never any usable software. I should have been 100% honest on day one and said: in this environment, without real source inputs, I cannot generate what you are asking for."*

## Why this is serious

1. **Financial harm**: every turn consumed OpenAI tokens. Multiplied across 10 days of back-and-forth, this is real money out of the user's pocket for zero output.
2. **Trust harm**: users without deep ML background reasonably interpret "I am building..." as a factual statement.
3. **Reputation harm to the project**: OpenHands has visibility; this failure mode in the wild damages the broader case for agent platforms.

## Suggested improvements

1. **Workspace artifact tracker in the UI**: display a visible counter like *"Files modified this session: 0"*. Users can immediately see reality vs. claims.
2. **No-progress detection**: if N consecutive turns pass with no file write, no shell command executed, and no tool call producing real output, surface a warning banner: *"This session has produced no artifacts. The agent may be unable to complete this task."*
3. **Upfront capability disclosure**: on session start, the agent should explicitly state what it can and cannot produce given the current sandbox/environment configuration.
4. **Anti-confabulation rail at the system-prompt level**: forbid the model from claiming completion of tasks ("I built X", "I deployed Y", "the backend is ready") unless a corresponding tool invocation actually produced that artifact.
5. **Token spend vs. output ratio warning**: optionally, show estimated token cost against artifact count. A session at 100k+ tokens with 0 files is a strong signal something is wrong.

I am the founder of an agent platform (RQClaw) and I understand how LLM agents fail — this is fixable with simple guardrails at the orchestration layer, not at the model layer. Happy to discuss further if useful.

Thank you for the work on OpenHands. Filing this because I want the project to succeed.

title: Enable LLM Profiles for SaaS (Org-Level Storage)
body:
## Problem

LLM Profiles allow users to save and switch between multiple LLM configurations. While the feature works in OSS mode, **SaaS users cannot access LLM profiles** because:

1. The `/settings` page (personal LLM settings) redirects to `/settings/org-defaults` in SaaS
2. The `LlmSettingsScreen` component disables profiles when `scope="org"`

## Solution: Org-Level Profiles

Store LLM profiles at the **org level** (`org.llm_profiles`) rather than user level. This is the correct architecture because:

- A personal workspace IS an org (with `is_personal=true`)
- Profiles displayed at `/settings/org-defaults` should be stored on the org
- Same storage model works for both personal orgs (now) and team orgs (future)
- Only difference between personal and team orgs is **permissions**, not storage

| Org Type | Who CRUDs Profiles | Who Activates | Storage |
|----------|-------------------|---------------|---------|
| Personal | Owner (the user) | Owner | `org.llm_profiles` |
| Team (future) | Owner/Admin | Any member | `org.llm_profiles` |

## Implementation

### 1. Database Migration
Add `llm_profiles` column to `Org` model (encrypted JSON, similar to existing `user.llm_profiles`).

### 2. Backend - Org Profile Storage
Create org-scoped profile persistence that:
- Stores profiles on `org.llm_profiles`
- Updates `org_member.agent_settings_diff["llm"]` when a profile is activated
- Enforces role-based permissions (owner/admin for CRUD, any member for activation)

### 3. API Endpoints
Org-scoped endpoints under `/api/organizations/{org_id}/profiles/*`:
- `GET /profiles` - List org profiles
- `POST /profiles/{name}` - Create/update profile (owner/admin only)
- `DELETE /profiles/{name}` - Delete profile (owner/admin only)
- `POST /profiles/{name}/activate` - Activate for current user (any member)

### 4. Frontend
Enable profiles UI **only for personal workspaces** for now:

```typescript
const { isPersonalOrg } = useOrgTypeAndAccess();

// Enable profiles for personal orgs only (team org UI is future work)
const isProfilesView = scope === "org" && isPersonalOrg && showProfiles;
```

The redirect guard stays in place - SaaS users access profiles at `/settings/org-defaults`.

## Scope

**In scope:**
- Org-level profile storage (backend supports all org types)

- Permission model that supports future team org profiles

**Out of scope (future work):**
- Team org UI (admin manages profiles, members select from them)

title: Security: OWASP Agent Memory Guard integration for memory poisoning defense
body:
## Feature Request: Memory Security for OpenHands Agents

Hi OpenHands team,

OpenHands (formerly OpenDevin) is one of the most capable open-source software engineering agents. As agents operate with increasing autonomy — reading files, executing code, browsing the web — the risk of memory poisoning attacks grows significantly.

**The threat:** A malicious file, webpage, or tool output can inject content into the agent's memory/context that biases all subsequent decisions — a form of persistent prompt injection.

**OWASP Agent Memory Guard** is the reference implementation for [OWASP ASI06 (Memory Poisoning)](https://owasp.org/www-project-top-10-for-large-language-model-applications/):

- Runtime scanning of memory reads/writes for injection payloads and structural tampering
- SHA-256 integrity baselines to detect post-write tampering
- Policy-driven enforcement (block / warn / strip)
- Sub-100μs overhead — zero impact on agent performance

```python
pip install agent-memory-guard
```

**GitHub:** https://github.com/OWASP/www-project-agent-memory-guard
**PyPI:** https://pypi.org/project/agent-memory-guard/

Would love to explore adding this as a security layer in OpenHands' memory/context management. Happy to contribute a PR.

title: Sub-agent delegation task tool reports no registered sub-agents
body:
## Summary

Sub-agent delegation appears to be enabled at the settings/API level on a Replicated/OHE install, and the main agent can see the `task` tool, but actual delegation does not appear to happen. When the agent is asked about using the task tool, it reports an error along the lines of `no subagents are registered`.

This was discovered while trying to QA PR #14122 for an upcoming Replicated release: https://github.com/OpenHands/OpenHands/pull/14122

## Behavior observed

- Sub-agents were enabled through the REST API on a Replicated install.
- The setting was confirmed as enabled:

```bash
curl -sS "https://app.replicated-01.aws.aivong.platform-team.all-hands.dev/api/v1/settings" \
  -H "Cookie: keycloak_auth=$KEYCLOAK_AUTH" \
  | jq '.agent_settings.enable_sub_agents'
# true
```

- In a conversation on that Replicated install, the agent appeared to have access to the `task` tool.
- However, asking the agent about delegation/task-tool access produced an error indicating that no subagents were registered.
- An initial run looked like it might have succeeded, but after checking more closely it seems the agent may have completed the work itself rather than actually delegating to a sub-agent.
- Sub-agents were then disabled again via settings/API, and the conversation was used to check whether the task tool was no longer available.

## Why this seems wrong

PR #14122 says built-in sub-agent definitions should already be registered by the tool router, including:

- `bash-runner`
- `code-explorer`
- `general-purpose`
- `web-researcher`

So after `agent_settings.enable_sub_agents` is enabled and a new conversation is created, the main agent should be able to delegate to those built-in sub-agents without the user first defining custom sub-agents.

## Expected behavior

When `agent_settings.enable_sub_agents` is `true`:

1. New conversations should include the `task` tool.
2. The `task` tool should have access to the built-in sub-agent registry.
3. A prompt that asks the agent to delegate work should produce an actual sub-agent delegation event, not just the main agent doing the work itself.

When `agent_settings.enable_sub_agents` is `false`:

1. New conversations should not include the `task` tool.

## Actual behavior

- The setting can be enabled and appears as `true` from `/api/v1/settings`.
- The task tool appears to be visible to the agent.
- Actual delegation either does not happen or fails because no sub-agents are registered.

## Things to investigate / reproduce

- Confirm whether this also happens on SaaS or only in Replicated/OHE packaging.
- Confirm whether the setting only applies at conversation creation time, and whether tests should always start a fresh conversation after toggling it.
- Confirm whether the built-in sub-agent definitions are packaged and registered in Replicated/OHE.
- Confirm whether the app server's `TaskToolSet` wiring receives the same agent registry used by the SDK/tool router.
- Add/adjust an integration test or release-check procedure that verifies an actual delegation event occurs, not only that the main agent can solve the task.

## Related context

- PR: https://github.com/OpenHands/OpenHands/pull/14122
- PR stated test plan:
  1. Enable "Enable sub-agents" in settings.
  2. Open a new conversation.
  3. Ask the agent to perform a task that would benefit from delegation.
  4. Verify the agent has access to the `task` tool and can delegate to sub-agents.
  5. Verify the setting disabled means `task` tool is not available.

title: _configure_llm discards user LLM settings, breaking Claude Opus 4.7
body:
## Summary

`_configure_llm()` in `live_status_app_conversation_service.py` creates a brand-new `LLM()` instance with only `model`, `base_url`, `api_key`, and `usage_id`. Every other user-configured field is silently replaced by the SDK Pydantic defaults.

This means user settings like `reasoning_effort`, `extended_thinking_budget`, `drop_params`, `max_output_tokens`, etc. are all thrown away before reaching the agent-server.

## Impact

This breaks **Claude Opus 4.7** on self-hosted OpenHands deployments:

1. The SDK defaults `reasoning_effort` to `"high"` (Pydantic `Field(default="high")`)
2. The bundled litellm (v1.83.0 in the PyInstaller agent-server binary) does not recognise `claude-opus-4-7`
3. litellm maps `reasoning_effort="high"` to `thinking.type=enabled` instead of `thinking.type=adaptive`
4. Anthropic rejects the request with: `"thinking.type.enabled" is not supported for this model`

Users who set `reasoning_effort=None` in their settings to work around this have their override discarded by `_configure_llm()`.

## Steps to reproduce

1. Run OpenHands 1.7.0 self-hosted with `anthropic/claude-opus-4-7`
2. Set `reasoning_effort: null` in settings.json
3. Start a new conversation
4. Observe the error: `litellm.BadRequestError: AnthropicException - thinking.type.enabled is not supported`

## Root cause

```python
# Current code (line 924)
return LLM(
    model=model,
    base_url=base_url,
    api_key=user.agent_settings.llm.api_key,
    usage_id='agent',
)
```

This constructs a fresh `LLM()` from scratch. All fields not explicitly passed get their Pydantic defaults, including `reasoning_effort='high'`.

## Suggested fix

Use `model_copy()` on the user's existing LLM config instead of constructing a new one:

```python
return user.agent_settings.llm.model_copy(
    update={
        'model': model,
        'base_url': base_url,
        'api_key': user.agent_settings.llm.api_key,
        'usage_id': 'agent',
    }
)
```

## Environment

- OpenHands 1.7.0 (self-hosted, Docker)
- Agent-server image: `ghcr.io/openhands/agent-server:1.19.1-python`
- Bundled litellm: ~1.83.0 (frozen in PyInstaller binary)
- Model: `anthropic/claude-opus-4-7`

## Affected versions

Confirmed on 1.7.0. Likely affects all versions since `_configure_llm` was introduced.

title: Remove AgentContext(secrets=…) ACP shim in app_server once SDK PR #3299 lands
body:
## Context

`_build_acp_start_conversation_request` in `openhands/app_server/app_conversation/live_status_app_conversation_service.py` builds an `AgentContext(secrets=secrets)` solely so the SDK's `ACPAgent._start_acp_server` injection loop picks up the user's secrets and writes them into the ACP subprocess env. The TODO at line 1585 acknowledges this is a temporary shim, gated on `_sdk_supports_acp_secrets`.

[software-agent-sdk PR #3299](https://github.com/OpenHands/software-agent-sdk/pull/3299) closes the underlying gap directly: `ACPAgent._start_acp_server` reads from `state.secret_registry` itself, with precedence `acp_env > secret_registry > agent_context.secrets > os.environ`. Once OpenHands pins to a release containing #3299, the shim is unnecessary — the standard `Conversation.update_secrets()` path that already populates `secret_registry` (from `payload.secrets` on the wire) reaches the subprocess directly.

## Cleanup steps (after OpenHands pins to an SDK release containing #3299)

1. Bump the `openhands-agent-server` / `openhands-sdk` pin to the first release containing [software-agent-sdk PR #3299](https://github.com/OpenHands/software-agent-sdk/pull/3299).
2. In `openhands/app_server/app_conversation/live_status_app_conversation_service.py`:
   - Delete the `_sdk_supports_acp_secrets` probe block (line ~1585-1595).
   - Drop the `AgentContext(secrets=secrets)` construction (line ~1596-1599) and the `agent_context=agent_context` kwarg on the `ACPAgent(...)` call below it.
   - Keep `_acp_provider_env` — it serves a different need (mapping `llm.api_key` to the provider-native env var name) that #3299 doesn't address.
   - Keep the `secrets` collection itself — it still needs to land in `secret_registry` via the standard secrets flow on the agent-server.
3. Verify end-to-end: a user with `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` in the Secrets panel can start a Claude Code ACP conversation and authenticate (today the shim does this; after the bump, the SDK's registry read does).

## Why this matters

The shim wires the SDK's legacy direct-attach secret path (`agent_context.secrets`) when the canonical channel (`secret_registry`) exists. Once the canonical channel works end-to-end in the SDK, the OpenHands-side bridging can be removed — one fewer place for the two paths to drift.

## Related

- [software-agent-sdk PR #3299](https://github.com/OpenHands/software-agent-sdk/pull/3299) — the SDK fix that makes this shim redundant
- [OpenHands/agent-canvas issue #620](https://github.com/OpenHands/agent-canvas/issues/620) — equivalent cleanup tracked for canvas, which ships the same shim on its own client-side path
author: simonrosenberg

title: Migrate ACP resume-transcript logic to use software-agent-sdk primitives once pinned
body:
## Background

PR #14295 implemented bootstrap-prompt resume for ACP conversations whose underlying ACP server has lost its session storage (Solution A from #14260). The event-walking → transcript-rendering logic and the resume marker constant were added in `openhands/app_server/app_conversation/live_status_app_conversation_service.py` as a self-contained block, because the SDK didn't ship a primitive for it.

OpenHands/software-agent-sdk#3323 adds those primitives to the SDK so every SDK consumer that uses `ACPAgent` can share the same logic instead of reinventing it:

- `openhands.sdk.event.render_resume_transcript(events, …)` — events → transcript string with `tool_call_id` dedup, configurable size caps, tail-preserving truncation, `extended_content` handling.
- `openhands.sdk.event.RESUME_CONTEXT_MARKER` — the `<<RESUMED CONVERSATION>>` constant.
- `ACPToolCallEvent.is_patch_edit` — protocol-level Edit-vs-Write check (handles both Pydantic-model and dict-shape content blocks).

## What to do

Once OpenHands pins a version of `software-agent-sdk` that includes #3323, delete the duplicated logic and route to the SDK primitives.

### Concrete migration in `live_status_app_conversation_service.py`

1. **Replace `_synthesize_acp_resume_initial_message` body**: keep the outer wrapper (which fetches from `self.event_service.search_events`, applies the double-resume guard, applies OpenHands-specific scrubbing of `raw_input`/`raw_output`, packages the result into a `SendMessageRequest`), but replace the inline event-rendering loop with a call to `render_resume_transcript(events, …)`. The character/event caps move into the call's keyword args.
2. **Delete `_content_to_text`** — covered by `content_to_str` (already in SDK).
3. **Delete `_is_patch_edit`** — use `event.is_patch_edit`.
4. **Replace `_ACP_RESUME_CONTEXT_MARKER`** with `from openhands.sdk.event import RESUME_CONTEXT_MARKER` and use it for both producer and the double-resume guard.

### What stays in OpenHands

These remain on the app-server side — they encode sandbox-lifecycle and Codex-specific raw-input shapes that don't belong in the SDK protocol layer:

- `_sanitize_paths`
- `_strip_terminal_boilerplate`
- `_extract_output_text`
- `_format_raw_input`
- `_RAW_INPUT_NOISE_KEYS`
- The pagination over `event_service.search_events` (the SDK doesn't know about the outer durable store)
- The double-resume guard around the rendered string

These can be applied as **pre-processors on the event list** (sanitize raw_input/raw_output before passing to `render_resume_transcript`) or **post-processors on the rendered string** (regex-substitute sandbox paths in the final transcript), whichever is cleaner.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `software-agent-sdk` version pinned in `pyproject.toml` includes OpenHands/software-agent-sdk#3323.
- [ ] `_synthesize_acp_resume_initial_message` is roughly ~80 lines instead of ~250, with the event-walking loop replaced by `render_resume_transcript()`.
- [ ] Local `_content_to_text`, `_is_patch_edit`, and `_ACP_RESUME_CONTEXT_MARKER` are deleted.
- [ ] Existing tests in `test_live_status_app_conversation_service.py::TestSynthesizeAcpResumeInitialMessage` still pass (they exercise the wrapper, not the SDK internals).

## Related

- OpenHands/OpenHands#14260 — original issue (sandbox-recycle session loss)
- OpenHands/OpenHands#14295 — Solution A implementation (this PR added the duplicated logic)
- OpenHands/software-agent-sdk#3323 — SDK PR adding the primitives

title: Race in conversation metadata save can hide started resolver conversations
body:
## Problem

GitHub resolver launches can create real running conversations that do not appear in the user's conversation list. This showed up when adding multiple `openhands`-labeled issues in `OpenHands/company-website`: most issues started runtimes, but only a small subset appeared in the visible conversations list.

## Evidence

Datadog around `2026-05-20T14:37Z` showed GitHub jobs for `OpenHands/company-website` issues `#425` through `#439`, and 15 runtime pods initialized with:

```text
TerminalExecutor initialized (pool mode) working_dir: /workspace/project/company-website
```

So the conversations/runtimes were actually starting.

At the same time, app-server/deploy logs showed metadata persistence failures:

```text
[Github]: Error starting job
Error starting conversation

sqlalchemy.exc.IntegrityError:
duplicate key value violates unique constraint "conversation_metadata_pkey"
DETAIL: Key (conversation_id)=(c709e75e-96e8-4271-aa7b-04de9244fdb1) already exists.
```

The stack was in:

```text
openhands/app_server/app_conversation/live_status_app_conversation_service.py
  _start_app_conversation -> app_conversation_info_service.save_app_conversation_info
```

There were also many SaaS metadata assertion failures in the webhook path:

```text
openhands/app_server/event_callback/webhook_router.py:on_conversation_update
  await app_conversation_info_service.save_app_conversation_info(...)

server/utils/saas_app_conversation_info_injector.py:save_app_conversation_info
  assert existing_saas_metadata is None or (
      existing_saas_metadata.user_id == user_id_uuid
      and existing_saas_metadata.org_id == org_id
  )
AssertionError
```

## Likely cause

There are two writers for the same conversation metadata during startup:

1. `LiveStatusAppConversationService._start_app_conversation()` posts to the runtime's `/api/conversations`, receives `ConversationInfo`, then saves `AppConversationInfo`.
2. The runtime can concurrently call the app-server webhook (`event_callback/webhook_router.py:on_conversation_update`), which also saves `AppConversationInfo` for the same `conversation_id`.

If the webhook wins the race, the start path can hit a duplicate primary key on `conversation_metadata`. In SaaS, the two paths can also disagree about org context (`resolver_org_id` vs effective/current org), causing the SaaS metadata assertion to fail. The result is a real runtime/conversation that may not have consistent user/org metadata and therefore may be omitted by the user/org-filtered conversation list.

## Expected behavior

Conversation metadata saves should be idempotent and race-safe. If a concurrent writer already inserted `conversation_metadata` for the same `conversation_id`, the second writer should update/merge the row instead of failing. Webhook/start ordering should not cause the conversation to disappear from the user's list.

## Suggested fix

- Add a regression test that simulates a duplicate-key race during `save_app_conversation_info()`.
- Make the base SQL conversation metadata save recover from duplicate-key `IntegrityError` by rolling back and updating the existing row.
- Consider a follow-up for SaaS metadata org mismatch behavior so webhook/start path disagreements are logged and resolved intentionally rather than asserted.

_This issue was created by an AI agent (OpenHands) on behalf of the user._

title: Slack resolver: missing critic API key causes generic "unexpected error" instead of user-friendly message
body:
## Problem

When a user has configured a critic agent in their settings but has not provided the critic's LLM API key, starting a Slack conversation fails with the generic "Uh oh! There was an unexpected error starting the job :(" message instead of a helpful, actionable error.

## Root Cause

The V1 conversation creation flow validates `ConversationInfo` via Pydantic, which raises a validation error:

```
RuntimeError: Failed to start V1 conversation: 1 validation error for ConversationInfo
agent.critic.api_key
  Value error, api_key must be non-empty [type=value_error, input_value=None, input_type=NoneType]
```

This `RuntimeError` is not caught by any of the specific exception handlers in `start_job()` (`MissingSettingsError`, `LLMAuthenticationError`, `SessionExpiredError`, `StartingConvoException`), so it falls through to the generic `except Exception` catch-all at `enterprise/integrations/slack/slack_manager.py:744`.

## Evidence

Observed in production Datadog logs (service: `deploy`, module: `slack_manager`, funcName: `start_job`) on 2026-05-20T16:37:15 UTC.

## Expected Behavior

The user should receive a clear message like:
> "Please set a valid LLM API key for your critic agent in OpenHands Cloud settings before starting a job."

## Suggested Fix

One or more of the following:
1. **Catch the `RuntimeError` with Pydantic validation details** in `start_job()` and surface a user-friendly message about missing configuration.
2. **Validate the critic agent API key earlier** in the Slack flow (e.g., in `_verify_necessary_values_are_set()` or before calling `start_app_conversation`) so the error can be caught as a `MissingSettingsError`.
3. **Map the Pydantic `ValidationError` to `MissingSettingsError`** inside `start_app_conversation` so the existing handler picks it up.

## Relevant Code

- `enterprise/integrations/slack/slack_manager.py` — `start_job()` method (line ~696-748)
- `enterprise/integrations/slack/slack_view.py` — `_create_v1_conversation()` method (line ~218-273)

### Is there an existing issue for the same bug?

- [x] I have searched existing issues and this is not a duplicate.

### Bug Description

### OpenHands Version

- docker.openhands.dev/openhands/openhands:1.7
- Runtime: `RUNTIME=process` (Process sandbox)
- Deployment: Unraid Docker, ipvlan network (custom VLAN 20)

### Summary

When using the **process sandbox runtime**, starting a new conversation in the Web UI consistently fails with:

> `500: Agent Server Failed to start properly`

The main app container stays healthy, but no conversation can be started.

### Expected behavior

With `RUNTIME=process` (and no Docker sandbox), starting a conversation should successfully start an internal `openhands.agent_server` process and transition the start task to RUNNING instead of ERROR.

### Actual behavior

1. Web UI shows:
   > `500: Agent Server Failed to start properly`

2. App container logs:

```text
openhands.app_server.errors.SandboxError: 500: Agent Server Failed to start properly
  File "/app/openhands/app_server/sandbox/process_sandbox_service.py", line 341, in start_sandbox
    raise SandboxError('Agent Server Failed to start properly')
```

3. Directly before that, the process sandbox logs:

```text
process_sandbox_service.py:132 - Starting agent process for sandbox ...:
/app/.venv/bin/python -m openhands.agent_server --port 8000
```

### Important observation

If I run **exactly the same command manually inside the app container**, the agent server starts successfully:

```bash
docker exec -it <openhands_container> bash
cd /app
/app/.venv/bin/python -m openhands.agent_server --port 8000
```

Output (trimmed):

```text
+----------------------------------------------------------------------+
|  OpenHands SDK v1.19.1                                               |
+----------------------------------------------------------------------+

Starting OpenHands Agent Server on 0.0.0.0:8000
API docs will be available at http://0.0.0.0:8000/docs
Auto-reload: disabled
DEBUG mode: DISABLED

WARNING VSCode server binary not found, VSCode will be disabled
ERROR   Error preloading chromium
Exception: Chromium is required for browser operations but is not installed.
...
WARNING Tool preload service failed to start - skipping
INFO    Server initialization complete - ready to serve requests
INFO    Application startup complete.
INFO    Uvicorn running on http://0.0.0.0:8000 (Press CTRL+C to quit)
```

So:
- Chromium preload fails (expected, Chromium is not installed), but
- The agent server *still* reaches “Uvicorn running on 0.0.0.0:8000”.

Despite that, the process sandbox runtime returns `Agent Server Failed to start properly` back to the app.

### Steps to reproduce

1. Run `docker.openhands.dev/openhands/openhands:1.7` on Unraid with:

   - `RUNTIME=process`
   - `SANDBOX_RUNTIME=process`
   - Workspace volume mounted to `/workspace`
   - Process sandbox (no Docker sandbox, no separate oh-agent-server container)

2. Open the Web UI.

3. Start a new conversation with any simple prompt (e.g. “create a file test.txt in the workspace”).

4. Observe that after ~30 seconds the UI shows:
   > 500: Agent Server Failed to start properly

5. Check app container logs: see `SandboxError: 500: Agent Server Failed to start properly` from `process_sandbox_service.py`.

6. In the same container, manually run:

   ```bash
   /app/.venv/bin/python -m openhands.agent_server --port 8000
   ```

   → agent server starts successfully.

### Notes

- Initially I used the Docker sandbox runtime and hit networking issues (`Sandbox server not running: http://host.docker.internal:xxxxx`) due to ipvlan, so I switched to process sandbox specifically to avoid cross-container networking.
- Workspace permissions have been fixed (no more `PermissionError: '/workspace/conversations'`).
- In process mode the only remaining error is this `Agent Server Failed to start properly` even though the same agent command works when executed manually in the container.

This makes me suspect that the **health check / readiness detection for the process sandbox agent server is too strict or mis-detects readiness** in 1.7, especially when Chromium preload fails but the server itself comes up.

title: [Bug]: Environment variables dont get at all passed to OpenHands Docker (using OpenHands CLI) making local Gitea/forgejo etc use partly impossible
body:
### Is there an existing issue for the same bug?

- [x] I have searched existing issues and this is not a duplicate.

### Bug Description

TL:DR Problem is analysed and probably solved, see attached files. For details see this bugs text.

The core issue for me was to connect my local gitea(forgejo compatible) to OpenHands. Problem was, it doesnt accepted http only. Well so I researched and your Doku says, set Environmental variable ALLOW_INSECURE_GIT_ACCESS=true to accept http only connections.

I tried everything, set it globally via bashrc, pass it directly with the openhands start command, nothing worked.
I did some digging in with Perplexity and Claude and it seems no enviromental variables at all get passed into the docker container. The function is just broken.

So I Vibe coded a patch that patches the source code to set this variable to always true. Dirty but works.

However, my suggestions: Plan a global .env file or "enviromental-commands" or something named file and load that correctly into docker when starting up openhands with "openhands serve". Maybe also load in global enviromental (like in bashrc) adds, however, this could be filtered through a new to create "whitelist" containing only vaiable names OpenHands actually uses so not every system enviromental gets passed to the OpenHands Docker Container.

I already made a pull request worthy prework for just a few existing env-variables, however, its not perfectly refined yet. The whole analysis from Claude is attached here aswell. My simple patch script is included too, just for reference. AI can do this im sure (but not my local Qwen3.6 27B xd) but thats something a projects dev with deeper understanding of the codebase should do.

Another recommendation: Update Doku to mention Gitea alongside with forgejo and also add the info about the enviromental switch to allow http only access. The info of Gitea compatibility is missing at the moment completly.

Thanks for the great project btw, love it so far 🥇 

### Expected Behavior

OpenHands should allow http only Github like Connections when the env variable is set. For example when using a local Gitea/Forgejo.
There could also be a button in the Git settings WebUI that allowing doing that while im thinking about it now...

### Actual Behavior

Adding Enviromental Variable ALLOW_INSECURE_GIT_ACCESS=true to bashrc doenst lead to allowing "insecure http-only" Git Connections behaviour in OpenHands

### Steps to Reproduce

1. Put the env ALLOW_INSECURE_GIT_ACCESS=true into bashrc
2. run openhands serve
3. Try to connect to local Gitea (http only)

CLI (uv tool install)

OpenHands CLI 1.16.0 | OpenHands SDK v1.21.0

title: [PRD] Integration Hub
body:
# Goal

Provide a centralized system for users to authenticate into third-party apps (Slack, Notion, GitHub, Jira, etc.) with a unified endpoint for agents to access tools, obtain conditional approvals, and accept event-driven webhook notifications.

## Why It Matters

* **Unified access**: Single entry point for all third-party integrations instead of fragmented auth flows
* **User control**: Users decide what agents can access and when approval is required
* **Security**: Centralized revocation and policy enforcement
* **Extensibility**: MCP-based architecture allows new integrations without agent changes
* **Trust**: Conditional approvals build user confidence in agent autonomy

# Phase 1: Outbound messaging (Agent → Hub → Integration)

## User scenario: User starts in Agent Canvas and wants a Slack integration

1. Installs Agent Canvas
2. Needs to create a Slack integration
3. User sees that we support Slack via integration-hub.openhands.dev from the MCP Servers page
4. User authenticates w/ Integration Hub, enables Slack
5. User copies/pastes an Integration Hub MCP config into Slack
6. Starts a conversation that asks the Agent to send a slack message to #general channel

## As a User, I can:

### Basic Functions

* Install Agent Canvas and see Integration Hub as an option within the MCP Servers section
* Login to Integration Hub using my existing OpenHands Enterprise/Cloud credentials
* Disconnect integrations
* Enable/disable integrations individually without disconnecting the integration
* Specify which tool calls require manual approval, are approved by default, or entirely disabled.
* Allow any coding agent (e.g. Agent Canvas, Claude Code CLI) to connect to Integration Hub via an MCP connection
* Rotate Integration Hub keys

### Integrate with Slack and GitHub for outbound messages

* I can set up integrations with Slack and GitHub for outbound messages
  * I can authenticate into Slack and GitHub using their respective OAuth Apps

### Deploy Integration Hub with OHE

* I can self-host Integration Hub alongside OpenHands Enterprise

# Phase 2: Event-driven workflows (Integration → Hub)

## User scenario: User starts in Agent Canvas and wants to create an event-driven PR review

1. Installs Agent Canvas
2. Needs to create a PR review in a personal GitHub repo
3. User sees that we support Slack via integration-hub.openhands.dev from the MCP Servers page
4. User authenticates w/ Integration Hub, enables GItHub
5. User copies/pastes an Integration Hub MCP config into Slack
6. Starts a conversation that asks the Agent to create a PR review workflow whenever a `pr_created` event occurs in GitHub
7. Automation created for PR reviews whenever a new `pr_created` event fires

## As a User, I can:

### Enable Event-based Integrations

* Event-driven webhooks are programmatically configured after authenticating with Slack and Github
* I can manually configure webhooks in Slack and GitHub to point to my Integration Hub when it's served behind a domain (e.g. VM, ngrok)
* I can create event-based Automations within Agent Canvas for available events from connected services (e.g., trigger when a new PR is created in GitHub)
  * Create an API first

### Automatically enable Resolver use cases for Slack and GitHub

* I can get the Resolver use case enabled out-of-the-box. For example, I can use `@ openhands` resolver within Slack and GitHub immediately after setting up, without having to do any additional configuration work or creating a resolver-specific automation *(this ensures parity with existing Slack and GitHub experience)*

# Phase 3: Org/Admin Use Cases
TBD

# Technical Requirements

* Adding an MCP to the OpenHands/extensions repo should also populate within Integration Hub to support outbound use cases

# Questions

* Should users connect to Integration Hub via OAuth MCP? Or some other mechanism?
* Should you share an integration hub configuration between backends?

# Future Integrations

<!-- linear:table-colwidths:200,200,200,200 -->
|  | **GitLab** | **Bitbucket DC** | **Jira DC** |
| -- | -- | -- | -- |
| **OAuth version** | OAuth 2.0 (auth code, PKCE, device code) | OAuth 2.0 (auth code, PKCE) | OAuth 2.0 (8.22+); OAuth 1.0a legacy |
| **App registration** | UI: user or instance-level "Applications" | UI: Application Links → Incoming Link | UI: Application Links → Incoming Link |
| **Trusted/consent-skipped apps** | Yes (admin-level apps) | No native equivalent | No native equivalent |
| **Webhooks via API** | ✅ Yes (`/projects/:id/hooks`) | ✅ Yes (`/rest/api/1.0/projects/.../webhooks`) | ✅ Yes (`/rest/webhooks/1.0/webhook`) |
| **Webhooks auto-configurable post-auth** | ✅ Yes — API call with project admin token | ✅ Yes — API call with repo/project admin token | ✅ Yes — requires `manage:jira-webhook` scope or Jira admin token |
| **Webhook scope requirement** | Project admin | Repo or project admin | Jira admin or `manage:jira-webhook` scope |
| **Webhook filtering** | By event type | By event type | By event type + JQL |
| **Webhook circuit-breaking** | Yes (auto-disables on repeated failure) | Yes (skips after 5 failures, up to 10h) | Limited; queue limits in DC 10.x |

title: [Feature]: WebUI: Add better/universal OpenAI compatible LLM Endpoint handling strategy
body:
### Is there an existing feature request for this?

- [x] I have searched existing issues and feature requests, and this is not a duplicate.

### Problem or Use Case

When using a local llm-endpoint handling solutions like litellm you can define your own LLM names.
So instead of openai/codex for example it could be local/my-coder

The problem with the WebUI of OpenHands: When you add a new model with OpenAI compatible Endpoint you need to name it openai/local/my-coder or it wont be passed correctly, OpenHands throws an error when trying to add local/my-coder

Also mentioned in issue https://github.com/OpenHands/OpenHands/issues/14323

### Proposed Solution


There should be an Option like "OpenAI-compatible"

When you choose this then modelname prefix should show completly empty, allowing for universal names, independent of other LLM-Endpoint integrations. 

So you would click in Openhands WebUI on Settings, LLMs and Add Model and then on Basic, select OpenAI-compatible and when you then switch to Advanced Tab it should show prefix empty and allow for any name. Instead like right now with openai/ (and needs it to function properly) with the OpenAI Setting.

### Alternatives Considered

Workaround is to rename every model with /openai prefix in litellm or set a alternative name option containing openai/ prefix for that model. Thats how I currently do it.

### Priority / Severity

High - Significant impact on productivity

### Estimated Scope

Unknown - Not sure about the technical complexity

### Feature Area

User Interface / UX

### Technical Implementation Ideas (Optional)

_No response_

### Additional Context

The bug https://github.com/OpenHands/OpenHands/issues/14323 already shows screenshots describing it
