title: ❓ Agent Canvas transition FAQ
body:
## Community FAQ

Dated: June 3rd, 2026

With the launch of Agent Canvas, we'd like to share an update on how we see Agent Canvas, Local GUI, and the CLI evolving over time. Some of these plans were previewed last month in the [Agent Canvas Initiative issue](https://github.com/OpenHands/OpenHands/issues/14374), and we'd like to provide more detail on where things stand today. 

Agent Canvas continues to move through BETA and towards a stable release. On June 3rd, we launched the BETA to the OpenHands Community. We invite contributions, bug fixes, and all feedback. We still have work to do around stability, but Agent Canvas has become a daily tool for the OpenHands team across both ad-hoc conversations and always-on automations. Community members have also been putting it through its paces and sharing valuable feedback as we continue to improve it.

> “Canvas is bomb!!!! this is perfect guys”
—Andrew C.
> 

> “But seriously this is some cool stuff…Its dedicated, fast, worry free and lets me bring my own keys!”
—Evan O.
> 

> “It’s a beautiful, you guys have done a great job. I love the product…I’ve drunk the kool-aid”
—Anthony T.
> 

The community is increasingly orienting around Agent Canvas as the long-term future of the OpenHands user experience, and we're organizing our projects and repositories around that direction. That raises important questions about how we maintain other parts of the OpenHands ecosystem, including Local GUI, the CLI, and the way our repositories are organized. We go into these details below:

### **What will go in the OpenHands/OpenHands repo?**

This is our flagship repository, built with contributions from more than 500 people and supported by a community that has helped it reach 75k stars. It will be everyone’s first introduction to the OpenHands community. So what goes here is important.

First, the README of OpenHands/OpenHands will point users to `npm install @openhands/agent-canvas` or `docker run ghcr.io/openhands/agent-canvas`. It makes sense that our primary repo would point folks to our primary interface!

Second, most of the code that currently resides in OpenHands/OpenHands will be deprecated. It’s a legacy frontend and a mostly-enterprise-licensed backend. We’re going to move this code elsewhere (along with the annoying dual license!)—see more below.

But in terms of what code should live in this repo going forward, we’re seeking feedback from the community. We see a few options:

- Option A: [Agent Canvas](https://github.com/OpenHands/agent-canvas) (the frontend code)
- Option B: [Software Agent SDK](https://github.com/OpenHands/software-agent-sdk) (which also contains the backend code, plus much more)

Agent Canvas is a natural choice, since that’s what folks will be installing. The SDK is also a natural choice, since that’s where the “core” of OpenHands lives.

What do you think? We’d like to get your feedback!

### **Where will the OpenHands/OpenHands code go?**

This code (often called “Local GUI”) will move to a new repo.

Existing installs (Docker Install or via `openhands serve`) will continue to work. And we’ll continue merging bug and vulnerability fixes while it remains in maintenance mode (see below).

### What will happen to the CLI?

Today, the CLI is composed of:

- A Terminal UI (TUI), similar to Claude Code
- A headless CLI (which works like `claude -p`)
- ACP mode (which allows it to run in your IDE)

As we focus development effort on Agent Canvas, we will put the TUI into maintenance mode. But we’ll continue to support headless/ACP modes.

### What will happen to the Software Agent SDK project?

OpenHands Software Agent SDK remains a first-class officially supported project. The SDK will continue to get regular updates, features, enhancements, and bug fixes by both the community and OpenHands staff.

If the code will move to the OpenHands/OpenHands repo, we’ll do our best to preserve commits/contributions/issues/etc.

### **What is “maintenance mode”?**

OpenHands commits to supporting projects for a period of time after they go into maintenance mode, to ensure users have time to migrate to the latest products, without disrupting their workflows.

While in maintenance mode, the TUI and Local GUI will receive:

- Dependency updates
- Critical bug fixes
- Support for new LLMs

But they will not get any new features or non-critical updates.

### **How long will OpenHands staff maintain Local GUI and CLI code?**

**Local GUI**

We plan to support Local GUI until the Agent Canvas has a way to support isolated, ephemeral sandboxes. This remains one of the biggest feature gaps relative to Local GUI, however we are considering different architectural options to make this support better.

**TUI**

The TUI will receive maintenance for at least 3 months, until October 1, 2026. Headless/ACP modes will continue to receive full support indefinitely.

### **How do I migrate from Local GUI to Agent Canvas?**

Agent Canvas should pick up most of your settings and existing conversations from your ~/.openhands directory. If you have trouble migrating, reach out to us on Slack!

title: batch_get_sandboxes 500s the conversation list when the runtime API is slow — missing the graceful fallback get_sandbox already has
body:
## Summary

When the remote runtime/sandbox API is slow or unreachable, `GET /api/v1/app-conversations` (and `/app-conversations/search`) return **HTTP 500** instead of degrading gracefully. A single slow upstream turns every conversation-list request into an error, even for conversations whose stored DB records are perfectly fine.

## Cause

In `openhands/app_server/sandbox/remote_sandbox_service.py`:

- `_send_runtime_api_request` catches `httpx.TimeoutException` / `httpx.HTTPError` but **re-raises** them (~lines 127–132).
- `_get_runtimes_batch` calls `response.raise_for_status()` (~line 268), so an upstream error propagates.
- `batch_get_sandboxes` calls `await self._get_runtimes_batch(...)` with **no try/except** (~line 669). The exception bubbles all the way out, failing the entire batch and the conversation-list request.

## The inconsistency

The single-sandbox path already degrades gracefully: `get_sandbox` wraps the runtime fetch in `try/except Exception` and falls back to `self._to_sandbox_info(stored_sandbox, None)` (~line 388). The data model already supports a `None` runtime (it maps to a missing/unknown status). The **batch** path is simply missing the same guard.

## Suggested direction (not prescribing implementation)

- In `batch_get_sandboxes`, wrap the `_get_runtimes_batch` call so that on failure it falls back to `runtimes_by_id = {}`. Every sandbox then degrades to `runtime=None` (mirroring `get_sandbox`), and the endpoint returns conversations with an unknown/missing runtime status instead of a 500.
- Optionally introduce a distinct "status unknown" value (vs. "missing") so a transient runtime-API outage isn't misreported as a deleted sandbox.

## Why it matters

This is defense-in-depth: it prevents a slow or unavailable runtime API from cascading into user-facing 5xx on the conversations list — independent of any fix on the runtime-API side.

title: Use shallow clone by default with a setting to fetch full Git history
body:
## Problem

Starting conversations from large repositories can be slow because OpenHands currently performs a full Git clone when a repository is selected.

For most tasks, OpenHands only needs the current branch and recent repository state. Fetching the full Git history by default adds unnecessary startup time, especially for very large repositories.

Some tasks still require full Git history — for example, tasks involving older commits, tags, merge bases, historical blame, changelog generation, or checking out arbitrary commits. Users should have a clear way to opt into the previous full-clone behavior when they need it.

## Proposed solution

Make shallow cloning the default for repository selections.

Add a setting under **Application → Git Settings** or a new **Repository Cloning** section:

**Fetch full Git history for repositories**

Default: **Off**

When this setting is off, OpenHands uses a shallow clone to speed up repository startup.

When this setting is on, OpenHands uses the previous full-clone behavior.

Suggested helper text:

> OpenHands uses shallow clones by default to speed up startup for large repositories. Turn this on if your tasks require full Git history, tags, merge bases, historical blame, or checking out older commits. Full clones may take longer for large repositories.

## User experience

Users should not need to understand Git clone flags to get faster repository startup by default.

Users who know they need full history should have a simple, visible setting that restores the old behavior.

The setting should avoid “workspace” language and describe the behavior in terms of repositories and Git history.

## You will know this succeeded when

- New repository selections use shallow clone by default.
- Users can enable **Fetch full Git history for repositories** to restore the previous full-clone behavior.
- The setting is persisted and respected for future repository selections.
- The setting applies consistently across repository-started conversations, including UI-created conversations and integration-triggered conversations.
- Users are warned in the UI that shallow clones may not support history-dependent operations.
- When OpenHands starts from a shallow clone, the agent receives context explaining that Git history may be incomplete and how to deepen or unshallow the repository if needed.
- Existing integration-provided system instructions are preserved and not overwritten.
- Full-clone mode preserves the current behavior.

## Acceptance criteria / test cases

- By default, repository startup uses `git clone --depth 1 ...`.
- When a selected branch is available, repository startup uses a shallow clone of that branch.
- When `git_full_clone` is enabled, repository startup uses the current full-clone behavior.
- Azure DevOps bearer-token clone flow respects the same shallow/full setting.
- The setting appears on the Application settings page with clear user-facing copy.
- The setting is saved, loaded, and reflected correctly in the UI.
- Shallow-clone agent guidance is appended without replacing existing integration-specific system-message suffixes.
- Unit tests cover shallow default, full-clone toggle, selected branch behavior, Azure DevOps clone path, and system-context appending.

title: Add fallback to MAX_CONCURRENT_CONVERSATIONS env var for max_concurrent_sandboxes
body:
## Problem

There is a database-level concurrent sandbox limit per organization that replaced the `MAX_CONCURRENT_CONVERSATIONS` environment variable. Currently, the `get_max_concurrent_sandboxes` methods hardcode a default of 10 when the database column is NULL, instead of falling back to the previously existing environment variable.

This means users who had configured `MAX_CONCURRENT_CONVERSATIONS` need to manually run database queries to restore their intended limits.

## Proposed Solution

1. **Environment variable fallback**: All `get_max_concurrent_sandboxes` methods should fall back to the `MAX_CONCURRENT_CONVERSATIONS` environment variable (rather than hardcoded 10) when the database column is NULL.

2. **Nullable columns with defaults**: A new database migration should be added so that the `max_concurrent_sandboxes` columns are nullable and have a default value of NULL. Existing values should also be set to NULL.

## Motivation

This change will prevent the need for manual database queries when deploying new versions or migrating configurations. Users can rely on environment variables as a fallback, which is more aligned with the previous behavior.

## References

- Related migration: `enterprise/migrations/versions/120_add_max_concurrent_sandboxes.py`

title: [Feature]: Optional reviewer-facing evidence gates for software-agent actions
body:
### Is there an existing feature request for this?

- [x] I have searched existing issues and feature requests, and this is not a duplicate.

### Problem or Use Case

OpenHands-style agents can write code, use command lines, browse, and operate in sandboxed environments. The final diff, terminal result, or browser outcome can be reviewed, but it can still be hard to answer a separate reviewer question:

The agent produced an output — but was it allowed to take that action?

This matters for higher-impact software-agent actions such as shell commands, file modifications, workflow/config changes, browser actions, or tool calls where a reviewer may want to see what evidence was checked before the action happened.

The use case is not to replace sandboxing, evals, or code review. It is to add a lightweight reviewer-facing audit artifact that makes agent action decisions easier to inspect and replay.

### Proposed Solution

Add an optional reviewer-facing evidence-gate artifact around agent actions.

A possible flow:

agent proposes action
→ optional pre-action evidence gate
→ ALLOW / BLOCK / ESCALATE
→ reviewer-facing stop reasons + checked evidence
→ tool call / shell step / browser action / code change

The artifact could include:

action type,

triggering task,

checked evidence or context fields,

decision: ALLOW / BLOCK / ESCALATE,

stop reason if blocked or escalated,

replayable decision record.

This could start as a lightweight trace/log/export artifact rather than a hard runtime enforcement feature. The goal is to help reviewers inspect why an agent action was considered acceptable, risky, or requiring escalation.

### Alternatives Considered

A reviewer can currently inspect the final diff, terminal logs, browser results, or conversation history. Those are useful, but they do not always provide a structured answer to whether the agent had enough evidence or permission to take a specific action.

Other alternatives include custom wrappers, external policy tools, or manual review checklists. The limitation is that they are usually inconsistent, not replayable, and not connected to the actual agent action trace.

Sandboxing, evals, and code review are still important, but they solve a different problem. This proposal is only about an optional reviewer-facing decision artifact around agent actions.

### Priority / Severity

Medium - Would improve experience

### Estimated Scope

Unknown - Not sure about the technical complexity

### Feature Area

Agent / AI behavior

### Technical Implementation Ideas (Optional)

A minimal version could start as an optional structured trace event emitted before selected high-impact actions. It does not need to block execution by default. The event could later be exported in logs or displayed in a reviewer UI.

### Additional Context

Related experimental project: https://github.com/safal207/pythiaLabs

Example snapshot output:
https://github.com/safal207/pythiaLabs/blob/main/docs/examples/agent-action-audit-snapshot-example.md

Workflow intake template:
https://github.com/safal207/pythiaLabs/blob/main/docs/examples/agent-action-workflow-intake-template.md

PythiaLabs explores deterministic evidence gates for high-risk AI-agent actions and replayable reviewer artifacts. This issue is only a question/proposal about whether a similar optional artifact would be useful around OpenHands-style workflows.

title: fix: log level warning → error for HTTP 4xx/5xx responses in automation service event forwarding
body:
## Why

`_send_source_to_automation_service` has three failure paths. PR #14820 raised the log level from `warning` to `error` for transport-level failures (`asyncio.TimeoutError`, `aiohttp.ClientError`), but the HTTP response failure path was left at `warning`:

\`\`\`python
# enterprise/server/services/automation_event_service.py
if resp.status >= 400:
    ...
    logger.warning(   # <-- should be logger.error
        f'[AutomationEventService] Automation service returned '
        f'{resp.status} for {source} org {org_id}: {body}'
    )
\`\`\`

A `>= 400` response (including 408 Request Timeout, 504 Gateway Timeout, 5xx errors) means the event was not delivered — same user impact as a transport failure. Logging it as `warning` is inconsistent with the convention established in #14820:

- `warning` = degraded but recoverable (retrying, falling back)
- `error` = operation failed, user impact, no recovery

## What to change

Change `logger.warning` to `logger.error` at the `resp.status >= 400` branch in `_send_source_to_automation_service`, and add a corresponding test to verify the level.

## Related

Surfaced during review of #14820.

title: Archive runtime workspace files before deleting remote sandboxes
body:
## Goal

Archive workspace files to durable object storage before a remote sandbox's workspace is destroyed, so the agent's work can become eval/dataset material instead of being irrecoverable.

## Update (2026-06-23, approved by Graham): primary trigger moved to runtime-api

Tracing the production lifecycle showed the app-server delete path does **not** run for the dominant case. The ~14-day reap that destroys workspace PVCs is performed by an autonomous runtime-api cleanup CronJob (`cleanup.py:399` `__main__` → `delete_old_runtimes()` → `remove_runtime_in_k8s()`; PVC deleted at `k8s.py:488`), which never calls the app-server. By reap time the pod is already scaled to `replicas: 0` (paused, `k8s.py:554`), so the in-pod agent-server is unreachable.

The primary archive trigger therefore moves to **runtime-api at pause/stop time** — tracked in [PLTF-3112](https://linear.app/all-hands-ai/issue/PLTF-3112/runtime-api-archive-workspace-to-object-storage-at-pausestop-time) (Platform team). This issue is re-scoped to the secondary path below.

## Scope (this issue): explicit-delete-while-running only

`RemoteSandboxService.delete_sandbox()` / `_finalize_sandbox_delete()` fire on explicit user/conversation delete or capacity eviction. When such a delete happens **while the runtime is still live**, archive the workspace via the OpenHands/software-agent-sdk#3779 endpoint before calling runtime-api `/stop`. This captures the user-initiated-delete case; the dominant idle/expiry case is covered by [PLTF-3112](https://linear.app/all-hands-ai/issue/PLTF-3112/runtime-api-archive-workspace-to-object-storage-at-pausestop-time).

Relevant code paths:

* `openhands/app_server/app_conversation/app_conversation_router.py` — `_finalize_sandbox_delete()` decides when the sandbox is no longer referenced by any conversation.
* `openhands/app_server/sandbox/remote_sandbox_service.py` — `RemoteSandboxService.delete_sandbox()` currently deletes the local sandbox record then calls runtime-api `/stop`.
* `openhands/app_server/file_store/google_cloud.py` — existing GCS file-store helper to reuse.

## Proposed implementation

1. Add an archive helper that fetches a workspace archive from the agent-server (OpenHands/software-agent-sdk#3779 endpoint) before sandbox deletion.
2. Upload the archive + a small manifest to configured object storage.
3. Reorder `RemoteSandboxService.delete_sandbox()` so it: resolves the stored sandbox + runtime data → archives workspace files → calls runtime-api `/stop` → deletes the local `StoredRemoteSandbox` row only after the archive + stop path complete acceptably.
4. If archive fails, leave the sandbox record intact and return failure so the delete can be retried (note: failure policy may differ from [PLTF-3112](https://linear.app/all-hands-ai/issue/PLTF-3112/runtime-api-archive-workspace-to-object-storage-at-pausestop-time), which must not strand reaped pods).
5. Reuse the archive enable/bucket/prefix config from [APP-2405](https://linear.app/all-hands-ai/issue/APP-2405/wire-runtime-file-archive-configuration-into-helm-and-replicated).

## Depends on / relates to

* Depends on OpenHands/software-agent-sdk#3779 for the agent-server archive endpoint.
* Depends on [APP-2405](https://linear.app/all-hands-ai/issue/APP-2405/wire-runtime-file-archive-configuration-into-helm-and-replicated) for deployment configuration.
* Complements [PLTF-3112](https://linear.app/all-hands-ai/issue/PLTF-3112/runtime-api-archive-workspace-to-object-storage-at-pausestop-time) (the primary pause-time path in runtime-api).
* Does not replace the repo snapshot/delta path in [ALL-2451](https://linear.app/all-hands-ai/issue/ALL-2451/collect-repo-snapshot-on-a-pr) (initial repo state for PR-linked tasks).

## Acceptance criteria

* An explicit delete of a still-running remote sandbox archives workspace files before runtime-api `/stop` is called.
* Archive failures prevent deletion unless an explicit future force path is introduced.
* The archive path includes enough metadata to identify environment, sandbox id, conversation id where available, and creation time.
* Unit tests cover success, archive failure, runtime `/stop` 404, and HTTP failure cases.
* Logs include sandbox id, archive URI, byte count if available, and elapsed time without exposing secrets.

title: Bug: Images Sent in Chat Are Not Forwarded to AI Agent Context
body:
## Thank you for reporting a bug! 🐛

---

### Is there an existing issue for the same bug?
- [x] I have searched existing issues and this is not a duplicate.

---

### Bug Description

When a user sends an image through the OpenHands chat interface, the image is displayed in the browser UI but **not forwarded to the AI agent's context**. This means:
- Images appear visually in the chat
- The AI agent never receives the image content  
- The AI cannot see or process images for understanding or tasks

### Expected Behavior

When a user sends an image in the chat, the AI should:
1. Receive the image content (as base64 or URL)
2. Be able to analyze and understand the image
3. Respond appropriately based on image content

### Actual Behavior

1. ✅ Image is uploaded and displayed in browser
2. ✅ Image URL is stored and sent to backend
3. ❌ AI agent context does not receive image content
4. ❌ AI cannot see or process the image

---

### Steps to Reproduce

1. Open OpenHands chat interface
2. Upload an image
3. Send a message referencing the image
4. Observe that the AI cannot see/describe the image

---

### OpenHands Version

- openhands-ai: 1.8.0
- openhands-agent-server: 1.28.1
- openhands-sdk: 1.28.1

---

### Technical Evidence

#### 1. Image Storage Exists (Frontend)

**`frontend/src/components/features/chat/uploaded-image.tsx`**
```typescript
export function UploadedImage({ image, onRemove, isLoading = false }: UploadedImageProps) {
  const url = URL.createObjectURL(image);
  setImageUrl(url);
}
```

#### 2. Images Are Sent to Backend

**`frontend/src/hooks/use-send-message.ts`**
```typescript
const content: Array<V1MessageContent> = [
  { type: "text", text: args.content },
];
if (args.image_urls && args.image_urls.length > 0) {
  content.push({
    type: "image",
    image_urls: args.image_urls,
  });
}
```

#### 3. Backend Receives and Stores Messages with Image Content

**`openhands/app_server/app_conversation/live_status_app_conversation_service.py` (lines 1852-1867)**
```python
for msg in pending_messages:
    content_json = [item.model_dump() for item in msg.content]
    response = await self.httpx_client.post(
        f{agent_server_url}/api/conversations/{conversation_id_str}/events,
        json={
            role: msg.role,
            content: content_json,  # ImageContent IS sent here
            run: True,
        },
        ...
    )
```

#### 4. Message Model Supports Images

**`openhands/app_server/app_conversation/app_conversation_models.py` (lines 361-365)**
```python
content: list[TextContent | ImageContent] = Field(
    description=The message content as a list of text and/or image content blocks.,
)
```

#### 5. Agent Server Receives Messages

**`openhands/agent_server/event_router.py` (line 194)**
```python
message = Message(role=request.role, content=request.content)
await event_service.send_message(message, request.run)
```

#### 6. SDK Has Vision Support (For Conversation Agent)

**`openhands/sdk/llm/llm.py` (lines 2013-2016)**
```python
def vision_is_active(self) -> bool:
    return not self.disable_vision and self._supports_vision()
```

**`openhands/sdk/llm/utils/image_inline.py` (lines 143-169)**
```python
def maybe_inline_image_urls(messages, vision_enabled: bool):
    # Converts http(s) URLs to base64 for LLM
```

---

### Root Cause

**The images ARE forwarded to the conversation agent (when vision is enabled), but they are NOT forwarded to the OpenHands AI agent context that processes user requests in this chat interface.**

This is an architectural separation:
1. **Conversation Agent** - Receives images via WebSocket/agent server
2. **OpenHands AI Agent (this interface)** - Does NOT receive image data in its context

---

### Possible Solutions

1. **Forward image data to AI context** - Modify the message handling to include image content in the AI's context
2. **Use vision-capable LLM** - Ensure the AI agent uses a vision-enabled model
3. **Implement multi-modal forwarding** - Add image content to the message context passed to the AI

---

title: Route startup/shutdown and Alembic INFO logs away from error status
body:
## Context

The `OpenHands Integrations Application Failures` monitor recently needed exclusions for startup/shutdown and migration noise that is INFO-level operational output, but is being ingested by Datadog as `status:error`:

- `"Uvicorn running on"`
- `"child process"`
- `"parent process"`
- `"Received SIGTERM"`
- `"alembic.runtime.migration"`

These should remain visible, but should not be classified as application failures.

## Investigation notes

The affected messages are not emitted as application errors:

- Uvicorn emits `"Uvicorn running on ..."`, `"Started parent process"`, `"Stopping parent process"`, `"Terminated child process"`, `"Waiting for child process"`, and `"Received SIGTERM, exiting."` via `logger.info(...)` in Uvicorn.
- The base app container currently starts Uvicorn directly:
  - `containers/app/Dockerfile`: `CMD ["uvicorn", "openhands.server.listen:app", ...]`
- The enterprise image also starts Uvicorn directly:
  - `enterprise/Dockerfile`: `CMD ["uvicorn", "saas_server:app", ...]`
- Direct Uvicorn startup bypasses the existing OpenHands `get_uvicorn_log_config()` path in `openhands/app_server/utils/logger.py`, so Uvicorn's default error logger writes INFO startup/shutdown records to stderr. Container log ingestion commonly maps stderr to `status:error` even when the Python log level is INFO.
- Alembic migration checks are also non-application-failure startup output. Current Alembic configs use stderr handlers and INFO/DEBUG Alembic levels:
  - `enterprise/alembic.ini`: root/alembic at DEBUG with `StreamHandler(sys.stderr)`
  - `openhands/app_server/app_lifespan/alembic.ini`: `logger_alembic` at INFO with `StreamHandler(sys.stderr)`

## Proposed fix

Audit startup logging so INFO records go through structured stdout logging rather than stderr/default Uvicorn formatting:

1. Start the app/enterprise servers through an entrypoint that passes OpenHands' Uvicorn log config, or provide an equivalent `--log-config`/programmatic `uvicorn.run(..., log_config=...)` for production containers.
2. Ensure Uvicorn INFO records are JSON/structured and written to stdout, while real ERROR/CRITICAL records still surface as errors.
3. Route Alembic migration INFO records through the application JSON logger/stdout, or raise `alembic.runtime.migration` to WARNING in production if these startup checks do not need INFO visibility.
4. Add/adjust tests around the production log config so Uvicorn startup/shutdown and Alembic migration records preserve level/status correctly.

## Acceptance criteria

- Uvicorn startup/shutdown lines listed above are ingested as INFO, not Datadog `status:error`.
- Alembic migration startup/check lines are ingested as INFO (or suppressed below monitor scope), not `status:error`.
- Real application errors still emit ERROR/CRITICAL status.

title: Normalize log severity for expected integration webhook skips
body:
## Context

The application-failure monitor previously needed exclusions for integration webhook routing/validation messages:

- `"not claimed and no personal org found"`
- `"No repository owner in github payload"`
- `"[Jira] No workspace name found in webhook payload"`

These are currently logged on normal skip/reject paths and can be confused with application failures by status-based monitors.

## Investigation notes

Current sources in `OpenHands/OpenHands`:

- `enterprise/server/services/automation_event_service.py`
  - `No repository owner in <provider> payload, skipping` is logged with `logger.warning(...)` when the webhook payload cannot be mapped to a repository owner.
  - `<provider> org <org> not claimed and no personal org found, skipping` is logged with `logger.warning(...)` when an otherwise parsed event is intentionally dropped because the repo/org is not claimed and no personal-org fallback exists.
- `enterprise/server/routes/integration/jira.py`
  - `[Jira] No workspace name found in webhook payload` is logged with `logger.warning(...)` before returning HTTP 403.

The `not claimed...skipping` case in particular appears to be an expected routing miss, not an application failure. The missing-owner and missing-Jira-workspace cases may still deserve warning-level visibility, but they should be structured as client/input validation outcomes rather than application errors.

## Proposed fix

Audit these expected integration skip/reject paths and make their severity/status intentional:

1. Downgrade expected skip paths to INFO, especially `not claimed and no personal org found`, where the app is behaving as designed.
2. For malformed/unauthorized payload paths that should remain WARNING, ensure JSON fields make them easy to exclude from app-failure monitors without string matching, e.g. `event_outcome=skipped|rejected`, `error_type=client_payload`, `provider=github|jira`, and `http.status_code=4xx`.
3. Avoid logging full webhook payloads at warning/error severity unless needed and safely redacted.
4. Add tests/assertions for the intended log level on each path.

## Acceptance criteria

- Expected unclaimed-org webhook skips are logged as INFO, not warning/error-status failures.
- Client/input validation rejects are distinguishable from server/application failures via structured fields.
- The monitor no longer needs broad string exclusions for these expected paths.

title: LLM Profile form renders the 'Authentication' (auth_type) field twice (duplicate llm schema sections not filtered by variant)
body:
## Summary

In the LLM Profile settings form (Settings -> LLM -> Add/Edit LLM Profile, **Basic** view), the **"Authentication"** field renders **twice**. Both copies are identical:

- label: **Authentication**
- marked **Optional**
- description: **"Authentication mode for the LLM."**
- the dropdown shows the value **`api_key`** selected (this is the `auth_type` choice value `api_key`, which is what makes the duplicate look like it's named "api_key")

Seen in OHE 1.38.1 (enterprise latest main) bundling agent-sdk 1.29.0.

## Repro

1. Open Settings -> LLM -> **Add LLM Profile** (or edit one), Basic view.
2. Observe two identical **Authentication** dropdowns, each with help text "Authentication mode for the LLM." and value `api_key`.

(There is also a React duplicate-key warning in the console: two sibling `<section>` elements get the same key `agent_settings:llm`.)

## Root cause (frontend double-render of a variant-tagged schema)

This is a **frontend double-render**, not a duplicated field in a single schema source.

The agent-schema endpoint (`GET /api/settings/agent-schema`) is built by `export_agent_settings_schema()` in software-agent-sdk (`openhands-sdk/openhands/sdk/settings/model.py:1924`). Because `AgentSettings` is a discriminated union of `OpenHandsAgentSettings` and `ACPAgentSettings`, and **both** define an `llm: LLM` field tagged with section key `"llm"`, the merged schema deliberately emits **two** sections with `key="llm"`:

- one with `variant="openhands"` (52 fields)
- one with `variant="acp"`       (52 fields, the "LLM (for metrics)" section)

Each contains the full LLM field set, including the `llm.auth_type` field (label "Authentication", desc "Authentication mode for the LLM.", `CRITICAL`) defined at `software-agent-sdk/openhands-sdk/openhands/sdk/llm/llm.py:242`. The SDK docstring for `export_agent_settings_schema` says sections carry a `variant` tag *"so the frontend can filter sections by the page's variant."*

The frontend never does that filtering:

- The LLM Profile form selects `sectionKeys: ["llm"]` — `frontend/src/routes/llm-settings.tsx:782-788`.
- `SdkSectionPage` filters sections **by key only** and keeps *every* section whose key is in `sectionKeys` — `frontend/src/components/features/settings/sdk-settings/sdk-section-page.tsx:273-277`.
- Nothing filters by `variant`; the frontend `SettingsSectionSchema`/`SettingsFieldSchema` types don't even include a `variant` field — `frontend/src/types/settings.ts:80-99`.

So both "llm" sections render, and every non-excluded LLM field renders twice. `llm.model` / `llm.api_key` / `llm.base_url` are hidden because they're in `LLM_EXCLUDED_KEYS` (`llm-settings.tsx:55`, they're rendered by the custom header instead), so those don't visibly double up. `llm.auth_type` is **not** excluded and is `CRITICAL`, so it appears twice in Basic. (`llm.subscription_vendor` is also `CRITICAL` but `depends_on=("auth_type",)`, and the frontend's boolean `depends_on` check hides it, so only `auth_type` shows.)

## Is it a regression?

Yes — visible only in builds bundling agent-sdk >= 1.29.0.

- The two-`llm`-sections schema has existed since SDK #2861 *"feat(sdk): split AgentSettings into LLM/ACP discriminated union"* (commit `9158a1dfa`, 2026-04-17). The frontend has ignored the `variant` tag since then (latent).
- It became **visible** with SDK #3367 *"Add LLM subscription auth endpoints"* (commit `a84f1e7ec`, 2026-06-12), which added the `CRITICAL`, non-excluded `llm.auth_type` field. Before #3367 the only critical LLM fields were model/api_key/base_url, all in `LLM_EXCLUDED_KEYS`, so the duplicate sections rendered nothing in Basic and the bug was invisible.

## Recommended fix (frontend)

Honor the SDK section `variant` tag in the frontend:

1. Add `variant?: string | null` to `SettingsSectionSchema` (and `SettingsFieldSchema`) in `frontend/src/types/settings.ts`.
2. In `SdkSectionPage`'s section filter (`sdk-section-page.tsx:273-277`), keep only sections whose `variant` is `null` (shared) **or** matches the page's active agent variant. The LLM Profile page is the `openhands` variant, so it keeps only the openhands "llm" section and drops the `acp` duplicate. This also removes the React duplicate-key warning.

Minimal alternative: dedupe the filtered sections by `key` in `SdkSectionPage` (keep first). But variant filtering is the intended mechanism and is forward-correct for a future ACP LLM page (which would want the `acp` "LLM (for metrics)" section instead).

No SDK change is required — emitting two variant-scoped "llm" sections is intentional; the frontend just needs to filter by `variant`.

## Evidence

`export_agent_settings_schema()` output (agent-sdk @ v1.28.0+ incl. #3367):

```
sections (key, variant, nfields):
  key='general'      variant=None        nfields=6
  key='llm'          variant='openhands' nfields=52
  key='condenser'    variant='openhands' nfields=8
  key='verification' variant='openhands' nfields=8
  key='acp'          variant='acp'       nfields=7
  key='llm'          variant='acp'       nfields=52   <-- duplicate key='llm'

both 'llm' sections contain:
  'llm.auth_type' label='Authentication' prom=CRITICAL desc='Authentication mode for the LLM.'
```

title: Resolver trigger macro is inferred from WEB_HOST and can't be configured per environment
body:
## Why
The resolver's trigger macro — the mention (`@openhands` vs `@openhands-exp`) and the issue label that fire it — is inferred from `WEB_HOST` by substring matching in `get_oh_labels()` (`enterprise/integrations/utils.py`). Only hosts containing `staging` or `local` get a distinct macro (`openhands-exp` / `@openhands-exp`); every other host falls back to the production `openhands` / `@openhands`.

This blocks running more than one non-production deployment cleanly:

- Any non-prod deployment whose host doesn't contain `staging`/`local` listens for the **same** `@openhands` as production. If it is installed alongside the production app on shared repos, it competes with prod and reacts to real issues/PRs.
- Adding a new environment requires editing `get_oh_labels()` each time, and the logic is fragile — it keys off accidental substrings of hostnames rather than an explicit setting.

Making the macro an explicit per-deployment value is safe: when the override is unset the existing host inference is preserved, so production and current staging/local behavior are unchanged.

## Validation
A fix should let each deployment declare its own macro via an environment variable (e.g. `OH_RESOLVER_LABEL`), falling back to today's `WEB_HOST` inference when the variable is absent. Acceptance:

- Override set (e.g. `OH_RESOLVER_LABEL=openhands-dev`) → `get_oh_labels()` returns `('openhands-dev', '@openhands-dev')`.
- Override unset on a `staging`/`local` host → still `('openhands-exp', '@openhands-exp')`.
- Override unset on any other host → still `('openhands', '@openhands')`.
- Covered by unit tests for `get_oh_labels()` across the three cases above.

title: [Bug]: Privilege Escalation and Host Takeover via Exposed Docker Socket in docker-compose.yml
body:
### Is there an existing issue for the same bug?

- [x] I have searched existing issues and this is not a duplicate.

### Bug Description

In the containers/dev/docker-compose.yml configuration, the host's Docker daemon socket is directly mounted into the openhands container (- /var/run/docker.sock:/var/run/docker.sock).

This violates container isolation principles and creates a severe privilege escalation/sandbox escape vulnerability (Confused Deputy). Because the LLM agent or untrusted code executed by the agent operates within this container, any malicious prompt injection or compromised workspace code can directly interact with the host's Docker daemon. An attacker can exploit this unrestricted socket access to spin up a new container with the --privileged flag and mount the host's root filesystem (/), thereby achieving complete root takeover of the underlying physical host.

### Expected Behavior

The OpenHands application should operate within a strictly isolated sandbox. The container should not have access to the physical host's Docker socket. If containerization features are required within the runtime environment, a secure Docker-in-Docker (DinD) approach or isolated runtime (e.g., Sysbox, gVisor) should be utilized instead of sharing the host's daemon.

### Actual Behavior

The host's /var/run/docker.sock is exposed to the internal container workspace. The internal agent environment implicitly possesses root-equivalent privileges over the physical host machine.

### Steps to Reproduce

1. Install and start OpenHands via the default containers/dev/dev.sh or docker-compose setup.

2. Trick the LLM agent (via prompt injection) or manually execute a script in the agent's workspace to interact with the mounted /var/run/docker.sock.

3. Send a request to the Docker API to create and start a new container using the ubuntu image, adding the --privileged flag and a volume mount -v /:/host_root.

4. Execute commands inside the newly created container to access or modify sensitive files on the host (e.g., /host_root/etc/shadow or /host_root/root/.ssh/authorized_keys), successfully taking over the host.

### OpenHands Installation Method

Other

### If you selected "Other", please specify

Docker Compose via containers/dev/dev.sh

### OpenHands Version

Latest main branch

### Version Confirmation

- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the LATEST version of OpenHands

### Model Name

N/A (This is an architecture/infrastructure vulnerability, independent of the LLM model used).

### Operating System

MacOS

### Browser (if using web UI)

N/A

### Logs and Error Messages

# N/A - This is a security design flaw, not an application crash. No error logs are generated during the exploit.

### Screenshots and Additional Context

This represents a critical security risk for users running OpenHands locally or on shared servers, as it completely negates the security boundaries of the containerized workspace. Refactoring the workspace to use a rootless DinD setup or removing socket bindings is highly recommended.

title: Multiple Command Injection vulnerabilities in openhands
body:
Posting here publicy because no one here seem to care about security.  
Private Security Advisory open for 6-7 months, no answer.

### Summary

Multiple Command Injection vulnerabilities in openhands <0.62.0 allow an attacker to run arbitrary system commands.

### Details

The vulnerability is caused by the usage of `subprocess.run` with shell enabled without any escaping protection (e.g. `shlex`, ref: <https://semgrep.dev/docs/cheat-sheets/python-command-injection>)

The vulnerability is present in the file *openhands/resolver/send_pull_request.py* and specifically in the functions:

- `initialize_repo`: here the payload can be inserted in the input value *base_commit*

```python
def initialize_repo(
    output_dir: str, issue_number: int, issue_type: str, base_commit: str | None = None
) -> str:
    """Initialize the repository.

    Args:
        output_dir: The output directory to write the repository to
        issue_number: The issue number to fix
        issue_type: The type of the issue
        base_commit: The base commit to checkout (if issue_type is pr)
    """
    src_dir = os.path.join(output_dir, 'repo')
    dest_dir = os.path.join(output_dir, 'patches', f'{issue_type}_{issue_number}')

    if not os.path.exists(src_dir):
        raise ValueError(f'Source directory {src_dir} does not exist.')

    if os.path.exists(dest_dir):
        shutil.rmtree(dest_dir)

    shutil.copytree(src_dir, dest_dir)
    logger.info(f'Copied repository to {dest_dir}')

    # Checkout the base commit if provided
    if base_commit:
        result = subprocess.run(
            f'git -C {dest_dir} checkout {base_commit}',
            shell=True,
            capture_output=True,
            text=True,
        )
        if result.returncode != 0:
            logger.info(f'Error checking out commit: {result.stderr}')
            raise RuntimeError('Failed to check out commit')

    return dest_dir
```

- `make_commit`: here the payload can be inserted in the input values *repo_dir*, *issue_type*, *git_user_name*, *git_user_email*

```python
def make_commit(
    repo_dir: str,
    issue: Issue,
    issue_type: str,
    git_user_name: str = 'openhands',
    git_user_email: str = 'openhands@all-hands.dev',
) -> None:
    """Make a commit with the changes to the repository.

    Args:
        repo_dir: The directory containing the repository
        issue: The issue to fix
        issue_type: The type of the issue
        git_user_name: Git username for commits
        git_user_email: Git email for commits
    """
    # Check if git username is set
    result = subprocess.run(
        f'git -C {repo_dir} config user.name',
        shell=True,
        capture_output=True,
        text=True,
    )

    if not result.stdout.strip():
        # If username is not set, configure git with the provided credentials
        subprocess.run(
            f'git -C {repo_dir} config user.name "{git_user_name}" && '
            f'git -C {repo_dir} config user.email "{git_user_email}" && '
            f'git -C {repo_dir} config alias.git "git --no-pager"',
            shell=True,
            check=True,
        )
        logger.info(f'Git user configured as {git_user_name} <{git_user_email}>')

    # Add all changes to the git index
    result = subprocess.run(
        f'git -C {repo_dir} add .', shell=True, capture_output=True, text=True
    )
    if result.returncode != 0:
        logger.error(f'Error adding files: {result.stderr}')
        raise RuntimeError('Failed to add files to git')

    # Check the status of the git index
    status_result = subprocess.run(
        f'git -C {repo_dir} status --porcelain',
        shell=True,
        capture_output=True,
        text=True,
    )

    # If there are no changes, raise an error
    if not status_result.stdout.strip():
        logger.error(
            f'No changes to commit for issue #{issue.number}. Skipping commit.'
        )
        raise RuntimeError('ERROR: Openhands failed to make code changes.')

    # Prepare the commit message
    commit_message = f'Fix {issue_type} #{issue.number}: {issue.title}'

    # Commit the changes
    result = subprocess.run(
        ['git', '-C', repo_dir, 'commit', '-m', commit_message],
        capture_output=True,
        text=True,
    )
    if result.returncode != 0:
        raise RuntimeError(f'Failed to commit changes: {result}')
```

- `update_existing_pull_request`: here the payload can be inserted in the input value *patch_dir*

```python
def update_existing_pull_request(
    issue: Issue,
    token: str,
    username: str | None,
    platform: ProviderType,
    patch_dir: str,
    llm_config: LLMConfig,
    comment_message: str | None = None,
    additional_message: str | None = None,
    base_domain: str | None = None,
) -> str:
    """Update an existing pull request with the new patches.

    Args:
        issue: The issue to update.
        token: The  token to use for authentication.
        username: The username to use for authentication.
        platform: The platform of the repository.
        patch_dir: The directory containing the patches to apply.
        llm_config: The LLM configuration to use for summarizing changes.
        comment_message: The main message to post as a comment on the PR.
        additional_message: The additional messages to post as a comment on the PR in json list format.
        base_domain: The base domain for the git server (defaults to "github.com" for GitHub, "gitlab.com" for GitLab, and "dev.azure.com" for Azure DevOps)
    """
    # Set up headers and base URL for GitHub or GitLab API

    # Determine default base_domain based on platform
    if base_domain is None:
        base_domain = (
            'github.com'
            if platform == ProviderType.GITHUB
            else 'gitlab.com'
            if platform == ProviderType.GITLAB
            else 'dev.azure.com'
        )

    handler = None
    if platform == ProviderType.GITHUB:
        handler = ServiceContextIssue(
            GithubIssueHandler(issue.owner, issue.repo, token, username, base_domain),
            llm_config,
        )
    elif platform == ProviderType.AZURE_DEVOPS:
        # For Azure DevOps, owner is "organization/project"
        organization, project = issue.owner.split('/')
        handler = ServiceContextIssue(
            AzureDevOpsIssueHandler(token, organization, project, issue.repo),
            llm_config,
        )
    else:  # platform == ProviderType.GITLAB
        handler = ServiceContextIssue(
            GitlabIssueHandler(issue.owner, issue.repo, token, username, base_domain),
            llm_config,
        )

    branch_name = issue.head_branch

    # Prepare the push command
    push_command = (
        f'git -C {patch_dir} push '
        f'{handler.get_authorize_url()}'
        f'{issue.owner}/{issue.repo}.git {branch_name}'
    )

    # Push the changes to the existing branch
    result = subprocess.run(push_command, shell=True, capture_output=True, text=True)
    if result.returncode != 0:
        logger.error(f'Error pushing changes: {result.stderr}')
        raise RuntimeError('Failed to push changes to the remote repository')
# ...
```

### PoC

Here I'm providing a simple proof of concept in the cli, however every invocation of the functions mentioned above is vulnerable.

This the payload used for the function *make_commit()*: `\"; id #`.  
As one of many examples, this payload can be set via openhands Local web GUI.

```console
Python 3.13.3 (main, Nov 24 2025, 20:53:35) [GCC 14.2.0] on linux
Type "help", "copyright", "credits" or "license" for more information.
>>> git_user_name = '\"; id #'
>>> import subprocess
>>> subprocess.run(
...             f'git -C fakerepo config user.name "{git_user_name}"',
...             shell=True,
...             check=True,
...         )
fatal: cannot change to 'fakerepo': No such file or directory
uid=1000(edoardottt) gid=1000(edoardottt) groups=1000(edoardottt),4(adm),24(cdrom),27(sudo),30(dip),46(plugdev),100(users),104(kvm),118(lpadmin),129(lxd),131(docker),133(libvirt)
CompletedProcess(args='git -C fakerepo config user.name ""; id #"', returncode=0)
```

### Impact

An attacker can execute arbitrary commands on the server host. All the CIA triad components are impacted.

### Credits

Edoardo Ottavianelli (@edoardottt)

### Expected Behavior

Care about users security

### Actual Behavior

ignore and write vulnerable software

title: [Bug]: V1 Web UI connects to agent-server via dynamic host port behind reverse proxy (Traefik), causing persistent "Network Error" / conversation stuck
body:
### Is there an existing issue for the same bug?

- [x] I have searched existing issues and this is not a duplicate.

### Bug Description

Title: [Bug]: V1 Web UI connects to agent-server via dynamic host port behind reverse proxy (Traefik), causing persistent "Network Error" / conversation stuck


Is there an existing issue for the same bug?


 I have searched the existing issues. Related/possibly duplicate: #12519, #12403, #12229.


Describe the bug

When deploying OpenHands V1 behind a reverse proxy (Traefik, via Dokploy) on a VPS, the application loads correctly, conversations are created, sandboxes spawn successfully, and skills load — but the conversation never becomes usable. The UI shows "Network Error" in the Changes panel and the message input stays "Disconnected" / "Waiting for sandbox".

Backend logs are completely clean (all 200 OK, no errors after the auth fix below).

The root cause is visible in the browser DevTools Network tab: the frontend issues requests directly to the agent-server using a dynamic host port instead of routing them through the reverse-proxied domain. Example failed request URL:

https://openhands.example.com:42031/api/git/changes?path=%2Fworkspace%2Fproject

The port (42031) is the randomly-assigned host port Docker maps to the agent-server container's 8000. This port:


is not in DNS,
is not exposed/routed by Traefik (only 443 → app:3000 is),
changes on every conversation,


so the browser request fails with a CORS preflight failure / connection error → "Network Error".

This matches the architecture limitation already documented in #12403 ("Bridge network uses dynamic host ports, making it incompatible with proxy patterns") and the symptom in #12519 ("Web UI connects to runtime WebSocket via localhost:<random_port> instead of remote host").

Current behavior


App UI loads fine over https://openhands.example.com (Traefik → app container :3000).
A new conversation is created (POST /api/v1/app-conversations → 201).
agent-server container spawns and reports healthy; 50 skills load successfully.
Browser then tries to reach the agent-server directly at https://openhands.example.com:<dynamic_port>/... and fails.
WebSocket connections to the app domain succeed (Finished), but the direct-to-agent-server XHR/preflight requests fail.
Result: "Network Error" + "Disconnected", conversation unusable.


Expected behavior

When OH_WEB_URL / a reverse-proxy deployment is configured, the frontend should route all agent-server traffic through the main app domain (proxied by the app server), never directly to a dynamic host port. A reverse-proxy deployment should not require the browser to reach arbitrary host ports.

How to reproduce


Deploy OpenHands V1 via Docker Compose behind Traefik (Dokploy), exposing only the app on a domain with HTTPS (port 3000 internal).
Configure an LLM (Anthropic Claude) in Settings.
Start a new conversation ("Start from Scratch").
Observe "Network Error" / "Disconnected".
Open DevTools → Network: failed requests target https://<domain>:<dynamic_port>/api/git/changes?....


OpenHands Installation

Docker Compose (self-hosted), behind Traefik reverse proxy managed by Dokploy.

OpenHands Version


App image: docker.openhands.dev/openhands/openhands:latest (SDK v1.27.0)
Agent server image: ghcr.io/openhands/agent-server:1.27.0-python


Operating System

Debian (VPS), Docker / Dokploy stack.

Logs, error messages, screenshots

Browser DevTools (Network tab), failed request General section:

Request URL: https://openhands.example.com:42031/api/git/changes?path=%2Fworkspace%2Fproject
Referrer Policy: strict-origin-when-cross-origin

agent-server container inspect (dynamic port mapping):

"8000/tcp":[{"HostIp":"","HostPort":"33587"}],
"8001/tcp":[{"HostIp":"","HostPort":"57999"}],
"8011/tcp":[{"HostIp":"","HostPort":"44743"}],
"8012/tcp":[{"HostIp":"","HostPort":"43617"}]

Note: the agent-server containers are always created on the default bridge (172.17.0.x), even when the main app is attached to custom Docker networks — consistent with #12229 (the dynamically-created oh-agent-server-* containers don't inherit the app's network / extra_hosts).

Additional context

To get this far, two non-documented fixes were required:


Webhook 401 Unauthorized: The agent-server signs webhook callbacks to the app (http://host.docker.internal:3000/api/v1/webhooks/...) using OH_SESSION_API_KEYS_0, but the app rejected them with 401 because it had no matching secret (no /.openhands/.jwt_secret). Setting a fixed JWT_SECRET env var on the app container resolved the 401s. It would help to document this for reverse-proxy / Compose deployments.
Dynamic-port problem (this issue): even with auth fixed and the conversation/skills working server-side, the browser cannot reach the agent-server because of the dynamic host port. APP_MODE=oss did not change this behavior. network_mode: host is not a viable workaround (breaks health checks per #12229 / #11907).


A reverse-proxy-friendly mode — where the app server proxies all agent-server/sandbox traffic under the main domain (e.g. /<conversation_id>/... paths) instead of the browser connecting to dynamic ports — would make V1 usable behind Traefik/nginx/Caddy, which is the standard self-hosting setup.

body:
### Is there an existing feature request for this?

- [x] I have searched existing issues and feature requests, and this is not a duplicate.

### Problem or Use Case

While studying the OpenHands architecture, I found myself trying to better understand the project's security model and threat assumptions, particularly around the relationship between:

1. The manager/orchestration layer
2. The Docker sandbox layer
3. Host-level process execution used to coordinate containers

At the moment, I may simply be missing the relevant documentation.

### Proposed Solution

A document (or section in the architecture docs) describing:

- The primary security boundary of OpenHands
- Which components are considered trusted
- Which responsibilities are delegated to Docker/container isolation
- Threat assumptions regarding subprocess execution and sandbox management
- Future hardening goals, if any

### Alternatives Considered

Current approaches rely on infrastructure logging, container logs, and custom observability integrations.
While effective, they often make it difficult to reconstruct agent reasoning and execution flow in a consistent way across deployments.

### Priority / Severity

Medium - Would improve experience

### Estimated Scope

Small - UI tweak, config option, or minor change

### Feature Area

Documentation

### Technical Implementation Ideas (Optional)

Introduce optional execution audit hooks within OpenHands that allow:

Tool invocation events to be recorded
Agent decision checkpoints to be emitted
Execution chains to be reconstructed after completion
External audit systems to subscribe to execution events

Possible implementation approaches:

1. Event-based audit interface

- Standardized execution events emitted by the runtime
- Tool started
- Tool completed
- Tool failed
- Agent decision generated

2. Replay metadata export

- Structured execution traces
- Tool inputs/outputs
- Model responses
- State transitions

3. Audit provider abstraction

- Local file backend
- OpenTelemetry integration
- Third-party observability systems

### Additional Context

I'm comparing governance, auditability, and security approaches across several agent frameworks and would love to better understand how the OpenHands team thinks about these architectural boundaries.

As agent frameworks mature and move into production environments, auditability and replayability may become increasingly important for debugging, governance, compliance, and operational trust.
I'm interested in hearing how the OpenHands team currently thinks about these capabilities and whether they align with the long-term roadmap.

title: API keys carry full user privileges — add scoped (reduced-privilege) credentials
body:
# API keys carry full user privileges — add scoped credentials ## Problem **Every API key inherits the complete permission set of the user who created it. There is no mechanism to issue a key with *fewer* rights than its owner.** This makes **all delegation all-or-nothing**: handing an API key to a script, an integration, a CI job, or the automation service hands over the user's *entire* account authority. ### The inverted-least-privilege trap The danger scales with the owner's privilege: > As an **org owner**, when I connect an automation I mint an API key. That key
carries my full org-owner rights, so the automation can do anything I can —
delete other members' automations, read all org data, manage membership —
even if it only needs to write to its own KV namespace. The people most
trusted to set up automations are exactly the ones whose delegated
credentials are most dangerous. A leaked or misbehaving key therefore has a blast radius equal to the *whole user account*, not the task it was issued for. ### Session keys are the same bug, automatically Sandbox **session API keys** are just keys minted on the user's behalf — they inherit full user permissions too (confirmed: validating one via `/api/v1/users/me` returns the owner's complete `permissions` list). Every running agent is, today, an over-privileged bearer of its owner's identity. This is the instance we tripped over, but it is one symptom of the general
problem. ## What's missing `api_keys` has `user_id`, optional `org_id`, and `expires_at` — but **no scope column**. There is nowhere to express "this key may do less than its owner." ## Proposed solution: scoped credentials Allow an API key (and a session key) to carry an explicit, **reduced** set of scopes. An owner can never grant *more* than they have — only *less*. ### Core invariant OpenHands stores scopes as opaque, namespaced strings OpenHands does **not** interpret scope meaning. It stores strings like `automation:kv:read:org`, attaches them at mint time, returns them at validation, and enforces only a *grant-time* gate (can't grant what you lack / what your role rank forbids). All semantic enforcement lives in the system that
owns the namespace. This is the OAuth **authorization-server / resource-server** split: * OpenHands = authorization server (identity, roles, mints keys, consent UI). * Extending systems = resource servers that declare and enforce their scopes. ### Minimal data model ``` api_keys (existing) default scope = "full" (back-compat) api_key_scopes (new) api_key_id ─ scope: text // opaque, namespaced ``` * Existing keys default to `full` → **no behavior change** on rollout. * Validation (`/users/me` or token-introspection) returns the scope list so
resource servers can enforce. ## Benefits ✅ **Least privilege at last** — delegate a capability, not the account
✅ **Smaller blast radius** — a leaked key does only what it was scoped for
✅ **Safe automation/integration delegation**, including for org owners
✅ **Downstream services can distinguish reduced-trust credentials**
✅ **Foundation, not a point fix** — every integration benefits ## First consumers (motivating, not the justification) 1. **Sandbox/automation runtime** — session keys scoped to what the agent
needs (e.g. its own KV namespace), not the owner's whole account. 2. **Automation KV org-debug tokens** (OpenHands/automation#201) — a clean
consumer once scoped keys exist. 3. **CI / integration tokens** — narrow, auditable, revocable. ## Extensibility (how extending systems contribute scopes) * **Stage 0 (foundation):** opaque `api_key_scopes` + return on validation;
resource servers enforce. UI can start API-only / on the resource server. * **Stage 1 (dynamic UI):** extending systems publish a **scope manifest**
(`/.well-known/openhands-scopes`) with scopes, a small set of intent
**presets**, and a `min_role_rank` gate. OpenHands renders consent UI
generically — no per-scope code. * **Stage 2 (optional):** push-based dynamic registration. ## UX guardrail Users pick **intents (presets)**, never raw scope strings; cap the visible
surface at \~3–5 presets. The expressive grammar stays an internal compile
target (avoids the AWS-IAM nightmare). ## Implementation phases 1. `api_key_scopes` + default `full` + return scopes on validation
*(pure foundation; no behavior change)* 2. Mint **session keys** with reduced scopes for sandboxes 3. Scope manifest contract + generic consent UI 4. (optional) dynamic registration ## Related * OpenHands/automation#201 — org-scoped KV tokens (a Phase-1 consumer) * Affects every integration handed an API key today ## Open questions 1. Is `full` (implicit, legacy) an acceptable default scope? 2. Namespacing `":::"` — OK? 3. Grant-time gate via existing ranked `role` (`min_role_rank`)? 4. Token-introspection endpoint vs. extending `/users/me` to carry scopes? --- *Filed by an AI agent (OpenHands) on behalf of the maintainer.*

title: DELETE /api/v1/sandboxes/{id}: path/handler param mismatch makes `sandbox_id` a required query param (and ignores the path)
body:
## Summary

The `DELETE /api/v1/sandboxes/{id}` route's path parameter (`{id}`) does not match its handler's argument name (`sandbox_id`). Since FastAPI binds path parameters by name, `{id}` is never bound and `sandbox_id` is instead treated as a **required query parameter**. As a result:

- `DELETE /api/v1/sandboxes/<id>` → **422 Unprocessable Entity** (`sandbox_id` query field required)
- `DELETE /api/v1/sandboxes/<id>?sandbox_id=<id>` → `200` (the path segment is ignored; only the query value is used)

The sibling routes `POST /{sandbox_id}/pause` and `POST /{sandbox_id}/resume` are correct (their path placeholder matches the handler arg `sandbox_id`), so only `delete_sandbox` is affected.

## Affected code

`openhands/app_server/sandbox/sandbox_router.py` (main @ `7b228db`):
https://github.com/OpenHands/OpenHands/blob/7b228db6ae143598b4caf65c6f7ed759b511f922/openhands/app_server/sandbox/sandbox_router.py#L108-L116

```python
@router.delete('/{id}', responses={404: {'description': 'Item not found'}})
async def delete_sandbox(
    sandbox_id: str,        # <-- arg name does not match the path param '{id}'
    sandbox_service: SandboxService = sandbox_service_dependency,
) -> Success:
    exists = await sandbox_service.delete_sandbox(sandbox_id)
    if not exists:
        raise HTTPException(status.HTTP_404_NOT_FOUND)
    return Success()
```

Compare `pause_sandbox` / `resume_sandbox` immediately above, which use `'/{sandbox_id}/...'` and bind correctly.

## Reproduction

```console
$ curl -i -X DELETE http://localhost:3000/api/v1/sandboxes/oh-agent-server-XXXX
HTTP/1.1 422 Unprocessable Entity
{"detail":[{"type":"missing","loc":["query","sandbox_id"],"msg":"Field required","input":null}]}

$ curl -i -X DELETE "http://localhost:3000/api/v1/sandboxes/oh-agent-server-XXXX?sandbox_id=oh-agent-server-XXXX"
HTTP/1.1 200 OK
{"success":true}
```

## Impact

- A REST client calling the route as documented (id in the path, per the OpenAPI schema and RESTful convention) gets a `422` and cannot delete a sandbox without discovering the undocumented query param.
- The generated OpenAPI schema is misleading: it advertises a `{id}` path param that is ignored, plus a required `sandbox_id` query param.
- Because the path value is unused, `DELETE /sandboxes/A?sandbox_id=B` deletes **B**, not A.

## Suggested fix

Rename the path parameter to match the handler argument (consistent with the `pause`/`resume` routes):

```python
@router.delete('/{sandbox_id}', responses={404: {'description': 'Item not found'}})
async def delete_sandbox(
    sandbox_id: str,
    ...
```

(or, alternatively, rename the handler arg to `id`).

## Environment

- openhands `1.8.0`, self-hosted V1 app-server (`docker.openhands.dev/openhands/openhands:latest`), Docker runtime, observed on `localhost:3000`.

title: [Bug]: Cloud Automation PR reviewer intermittently posts no review — SecretStr webhook serialization error (non-blocking) + 600s run ceiling killing stalled agent loop (blocker)
body:
## Summary

Cloud Automation PR-reviewer runs intermittently fail to post a review: the bot posts a `🔍 Review in progress…` comment but never posts the review (Step 4) and never updates the comment to `✅ Review complete.` (Step 5). The agent conversation stalls and is killed. On the same PR, some reviews succeed and some don't (see e.g. OpenHands/evaluation#588, where 22:08/22:53/23:08 reviews completed but 23:20/23:34 were orphaned at "in progress").

Investigation with Datadog (prod-runtime `runtime-pods` + prod-core `automation` service) points to **two distinct runtime-side bugs**, only one of which actually blocks the review.

## Bug 1 (non-blocking but noisy): `Object of type SecretStr is not JSON serializable` in the conversation event webhook poster

The agent-server posts conversation events to `${OH_WEBHOOKS_0_BASE_URL}/api/v1/webhooks/events/{conversation_id}`. A Pydantic `SecretStr` is leaking into the event payload, and `json.dumps()` cannot serialize it, so **every** event post fails from the first event onward:

```
warn: Webhook post attempt 1 failed: Object of type SecretStr is not JSON serializable
warn: Webhook post attempt 2 failed: Object of type SecretStr is not JSON serializable
warn: Webhook post attempt 3 failed: Object of type SecretStr is not JSON serializable
warn: Webhook post attempt 4 failed: Object of type SecretStr is not JSON serializable
error: Failed to post events to webhook https://app.all-hands.dev/api/v1/webhooks/events/{conversation_id} after 4 attempts
```

This fires on a ~5s loop for the entire lifetime of the conversation. It is systemic: 100+ error lines across 3+ distinct `runtime-*` pods in 6h, and it has been occurring since at least 2026-06-22T02:02:41Z (24h+). Interleaved `401 Unauthorized` responses are also logged against the same `webhooks/events/{conversation_id}` URL.

**Important: this bug is NOT what blocks the review.** I confirmed this by comparing a *completing* conversation (95bfb430, pod `runtime-gvrbjukuamrmrdwj`) with a *stuck* conversation (3b8197b5, pod `runtime-xuheokibrcpgudko`): **both** pods emit the `SecretStr is not JSON serializable` errors, yet the completing conversation still posted its review and reached "✅ Review complete." The agent runs locally in the sandbox and posts the GitHub review via a direct `curl` to api.github.com, which does not depend on the event-streaming webhook. So Bug 1 breaks the UI event stream (and wastes CPU on retries) but does not itself prevent the review.

## Bug 2 (the actual blocker): agent stalls in an empty-LLM-response loop, then the 600s run ceiling kills it before recovery

This is what differs between completing and stuck runs.

**Completing run (95bfb430):** `start_bash_command` at 23:07:58 → conversation created 23:08:15 → review posted ~23:16 (~487s in, under the 600s budget) → SIGTERM at 23:17:07 (normal post-completion sandbox teardown). No `Command timed out`, no empty-response loop.

**Stuck run (3b8197b5):** `start_bash_command` at 23:32:47 → conversation 23:33:04 → at 23:40:16 (430s in) the agent enters an empty-response loop:

```
warn: LLM produced empty response - continuing agent loop
warn: LLM response contained no tool call and no content - sending corrective feedback
```

Then at 23:42:47 — **exactly 600s after `start_bash_command`** — the run's bash command is killed:

```
warn: Command timed out after 600 seconds: mkdir -p /workspace/project && tar xzf /tmp/automation-<run_id>.tar.gz ... && ([ ! -f setup.sh ] || bash setup.sh) && <entrypoint>
```

followed by `Received signal SIGTERM (15), shutting down...`. No `api.github.com` / `/pulls/` / `/reviews` activity was ever logged — the review was never posted.

### Why only sometimes

The review automation's entire execution (tarball extract + `setup.sh` + SDK install + agent review + GitHub POST) is one bash command bounded by `max_run_duration` = **600s** (`OpenHands/automation` → `execution.py::execute_in_context` → `_start_bash(timeout=...)`; `dispatcher.py` → `effective_timeout = min(automation.timeout, max_run_duration)`; `config.py` `max_run_duration: int = 600`, env `AUTOMATION_MAX_RUN_DURATION`). `presets/{prompt,plugin}/setup.sh` reinstalls `openhands-sdk`/`openhands-tools`/`openhands-workspace` from PyPI on every run, consuming a large fixed chunk of that 600s. So the agent has only a few minutes for the actual review. When the LLM starts returning empty responses (intermittent provider behavior), the agent burns the remaining budget in the corrective-feedback loop and the 600s ceiling kills the run before it reaches Step 4/5. When the LLM behaves, the review completes under budget. Hence the intermittent symptom on the same PR.

Datadog shows this is not isolated: 50+ `Run timed out (exit_code=-1)` on the prod-core `automation` service and 24 `Command timed out after 600 seconds` on prod-runtime in 6h, across multiple orgs/users.

## Expected behavior

- **Bug 1:** event payloads posted to `webhooks/events/{conversation_id}` should serialize `SecretStr` (and `set` / other non-JSON-native types) safely — e.g. `model_dump(mode="json")` / `pydantic.TypeAdapter(...).dump_python(..., mode="json")`, or `json.dumps(..., default=str)` as a safety net — so the UI event stream works and the retry storm stops.
- **Bug 2:** either raise the run budget for review-class automations (raise `AUTOMATION_MAX_RUN_DURATION`, or make `max_run_duration` per-automation so heavy reviews can legitimately request more time) and/or stop spending the time budget on per-run SDK install (cache/pre-bake the venv in the runtime image, or run `setup.sh` before the timed entrypoint starts). Additionally, the agent loop should break out of (or bounded-retry) the empty-LLM-response loop instead of looping until the 600s ceiling kills it.
- **Defense in depth:** when a review-trigger run is marked FAILED/timed-out, the watchdog should update the orphaned `🔍 Review in progress…` comment to a `⚠️ Review did not complete` message (with a conversation link), so PRs are never silently stuck.

## Reproduction

1. Trigger a Cloud Automation PR review on a non-trivial PR (label `review-this` / request review from the bot).
2. Tail Datadog: `cluster_name:prod-runtime "SecretStr is not JSON serializable"` (Bug 1, on nearly every run) and `service:automation cluster_name:prod-core "Run timed out"` + `cluster_name:prod-runtime "Command timed out after 600 seconds"` (Bug 2).
3. For a run that gets stuck, confirm on its `runtime-*` pod: `LLM produced empty response` loop → `Command timed out after 600 seconds` → `SIGTERM`, and no `api.github.com` review POST. The PR comment stays at `🔍 Review in progress…`.

## Environment

- OpenHands Cloud, prod-runtime `runtime-pods` + prod-core `automation` service.
- Reviewer = Cloud event-triggered automation (`pull_request.labeled` on `review-this`), prompt preset (`presets/prompt/sdk_main.py` + `setup.sh`).
- Evidence window: 2026-06-22, multiple conversations/pods/orgs.

## Suggested fix order

1. Fix Bug 1 (SecretStr-safe serialization in the event-webhook poster) — eliminates the retry storm and restores the UI event stream. Low risk.
2. Break/bound the empty-LLM-response loop in the agent loop so a flaky LLM response can't consume the entire run budget.
3. Raise/cache the run budget (raise `AUTOMATION_MAX_RUN_DURATION` or make per-automation; pre-bake/cache the SDK venv so `setup.sh` isn't re-installing from PyPI every run).
4. Watchdog-driven orphaned-comment cleanup for FAILED review runs.

---

_Note: This issue was created by an AI agent (OpenHands) on behalf of the user investigating the failing reviewer._

title: Improve MCP setup feedback when a server cannot connect
body:
## Problem

When a user adds an MCP server, the UI does not clearly show whether it connected successfully. If setup fails, the server's tools may simply be missing later, leaving the user unsure what happened or how to fix it.

## Desired experience

- Show a clear success or failure state after adding/editing a server, perhaps with a test connection button.
- Explain failures in plain language, such as connection, timeout, or authentication problems.
- Show server health in the MCP server list.
- Warn in the conversation when a configured server is unavailable.
- Never expose secrets or sensitive configuration details.

## Acceptance criteria

Users can tell whether each MCP server is usable, understand what to do when one fails, and are not left interpreting missing tools as expected behavior.

title: Recommend/document sem as an MCP server for entity-level code intelligence (graph-aware context + impact)
body:
### Is there an existing feature request for this?

- [x] I have searched existing issues and feature requests, and this is not a duplicate.

### Problem or Use Case

OpenHands agents reason about code structure mostly through file reads and grep/search. That misses cross-file callers and can infer relationships that do not exist, so an edit can break callers the agent never saw. Packing context also means pulling whole files, which is token-heavy and low-signal.

### Proposed Solution

Recommend and document [sem](https://github.com/Ataraxy-Labs/sem) as an MCP server for entity-level code intelligence. sem builds a real cross-file call and import graph and exposes `sem_context` (pack a target entity plus its real callers and callees into a token budget), `sem_impact` (deterministic "what breaks if I change this"), and `sem_entities` (intent search / list). It works today through OpenHands' existing `[mcp]` config:

```toml
[mcp]
stdio_servers = [
  {name = "sem", command = "npx", args = ["-y", "@ataraxy-labs/sem", "mcp"]}
]
```

Ask: add sem to a recommended-MCP-servers list and/or a short MCP docs page (there is not one yet). Happy to open the PR.

### Alternatives Considered

Built-in tree-sitter/grep context (current): fast, but no cross-file graph and cannot answer impact deterministically. Per-language LSPs: heavier to wire into an agent loop than one MCP server.

### Priority / Severity

Nice to have

### Estimated Scope

Small (docs plus a recommended-server entry; sem already runs via the existing `[mcp]` config)

### Feature Area

Agent / Integrations

### Technical Implementation Ideas (Optional)

sem is a stdio MCP server, so no core changes are needed. Optional follow-ups: a curated MCP-servers doc page (none exists today) and a recommended-servers entry.

### Additional Context

Repo: https://github.com/Ataraxy-Labs/sem . sem is deterministic and cross-file, so it complements OpenHands' built-in search tools rather than overlapping them.

title: [Bug]: .openhands/setup.sh from repository not working
body:
### Is there an existing issue for the same bug?

- [x] I have searched existing issues and this is not a duplicate.

### Bug Description

When checking out a branch from a repo, the agent should automatically run `.openhands/setup.sh`, but this is currently broken.

### Expected Behavior

`.openhands/setup.sh` should run as documented here: https://docs.openhands.dev/openhands/usage/customization/repository#setup-script
For the example below, a file called `somefile.txt` should be created.

### Actual Behavior

The script is not executed. The script under "steps to reproduce" does not create a file `somefile.txt`.

### Steps to Reproduce

Make a repo with an `.openhands/setup.sh`, e.g. with the content:
```
#!/bin/bash
touch somefile.txt
```

### OpenHands Installation Method

Local GUI (Docker web interface)

### If you selected "Other", please specify

_No response_

### OpenHands Version

1.8.0

### Version Confirmation

- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the LATEST version of OpenHands

### Model Name

_No response_

### Operating System

_No response_

### Browser (if using web UI)

_No response_

### Logs and Error Messages

_No response_

### Screenshots and Additional Context

Look at this code in `openhands/app_server/app_conversation/app_conversation_service_base.py` from `maybe_run_setup_script`:
```python
        await workspace.execute_command(
            f'chmod +x {setup_script} && source {setup_script}',
            cwd=project_dir,
            timeout=600,
        )
```
`source` is a command that only exists in `bash`, but this command is probably executed in `sh`.
Not sure if there is any way to let the setup script export environment variables which would also be available for the agent. Would certainly be nice.
The docs (https://docs.openhands.dev/openhands/usage/customization/repository#setup-script) suggest that you can change the current directory in the script, which would have an effect for the agent. That's very similar to sharing environment variables, since both depend on the shell interpreter.

I tested a partial fix by changing:
`f'chmod +x {setup_script} && source {setup_script}',` to `f'chmod +x {setup_script} && . {setup_script}',`. That works, but current dir and environment variables wouldn't be shared. Still, better than before.
