title: Add managed LiteLLM key refresh and startup self-healing
body:
## Problem

Some OpenHands Cloud automations can fail before producing useful events when the managed LiteLLM key stored for the automation-running org member no longer exists in LiteLLM. In the observed failure, conversation startup/title generation failed with `token_not_found_in_db` for a managed key (`sk-...JUrQ`), causing automation runs to fail before profile-rotation logic could recover.

The current UI/API has a BYOR key refresh endpoint, but there does not appear to be a dedicated endpoint to refresh the managed conversation key (`org_member.llm_api_key`) used by normal SaaS conversation startup.

## Proposed stacked work

1. Add a managed LiteLLM key refresh endpoint for the authenticated user/effective org. It should only operate on managed keys and must not overwrite BYOK/BYOR keys.
2. Add startup self-healing that minimally verifies managed keys before conversation startup and invokes the managed refresh logic when the key is missing from LiteLLM.

## Requirements

- Only refresh keys for managed LiteLLM/OpenHands-provider configurations.
- Never validate or replace user-provided BYOK provider keys against LiteLLM.
- Avoid deleting the old key before the replacement has been generated and persisted where possible.
- Add tests for both explicit refresh and startup self-healing.

title: [AgentProfile][cloud] Implement Agent Profiles on the OpenHands cloud/SaaS surface
body:
**Epic:** OpenHands/software-agent-sdk#3713 · **Umbrella:** OpenHands/software-agent-sdk#3730 · **Thin-boundary contract:** https://github.com/OpenHands/software-agent-sdk/issues/3730#issuecomment-4841528619

This is the concrete OpenHands-side implementation issue for **Agent Profiles on the cloud / SaaS surface** (the umbrella's Phase 5). It consolidates the three SDK tracking sub-issues (software-agent-sdk#3832 / #3833 / #3834) into one buildable plan, adds the prerequisite SDK refactors, covers the migration + **retirement of the active-LLM-profile pointer** (§8; epic #3713 Phase 6), and lists the coordinated agent-canvas un-gating.

Agent Profiles already work **locally** end-to-end (SDK substrate `openhands.sdk.profiles` shipped in **v1.29.0**, agent-server router, agent-canvas UI in PR OpenHands/agent-canvas#1440/#1446). **Cloud is unbuilt** — `git grep agent_profile` on OpenHands `main` (`0571ff530`) returns **0 hits**.

The single most important directive: **cloud already implements LLM Profiles, and an Agent Profile is the same kind of resource one level up (it *references* an LLM profile). Mirror the LLM-profile cloud pattern in every way that applies; deviate only with a stated reason.** Every decision below cites the LLM-profile precedent it mirrors.

---

## Design summary (resolved decisions)

### 1. Storage shape → dedicated `org.agent_profiles` `EncryptedJSON` column (NOT embedded in `agent_settings`)

**Mirror `org.llm_profiles` exactly.** LLM profiles are a named-collection-with-active-pointer stored in their own encrypted column, not inside `agent_settings`:

- `enterprise/storage/org.py:72-74` — `llm_profiles: Mapped[dict[str, Any] | None] = mapped_column(EncryptedJSON, nullable=True)`.
- Migration `enterprise/migrations/versions/116_add_llm_profiles_to_org.py` — `op.add_column('org', sa.Column('llm_profiles', sa.String(), nullable=True))` (EncryptedJSON serializes to String at rest), no backfill, NULL → empty collection lazily.

Add a parallel **`org.agent_profiles: Mapped[dict | None]` `EncryptedJSON` column** + an alembic migration mirroring `116` (next head is `127` → new revision `128`, `down_revision='127'`). JSON envelope `{profiles: {<id>: AgentProfile}, active: <id> | null}`, **id-keyed** (the SDK keys the active pointer on `id`, and `LaunchedAgentProfile.agent_profile_id` is a UUID — see §5).

**Why `EncryptedJSON` even though `AgentProfile` is secret-free:** parity with `llm_profiles` keeps the at-rest story uniform, and `OpenHandsAgentProfile.skills[].mcp_tools` carries cipher-encrypted env/headers (`AgentProfileStore.save` redacts-or-encrypts these, software-agent-sdk `agent_profile_store.py:121-170`).

**Why NOT embed in `org.agent_settings`:** `agent_settings` is the **resolved** blob that `create_agent` consumes; Agent Profiles are **creation-time templates that resolve *into* that blob** via `resolve_agent_profile`. Embedding templates in the resolved blob conflates the two and breaks the SDK's clean `profile → AgentSettingsConfig → create_agent` pipeline. The FK lifecycle (delete-409 / cascade-rename, §4) also needs profiles as first-class addressable rows.

### 2. Active pointer → per-member `active_agent_profile_id`; **NEW field, do not overload `llm_profiles.active`**

The SDK separates these (`active_agent_profile_id` is a distinct field on `PersistedSettings`, software-agent-sdk `persistence/models.py:145-152`, separate from the LLM `active_profile`). The org envelope's `active` is the **org default**; the **effective active is per-member** (each member picks their own).

**Recommended: a dedicated `OrgMember.active_agent_profile_id: Mapped[str | None]` column.** Precedent: per-member profile state already lives as dedicated `OrgMember` columns (`enterprise/storage/org_member.py:28-30` — `_llm_api_key`, `has_custom_llm_api_key`). Written at `/activate`, read in `SaasSettingsStore.load` and at conversation-start. *(Alternative considered: a reserved key inside `OrgMember.agent_settings_diff` to avoid a second migration — rejected because `agent_settings_diff` is specifically the `agent_settings` overlay and `active_agent_profile_id` is a settings-level sibling; mixing it in risks colliding with the `deep_merge`.)*

The `GET /api/agent-profiles` list response returns the **effective** active id (member pointer, falling back to org `active`), exactly as `org_profiles.py:181` returns `active_profile=profiles.active`. (Router path settled in the task breakdown below.)

**`active_agent_profile_id` is the *sole* launch authority — the active *LLM* profile is deprecated, not a peer.** Once a member has an active Agent Profile, its `llm_profile_ref` (OpenHands) / `acp_model` (ACP) pins the model; the standalone active-LLM-profile pointer (`org.llm_profiles.active` / the per-member materialized `agent_settings_diff['llm']` / `ProfileListResponse.active_profile`) is **not** consulted at launch and is being retired (see §8 and epic #3713 Phase 6). For ACP-kind active profiles there is no LLM profile at all, which makes the point sharp. The earlier framing of "the org `active` LLM as a coexisting default" is wrong — there is one active pointer, and it is the Agent Profile.

### 3. Where resolution runs → **resolve at conversation-start (and in `load()` for the default), not eager-materialize at activate**

**This is the one deliberate divergence from the LLM-profile precedent — stated explicitly.**

LLM-profile `activate` **eagerly materializes**: it writes the resolved `llm` into the calling member's `agent_settings_diff['llm']` and lifts the key into `OrgMember._llm_api_key` (`enterprise/server/routes/org_profiles.py:296,321-346`), so conversation-start just reads `agent_settings.llm` (`live_status_app_conversation_service.py:1214-1249` `_configure_llm`).

Agent Profiles instead **store only the `active_agent_profile_id` pointer and resolve lazily**, because:
1. **Per-member MCP filtering.** `resolve_agent_profile` filters the user's `mcp_config` by `mcp_server_refs`; `mcp_config` is member-private and mutated over time (`MEMBER_PRIVATE_AGENT_KEYS`, `saas_settings_store.py:43`). Freezing the filtered set at activate-time would go stale. The *same* org-owned profile must re-filter against each member's *current* `mcp_config` at launch.
2. **Revision provenance.** Fresh resolution keeps `LaunchedAgentProfile.revision` (§5) accurate and lets profile edits propagate without re-activation.
3. **Parity with the local contract canvas already speaks.** The local agent-server `activate` is **pointer-only** (returns `agent_settings_applied=False`, software-agent-sdk `agent_profiles_router.py:512-560`); conversation-start does the resolve. Cloud must match so OpenHands/agent-canvas#1440's `agent_profile_id`-at-start wiring works unchanged.

**Two integration seams (mirror how the active LLM is both baked-at-activate AND read-at-start):**
- **`SaasSettingsStore.load()`** — after the org⊕member compose (`saas_settings_store.py:189-192` `deep_merge`) and before `Settings(**kwargs)` (`:265`): if the member has `active_agent_profile_id`, resolve it and use the resulting `AgentSettingsConfig` as the effective `agent_settings`, **replacing** the composed blob (so the active profile is authoritative and the LLM-profile-materialized `agent_settings.llm` is intentionally superseded). This gives the Settings page / switch-tools the resolved default. (This is the seam software-agent-sdk#3833 specifies.) The legacy active-LLM materialization survives **only** as the pre-migration fallback for rows that don't yet have an `active_agent_profile_id` (see §8).
- **Conversation-start** — honor an explicit per-request `agent_profile_id` (canvas sends it, XOR `agent_settings`) that launches **that one conversation** from the chosen profile **without mutating the member's active pointer** (a one-off override; the saved default is untouched), and **stamp `LaunchedAgentProfile`** (§5). This is what enables "launch a new conversation from a non-active profile" (OpenHands/agent-canvas#1446).

**The resolver is already store-injectable — call it, do not re-derive it** (`resolve_agent_profile(profile, *, llm_store, mcp_config, cipher) -> AgentSettingsConfig`, software-agent-sdk `profiles/resolver.py:266-272`):
- `llm_store`: a thin adapter exposing `.load(name, *, cipher) -> LLM` over `org.llm_profiles` (the resolver only calls `llm_store.load`, `resolver.py:290`). Org-owned LLM profiles ↔ org-owned agent profiles (§4).
- `mcp_config`: the member-effective (org⊕member) **decrypted** `MCPConfig`.
- `cipher`: the SaaS `EncryptedJSON` cipher (decrypts the LLM profile + `skills[].mcp_tools`).
- Dangling `llm_profile_ref` → SDK `ProfileNotFound` → surface as 4xx; dangling `mcp_server_refs` → SDK `DanglingMcpServerRef` → 4xx. **Never silently fall back to defaults.**

**Control-plane resolves; the per-sandbox runtime needs NO profile store.** The resolved `AgentSettingsConfig` feeds the **unchanged** `create_agent`, exactly as today's resolved `agent_settings` does. Do **not** mount `agent-profiles_router` in the sandbox agent-server. (Confirmed against how the active LLM is resolved control-plane-side and only *mirrored* into the sandbox for the `switch_llm` tool via `_seed_sandbox_profiles`, `live_status_app_conversation_service.py:957`.)

### 4. Org⊕member resolution rule

- **Profile definitions are org-owned** (`org.agent_profiles`), mirroring org-owned `org.llm_profiles`. CRUD requires `EDIT_ORG_SETTINGS`; read requires `VIEW_ORG_SETTINGS` (`org_profiles.py` permission model).
- **`llm_profile_ref` resolves against the org's LLM profiles** (`org.llm_profiles`) — both collections org-owned. **FK guard at the router, reusing the SDK helpers** (`find_referrers` / `ProfileReferenced` / `cascade_rename`, software-agent-sdk `profiles/profile_refs.py`): deleting an `org.llm_profiles` entry referenced by any `org.agent_profiles` → **409** naming referrers; rename → cascade under the org row lock (`_org_profiles_transaction`'s `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE`, `org_profiles.py:147-149`). `mcp_server_refs` are **not** FK-constrained at save — checked at resolve-time only.
- **`mcp_server_refs` resolve per-member.** Because `mcp_config` is member-private, the same org profile referencing server `"X"` binds to *each member's own* `"X"`. This asymmetry (org-shared profile, member-private MCP binding) is intentional — document it in the editor.
- **Reuse the org/member agent-kind overlay learnings (OpenHands#14678 / PR #14680).** A resolved Agent Profile produces a full `AgentSettingsConfig` of one `agent_kind`; it must replace `agent_settings` wholesale, not deep-merge a member ACP profile onto an org OpenHands base (the cross-variant `agent_kind` mongrel #14678 fixed). When an active profile resolves, it **replaces** the composed `agent_settings`, sidestepping the overlay-merge entirely.

### 5. Provenance → stamp `LaunchedAgentProfile {agent_profile_id, revision}` on `AppConversationInfo`

`LaunchedAgentProfile` (software-agent-sdk `profiles/agent_profile.py:212-226`): `agent_profile_id: UUID`, `revision: int`.

**Ride the `tags` dict with a typed `@computed_field` — the exact `acp_server` precedent:**
- `openhands/app_server/app_conversation/app_conversation_models.py:34` — `ACP_SERVER_TAG_KEY = 'acpserver'`.
- `:143` — `tags: dict[str, str]`; `:148-162` — `@computed_field def acp_server(self) -> str | None: return self.tags.get(ACP_SERVER_TAG_KEY)`.

Set `tags['agent_profile_id']` + `tags['agent_profile_revision']` at start (alongside the existing `acpserver` tag in `live_status_app_conversation_service.py`) and expose a `launched_agent_profile` computed field projecting them. **Gotcha:** `_to_info` rebuilds only declared columns, so a stored field without a column round-trips to `None` on the list endpoint — `tags` already round-trips, so this is **zero-migration**. (Switch to a declared column only if conversations must be *queried/filtered* by profile.) Canvas reads exactly `launched_agent_profile { agent_profile_id, revision }` (OpenHands/agent-canvas#1440).

### 6. Secrets

- **AgentProfiles store no creds.** ACP provider creds ride the **per-user Secrets panel** (`custom_secrets` → `request.secrets` → `state.secret_registry`), which `update_all_members_settings_async` never broadcasts. Verification is **secret-free** (no `critic_api_key`; reuses the profile's LLM key — software-agent-sdk `agent_profile.py:42-44`).
- The member-private ACP-creds pre-req from the umbrella is **already closed**: `acp_env` was removed entirely in SDK 1.29.0; ACP creds are ordinary global secrets (residual comment/test cleanup tracked in OpenHands#14921). No keyset change needed here.

### 7. ACP on cloud

- **Fix the `_merge_custom_mcp_config` ACP early-return** (software-agent-sdk#3705 remainder, still deferred on `main`): `live_status_app_conversation_service.py:1288-1289` returns immediately for `ACPAgentSettings`, dropping the user's/profile's MCP. A resolved ACP profile's ref-filtered `mcp_config` must reach `create_agent` — carry it on the `ACPAgentSettings` itself (it survives the early-return) and/or remove the ACP-only drop.
- **Out of scope:** machine-bound Gemini *personal* auth (encrypted to the host machine; impossible to inject in cloud/Docker). Codex (`auth.json`) and Claude (env token) cred injection are in scope via the secret channel.

### 8. Migration + deprecation of the active-LLM-profile pointer

Agent Profiles make the active **Agent** Profile the sole launch authority, so the standalone active **LLM** profile pointer is **deprecated** — the marker, not the profiles. LLM profiles stay as building blocks (referenced by `llm_profile_ref`, used by the per-conversation model picker / `switch_llm`); "current model" becomes per-conversation state. Cross-repo deprecation is tracked in **epic #3713 Phase 6**; this issue owns the cloud half.

**Migration (one-shot backfill + lazy on access), behavior-preserving:**
- Ensure a Default **LLM** profile exists — cloud already seeds one from the legacy `llm` (`saas_settings_store.py:252-259`).
- Seed exactly **one** Default **Agent** profile per org, **derived from the org's current `agent_settings`** — branch on `agent_kind` (an ACP org gets an ACP-kind default, **not** a wrong OpenHands one) and **do not** reset condenser/verification/suffix to fixed defaults — with `llm_profile_ref` = the org's active LLM profile. Reuse the hoisted `_build_seed_profile`; **do not** write a bespoke transform. (Deriving from current settings is strictly safer than fixed defaults: for an un-customized org it *is* the defaults, and it avoids silently demoting ACP users / wiping customizations.)
- Set each member's `active_agent_profile_id` to it. Per-member divergence (a member whose materialized `llm` differs from the org default) lives cleanly in the per-member pointer — a cleanup of today's org-marker-vs-member-materialization mismatch (`org_profiles.py:296` org-wide `active` + `:344-346` per-member materialize).

**Staged retirement** (physical removal gated on the backfill covering every row):
1. Stop honoring `org.llm_profiles.active` as launch authority (active Agent Profile wins; the legacy active-LLM materialization is the fallback **only** for rows without `active_agent_profile_id`).
2. Backfill the default Agent profiles.
3. Repoint the cloud model picker / `/switch_profile` to per-conversation; `/profiles/{name}/activate` collapses to no-op / building-block default.
4. Drop `ProfileListResponse.active_profile` + the materialize-on-`/activate`.

---

## Prerequisite SDK work (land in software-agent-sdk FIRST)

These keep the cloud router a thin store+auth+wiring shim. They are **stubs/refactors to propose in the SDK**, not cloud code. Per the thin-boundary contract, today some lifecycle logic lives **only** in the local agent-server router — extract it so both routers stay thin.

- [ ] **Extract an `AgentProfileStore` Protocol/ABC.** It's a concrete file-backed class today (`agent_profile_store.py:46`), with no interface — and `profile_refs._scan_referrers` / `_rewrite_refs` reach into file internals (`store.base_dir.glob("*.json")`, `store._atomic_write`, `profile_refs.py:63-111`). Define a Protocol (`list`, `save`, `load`, `delete`, `rename`, `list_summaries`, `name_for_id`) so the file store and a cloud DB store are interchangeable, and re-express the `profile_refs` FK scans over `list_summaries()` (interface-level) rather than file globs.
- [ ] **Hoist router-only lifecycle helpers into the SDK (store-agnostic):**
  - `_build_seed_profile` — the `AgentSettingsConfig → AgentProfile` seed transform (`agent_profiles_router.py:199-240`); pure, no I/O; belongs beside the resolver.
  - The **mint-id / keep-id-on-overwrite / bump-revision** policy (`agent_profiles_router.py:418-427` + `_existing_identity:287-307`) → an SDK helper like `save_profile_preserving_identity(store, profile, *, max_profiles)` over the Protocol.
  - `_profile_verification` — `VerificationSettings → ProfileVerificationSettings` projection (`:182-196`).
  - The **422 secret-safe error-shaping** (`:388-405`, strips `msg`, keeps `loc`/`type`) → a small reusable helper.
  - Unify `_decrypt_mcp_tools` / `_decrypt_profile_mcp_tools` (`:134-179`) with the resolver's `_decrypt_skill_mcp_tools` (they duplicate it).
- [ ] Track these under epic #3713; the cloud tasks below depend on them landing + a patch release.

---

## OpenHands task breakdown (ordered, checkboxed)

Each task names the **parallel LLM-profile file** as the template.

- [ ] **DB model + migration.** Add `org.agent_profiles` `EncryptedJSON` column → template `enterprise/storage/org.py:72-74`. Add `OrgMember.active_agent_profile_id` column → template `enterprise/storage/org_member.py:28-30`. Alembic migration (revision `128`, revises `127`) → template `enterprise/migrations/versions/116_add_llm_profiles_to_org.py`.
- [ ] **Store / service.** DB-backed `AgentProfileStore` conforming to the extracted SDK Protocol, over the `org.agent_profiles` envelope; `_load_agent_profiles(org)` + an `_org_agent_profiles_transaction` doing `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE` on the org row → template `enterprise/server/routes/org_profiles.py:107-162`.
- [ ] **`/api/agent-profiles` router.** CRUD + `/{id}/activate` + `/{name}/materialize`, mounted in `enterprise/saas_server.py` → template `saas_server.py:163-164`. `VIEW/EDIT_ORG_SETTINGS` perms + the locked org-row transaction → template `org_profiles.py`. **Each endpoint delegates** validation to `validate_agent_profile`, resolution to `resolve_agent_profile` / `resolve_agent_profile_dry_run`, FK to `find_referrers`/`cascade_rename`, identity-stamping to the hoisted helper. Secret-free profiles → no api-key masking needed (unlike `org_profiles.py:321-346`).
  - **URL-shape decision (stated deviation from `org_profiles.py`):** canvas's `AgentProfilesClient` (ts-client 1.26.0) calls a **flat** `GET/POST/DELETE /api/agent-profiles[/{name}]`, `POST /{name}/rename`, `POST /{id}/activate` (by UUID), `POST /{name}/materialize` — **no `org_id` in the path** (`agent-profiles-service.api.ts:37-86`). Serve the router at the **flat member-facing path, deriving the org from the authenticated session**, so canvas works unchanged. This deviates from `org_profiles.py`'s `org_id`-in-path on one axis only (URL shape), justified because the surface is **member-facing** (each member activates their own profile, §2), not org-admin management. Mirror everything else about `org_profiles.py` (column, store, transaction, perms, FK). *(Alternative: org-scoped `/api/organizations/{org_id}/agent-profiles` exactly mirroring `org_profiles.py` — then canvas needs a cloud-routing branch in `AgentProfilesService`. Not recommended.)*
- [ ] **`active_agent_profile_id` pointer.** `/activate` writes the per-member `OrgMember.active_agent_profile_id` (and may set the org-default `agent_profiles.active`); **pointer-only, no materialization** (§3) → contrast template `org_profiles.py:268-352` (which materializes). List endpoint returns the effective active id.
- [ ] **FK lifecycle.** Wire `org.llm_profiles` delete/rename (`org_profiles.py:244-262` / `:355-378`) to the SDK FK guard: delete referenced → 409 (`ProfileReferenced`), rename → `cascade_rename` under the org lock. `mcp_server_refs` checked at resolve-time only.
- [ ] **Org/member scoping.** Org-owned definitions; member-private active pointer + member-private MCP binding; replace (not merge) `agent_settings` when a profile resolves → reuse OpenHands#14678 / PR #14680 learnings.
- [ ] **Conversation-start resolve + provenance.** (a) Wire `resolve_agent_profile` into `SaasSettingsStore.load` between `:192` and `:265`, with the `llm_store` adapter over `org.llm_profiles` + member-effective decrypted `mcp_config` + cipher → seam template `saas_settings_store.py:234-244` (where `llm_profiles` is surfaced). (b) Accept an explicit `agent_profile_id` at conversation-start (XOR `agent_settings`) — a **one-off override that does not mutate** the member's active pointer — and stamp `LaunchedAgentProfile` from it → integration point `live_status_app_conversation_service.py` (where `acpserver`/`llm_model` are set, `:505-516`).
- [ ] **ACP-on-cloud.** Fix the `_merge_custom_mcp_config` ACP early-return (`live_status_app_conversation_service.py:1288-1289`) so a resolved ACP profile's MCP reaches `create_agent`; route ACP creds via the secret channel. Out of scope: Gemini personal auth.
- [ ] **Migration + active-LLM-profile deprecation (cloud) — see §8.** Backfill one Default Agent profile per org, derived from current `agent_settings` (kind-aware) + `llm_profile_ref` = active LLM profile, and set each member's `active_agent_profile_id`. Then stage the retirement of `org.llm_profiles.active` as launch authority → repoint the model picker / `/switch_profile` per-conversation → drop `ProfileListResponse.active_profile` + the materialize-on-`/activate`. Coordinated with the SDK/canvas deprecation in **epic #3713 Phase 6**.
- [ ] **agent-canvas un-gating (coordinated follow-up — OpenHands/agent-canvas, on top of #1440).** The Agent Profiles UI is **already cloud-ready by construction** — `AgentProfilesService` news up `AgentProfilesClient` against the active backend host with **no `backend.kind` gate** (`agent-profiles-service.api.ts:37-86`), the route `/settings/agents` (`routes.ts:26`), the nav item (`constants/settings-nav.tsx:22-27`), and `useAgentProfiles` (`enabled: true`, `use-agent-profiles.ts:25`) all render/fire on cloud today; they only fail because cloud doesn't serve the endpoints. So once cloud serves the wire contract above, the canvas coordination is small:
  - Flip the one explicit cloud exclusion: `use-create-conversation.ts:57` `enabled: backend.kind !== "cloud"` (so cloud fetches profiles + defaults new conversations to `active_agent_profile_id`, `:78`).
  - Thread `agent_profile_id` through the **cloud** start path so the pre-start profile picker launches a one-off conversation from a chosen profile **without** activating it globally: the cloud branch `agent-server-conversation-service.api.ts:379` builds `AppConversationStartRequest` **without** the id and calls `createCloudAppConversation` (`src/api/cloud/conversation-service.api.ts`, `POST /api/v1/app-conversations`). Extend both to carry `agent_profile_id` (the local branch already does, via `buildStartConversationRequest`, `agent-server-adapter.ts:926-931`). → **Cloud's `POST /api/v1/app-conversations` start request must accept `agent_profile_id`** (XOR `agent_settings`).
  - Cloud conversation list/get responses must emit `launched_agent_profile { agent_profile_id, revision }` — canvas normalizes it server-authoritatively at `agent-server-conversation-service.api.ts:185-194` (read `:252`).
  - Page-retirement OpenHands/agent-canvas#1452 (retire the now-dead global `/settings/agent` · `/condenser` · `/verification` pages + migrate the `mock-llm-acp-agent` e2e) is **hard-gated on this issue** — do it once cloud has the library.

---

## Do NOT re-implement — review gate (restating the thin-boundary contract)

The cloud diff should be **DB store + auth + wiring only**. A reviewer should be able to `git grep` the PR clean of re-implemented domain logic.

**✅ MUST import from `openhands.sdk.profiles` (shipped v1.29.0):** `AgentProfile` union + `validate_agent_profile`; `resolve_agent_profile` / `resolve_agent_profile_dry_run` + `AgentProfileDiagnostics` (already store-injectable — takes `llm_store`/`mcp_config`/`cipher`); `find_referrers` / `cascade_rename` / `ProfileReferenced`; `LaunchedAgentProfile`; `PROFILE_NAME_PATTERN`, `ProfileLimitExceeded`, `ProfileNotFound`, `DanglingMcpServerRef`, the schema-version constants; plus the SDK-hoisted seed / identity-stamp / 422-shaping helpers.

**❌ MUST NOT (auto-reject):** re-deriving the `llm_profile_ref` + `mcp_server_refs` → `AgentSettingsConfig` join · re-implementing delete-409 / cascade-rename · hand-building `AgentSettingsConfig` from a profile · a divergent provenance shape (anything other than `launched_agent_profile { agent_profile_id, revision }`) · forking `PROFILE_NAME_PATTERN` / the limit / the seed · mounting a profile store in the sandbox runtime.

**🟦 Cloud MAY implement (the irreducible shim):** the DB-backed `AgentProfileStore` (CRUD / `list_summaries` / rename / delete + the `active_agent_profile_id` pointer), org/member-scoped; the HTTP layer (auth, org scoping, RBAC) delegating to the imports; the conversation-start wiring (accept the one-off `agent_profile_id` override, call the resolver, stamp + emit provenance); the org⊕member resolution policy.

---

## Links

- Epic: OpenHands/software-agent-sdk#3713 (incl. **Phase 6 — retire the active-LLM-profile pointer**, the cross-repo deprecation this issue's §8 implements cloud-side)
- Umbrella: OpenHands/software-agent-sdk#3730 · design note (storage/resolution settled) https://github.com/OpenHands/software-agent-sdk/issues/3730#issuecomment-4762519733 · **thin-boundary contract** https://github.com/OpenHands/software-agent-sdk/issues/3730#issuecomment-4841528619
- SDK tracking sub-issues this consolidates: OpenHands/software-agent-sdk#3832 (container+column+migration+router+FK), #3833 (resolve wiring), #3834 (provenance)
- SDK substrate v1.29.0; DI seam OpenHands/software-agent-sdk#3816; ACP-merge remainder OpenHands/software-agent-sdk#3705
- Canvas consumers: OpenHands/agent-canvas#1440, OpenHands/agent-canvas#1446; page-retirement follow-up OpenHands/agent-canvas#1452
- Org/member overlay learnings: OpenHands#14678 (PR #14680); member-private ACP creds OpenHands#14921

---
*Verified against OpenHands `main` `0571ff530` and the pinned `openhands-sdk==1.29.0`. Every architectural claim is grounded in a file:line read during the design pass.*

title: OHE - Organization shared secrets and MCP servers
body:
# PRD: Org-Shared Secrets & MCP Servers ## Goal Allow Admins/Owners of an OHE Org to define a secret or MCP server as org-shared, so the resource can be used by all members of the org without exposing its value. ## Problem Today, secrets and MCP servers are private to the user who created them. Teams that rely on shared credentials (e.g., a shared API key, a company MCP endpoint) must ask every member to re-enter the same values individually — creating duplication, drift, and unnecessary exposure of raw credentials across multiple people. ## Scenario **Organization's Code Review Bot**
You create an Automation that performs a code review. Instead of inheriting an individual human user's GitHub identity, you configure a GitHub App credential as an Org-wide secret. The automation then uses that secret to perform the code review on behalf of the GitHub App -- not the user's identity. When that credential expires or needs to be rotated, OHE Org Admins/Owners only need to update the secret in one place since it's configured as an Org-wide Secret. This helps avoid scenarios like  a human user leaving the organization, and thus causing the Code Review Automation failing to access GitHub. **Configure a Shared Service as MCP configuration**
If I wanted to configure a shared service (need example) then a Shared MCP configuration could enable it. I may want users to operate on behalf of a different identity. ## I Can * When adding a secret or MCP server, choose **Personal** (default) or **Shared with org.** * *(Admin / Owner only)* Only Admins and Owners can create Org secrets and MCPs. * Use any org-shared secret or MCP server in my conversations and automations, regardless of who created it * See the names of org-shared secrets and MCP servers. It's clear which of these are Org-scoped vs. Personal-scoped. * Edit/replace the a secret value (but never see or view the actual value associated with that secret) * *(Admin / Owner only)* Delete an org-shared secret or MCP server **Important: Nobody** — including admins and owners — can view the value or configuration of a secret or MCP server once it has been saved. ## Questions to Validate * Is org-shared secrets and MCP servers actually desirable, or do teams prefer each member to hold their own copy? * Yes, confirmed with at least two customers * Should any org member (including Members) be able to create org-shared secrets and MCP servers, or should this be restricted to Admins and Owners? * For now, Admins/Owners can create and scope Org-level secrets. We will eventually need to create fine-grained permissions so a Member user could create Org-level secrets, but not inherit Admin permissions like Creating Users. * Do automations need to access org-shared secrets and MCP servers, and if so, how should authorization work (e.g., does the automation run as the creating user, the org, or a service identity)? * Automations should be able to access Org-shared secrets and MCP servers * What would be required to make this feature acceptable to internal security teams? (e.g., SSO-gated access, encryption at rest guarantees, approval workflows before a secret goes org-wide) * What type of auditing is required? (e.g., who created a shared secret/MCP, when it was last used, who used it, when it was deleted and by whom) * We should log when secrets are used too (and convo ID) ## Why It Matters * **Reduces credential sprawl** — one canonical shared secret instead of N copies across N users, lowering the blast radius if a credential is compromised * **Faster onboarding** — new org members immediately inherit shared MCP servers and secrets without a manual setup step * **Enables org-level automation** — automations that act on behalf of the org (e.g., CI bots, scheduled agents) can use shared credentials without tying them to a specific user's account * **Preserves zero-knowledge privacy** — the "write-once, never read" model keeps raw values out of admin hands while still enabling controlled access

title: Make repository selection optional for Jira and Jira DC resolvers
body:
## Summary

Both the **Jira** and **Jira DC** resolvers currently refuse to start a conversation unless they can infer and verify **exactly one repository** from the triggering issue/comment. This is stricter than necessary and blocks legitimate use cases:

- Repo-less tasks (e.g., "translate this comment to German and post it back")
- Multi-repo workflows (e.g., "compare the implementations in frontend-app and backend-api")
- Ambiguous mentions that the agent could clarify at runtime using skills

The resolvers should instead allow **zero, one, or multiple repos**, and defer resolution to the agent when unclear — mirroring how the GitHub resolver already works (repo is provided by the webhook context) and how Slack allows a "No Repository" option.

## Current Behavior

### Jira (Cloud)
- `JiraFactory._select_single_repo()` (`enterprise/integrations/jira/jira_view.py:402-427`) raises `RepositoryNotFoundError` if `len(verified_repos) != 1`.
- Zero repos → "Could not determine which repository to use."
- Multiple repos → "Multiple repositories found: …. Please specify exactly one."
- The agent/conversation is never started.

### Jira DC (Data Center)
- `JiraDcManager.is_job_requested()` (`enterprise/integrations/jira_dc/jira_dc_manager.py:487-524`) returns `False` unless `len(verified_repos) == 1`.
- Zero repos → posts "Could not access any of the mentioned repositories" (or "Could not determine which repository to use") and stops.
- Multiple repos → posts "Multiple repositories found…" and stops.
- `JiraDcNewConversationView.create_or_update_conversation()` (line 86) has a second guard that raises `StartingConvoException('No repository selected…')`.

Both use `infer_repo_from_message()` (`enterprise/integrations/utils.py:173`) to extract candidate repos from free text.

## Why This Is Too Restrictive

1. **Repo-less tasks are blocked.** Example from a real C24 support bundle: user wants to "translate this comment" — no repo needed. Today: refused.

2. **The agent could resolve ambiguity at runtime.** If two repos are mentioned, the agent could read the issue, ask a clarifying question in a Jira comment, or infer from context (linked PRs, previous comments). Today: hard refusal upfront.

3. **Contrast with other integrations:**
   - **GitHub/Bitbucket DC:** repo comes from the webhook payload (inherently unambiguous).
   - **Slack:** offers an explicit "No Repository" button and starts the conversation in an empty workspace; the agent can clone repos later via skills.
   - **Jira should be at least as flexible as Slack.**

4. **The agent has the tools to handle this.** Once started with credentials, the agent can:
   - Use the git-provider skill to search/verify/clone repos.
   - Post a Jira comment asking the user for clarification.
   - Proceed without a repo if the task doesn't require one.

   Refusing before the agent even runs discards these capabilities.

## Related Issues

- **Linear APP-1068**: "Jira missing repo information should be optional" — already identified for the regular Jira integration.
- **Trailing punctuation regex bug** (not yet filed): `infer_repo_from_message` fails to match repos followed by `?`/`!`/`;` due to a too-narrow right-boundary in `direct_pattern` (line 215). Example: `"in repo BANKAPP/bank-android?"` extracts nothing. This is a separate one-line fix but contributes to the perception that repo inference is fragile.

## Proposed Solution

### High-Level Behavior
- **≥1 repo confidently inferred** → clone it (or them, if multi-repo is supported) and start.
- **0 repos** → start the conversation in an empty workspace (or with an initialized git repo, mirroring Slack's "No Repository" path). Let the agent decide: read the issue, use skills to clone, or ask the user.
- **Ambiguous/multiple** → start anyway; optionally post a clarifying comment, but don't block.

### Code Changes Required

#### Both Integrations
1. **`enterprise/integrations/utils.py`** — fix the trailing-punctuation regex bug:
   ```python
   # Line 215: broaden right boundary to allow ?!; as delimiters
   r'(?=\s|$|}}|[\]\)\'",.:;!?`])'  # right boundary
   ```
   Strip any trailing `.` from the captured repo name (mirror the existing `.git` cleanup).

#### Jira (Cloud)
2. **`enterprise/integrations/jira/jira_view.py`**:
   - `_select_single_repo()` (line 402): instead of raising on zero or multiple, log and return `None` (or the first verified repo, or all of them). Caller must handle `None`.
   - `_infer_repository()` (line 431): catch `RepositoryNotFoundError` and return `None` instead of propagating.
   - `create_view()` (line 464): allow `view.selected_repo = None`.
   - `JiraNewConversationView.create_or_update_conversation()` (line ~184): drop the `if not self.selected_repo: raise StartingConvoException(…)` guard.
   - `_create_v1_conversation()`: pass `selected_repository=None` when appropriate; ensure credentials are still injected even without a repo (this path already exists for Slack "No Repository").

#### Jira DC
3. **`enterprise/integrations/jira_dc/jira_dc_manager.py`**:
   - `is_job_requested()` (line 487): change the zero/multiple logic from `return False` to `return True` (with optional clarifying comment for the user). Set `jira_dc_view.selected_repo = None` or `verified_repos[0]` as appropriate.
   - **OR** keep the current short-circuit but add a fallback: if zero verified, still return `True` and proceed with no repo.
4. **`enterprise/integrations/jira_dc/jira_dc_view.py`**:
   - `JiraDcNewConversationView.create_or_update_conversation()` (line 86): drop the `if not self.selected_repo: raise StartingConvoException('No repository selected…')` guard.
   - `_create_v1_conversation()`: handle `selected_repository=None` gracefully.

### Multi-Repo Support (Optional, Larger Lift)
- `AppConversationStartRequest` currently takes a single `selected_repository`. True multi-repo cloning (passing a list, auto-cloning all) is a broader runtime change.
- **Pragmatic first step:** auto-clone at most one unambiguous repo; let the agent clone additional repos via skills.

## Benefits

1. **Unblocks legitimate use cases** (repo-less tasks, multi-repo, agent-driven clarification).
2. **Parity with Slack's flexibility** (no hard refusal for missing/ambiguous repo).
3. **Leverages the agent's capabilities** (skills, clarifying questions, context inference) instead of discarding them.
4. **Simpler failure mode:** if the agent truly needs a repo and none is available, it can post a Jira comment asking — a better UX than a pre-flight refusal.

## Testing Strategy

1. **Repo-less task:** Jira issue with `"@openhands translate this comment to German"` (no repo mention). Verify: conversation starts, agent responds (even if it says "I need more context").
2. **Trailing punctuation:** `"@openhands clone BANKAPP/bank-android?"` (with `?`). Verify: repo is extracted and cloned (once regex is fixed).
3. **Multiple repos:** Issue mentions two repos. Verify: conversation starts (agent may ask which one, or clone both if multi-repo is supported).
4. **Zero matches, git provider connected:** Verify: conversation starts in empty workspace; agent can use skills to search/clone.

## Open Questions

1. **Multi-repo cloning:** Do we want to support auto-cloning multiple inferred repos in the initial request, or defer that to agent-driven skill usage?
2. **UI/messaging:** When starting with zero/multiple repos, should we always post an initial Jira comment to set expectations (e.g., "Starting without a pre-selected repo; I'll infer from context"), or only when truly ambiguous?
3. **Backward compat:** Are there workflows that rely on the hard refusal as a safety check (e.g., "don't start unless a repo is explicit")? If so, could we make it a workspace/org setting?

---

**Related Linear Issue:** [APP-1068](https://linear.app/all-hands-ai/issue/APP-1068/jira-missing-repo-information-should-be-optional)  
**Affected Files:**
- `enterprise/integrations/utils.py:173,215` (regex bug + shared inference)
- `enterprise/integrations/jira/jira_view.py:402,431,464,184` (regular Jira guards)
- `enterprise/integrations/jira_dc/jira_dc_manager.py:487` (Jira DC gate)
- `enterprise/integrations/jira_dc/jira_dc_view.py:86` (Jira DC guard)

title: Jira/Jira DC: repo extraction fails with trailing punctuation (?!;)
body:
## Summary

The `infer_repo_from_message()` function fails to extract repository names when they are immediately followed by common punctuation marks (`?`, `!`, `;`). This affects both Jira and Jira DC integrations when users mention repos in natural language.

## Root Cause

The `direct_pattern` regex in `enterprise/integrations/utils.py` (line 215) has a right boundary that only allows a limited set of delimiters:

```python
r'(?=\s|$|}}|[\]\)\'",.:` ])'  # right boundary
```

This set **excludes** `?`, `!`, and `;` — so a repo mention like `owner/repo?` fails to match entirely.

## Evidence (Synthetic Example)

### Test Case 1: Question Mark
**Input:** `"Can you work on ACME-PROJECT/mobile-app?"`

**Expected:** `['ACME-PROJECT/mobile-app']`

**Actual:** `[]` (no match)

### Test Case 2: Exclamation Point
**Input:** `"Please fix ACME-PROJECT/backend-api!"`

**Expected:** `['ACME-PROJECT/backend-api']`

**Actual:** `[]` (no match)

### Test Case 3: Semicolon
**Input:** `"Check these repos: ACME-PROJECT/frontend; ACME-PROJECT/docs"`

**Expected:** `['ACME-PROJECT/frontend', 'ACME-PROJECT/docs']`

**Actual:** `[]` (no matches)

### Test Case 4: Period (Additional Bug)
**Input:** `"See ACME-PROJECT/docs."`

**Expected:** `['ACME-PROJECT/docs']`

**Actual:** `['ACME-PROJECT/docs.']` (trailing `.` incorrectly included in repo name)

## Impact

When a Jira or Jira DC user mentions a repository followed by these punctuation marks, the integration:

1. Fails to extract the repo name
2. Either refuses to start (current behavior for both integrations — see issue #15050)
3. Or extracts noise patterns (e.g., other `word/word` tokens in the issue description like `feature/branch`, `bug/fix`, `old/new`) as false-positive repo candidates
4. Produces confusing error messages like "Could not access any of the mentioned repositories: feature/branch, bug/fix, old/new" (listing the noise, but not the real repo)

## Reproducible Test

```python
import re

direct_pattern = (
    r'(?:^|\s|{{|[\[\(\'":`])'  # left boundary
    r'([a-zA-Z0-9_.-]+)/([a-zA-Z0-9_.-]+)'
    r'(?=\s|$|}}|[\]\)\'",.:`])'  # right boundary (current, buggy)
)

tests = [
    ('in repo ACME-PROJECT/mobile-app?', [('ACME-PROJECT', 'mobile-app')]),
    ('in repo ACME-PROJECT/mobile-app', [('ACME-PROJECT', 'mobile-app')]),
    ('in repo ACME-PROJECT/mobile-app!', [('ACME-PROJECT', 'mobile-app')]),
    ('in repo ACME-PROJECT/mobile-app;', [('ACME-PROJECT', 'mobile-app')]),
]

for text, expected in tests:
    matches = re.findall(direct_pattern, text)
    status = "✓" if matches == expected else "✗"
    print(f"{status} {repr(text)}")
    print(f"  Expected: {expected}")
    print(f"  Got:      {matches}\n")
```

**Output:**
```
✗ 'in repo ACME-PROJECT/mobile-app?'
  Expected: [('ACME-PROJECT', 'mobile-app')]
  Got:      []

✓ 'in repo ACME-PROJECT/mobile-app'
  Expected: [('ACME-PROJECT', 'mobile-app')]
  Got:      [('ACME-PROJECT', 'mobile-app')]

✗ 'in repo ACME-PROJECT/mobile-app!'
  Expected: [('ACME-PROJECT', 'mobile-app')]
  Got:      []

✗ 'in repo ACME-PROJECT/mobile-app;'
  Expected: [('ACME-PROJECT', 'mobile-app')]
  Got:      []
```

## Proposed Fix (Regex Only)

Change line 215 in `enterprise/integrations/utils.py`:

```python
# Before (current)
r'(?=\s|$|}}|[\]\)\'",.:` ])'  # right boundary

# After (fixed)
r'(?=\s|$|}}|[\]\)\'",.:;!?`])'  # right boundary — added ;!?
```

Additionally, strip any trailing `.` from captured repo names (mirror the existing `.git` cleanup around line 233):

```python
for owner, repo in re.findall(direct_pattern, normalized_msg):
    repo = re.sub(r'\.git$', '', repo)
    repo = re.sub(r'\.$', '', repo)  # NEW: strip trailing period
    full_match = f'{owner}/{repo}'
    # ... rest of logic
```

## **Recommendation: Don't Fix This in Isolation**

This one-line regex fix would unblock the specific punctuation failure, but it's **symptomatic of a broader design issue**: both Jira integrations currently **refuse to start** unless they can infer and verify exactly one repository from free text. This means:

- Repo-less tasks are impossible (e.g., "translate this comment to Spanish")
- Ambiguous cases are rejected upfront instead of letting the agent clarify at runtime
- Small extraction bugs like this one cause hard failures

**Instead of patching the regex, we should fix the root problem: make repository selection optional** (tracked in #15050). Once repos are optional:

- The regex bug becomes a performance optimization (nicer auto-clone UX) rather than a failure mode
- Users can still proceed when extraction fails
- The agent can use skills to search/verify/clone repos at runtime

If we fix the regex first, we still leave users blocked on repo-less tasks and ambiguous mentions — solving 10% of the problem while leaving 90% unfixed.

## Affected Code

- **File:** `enterprise/integrations/utils.py`
- **Function:** `infer_repo_from_message()` (line 173)
- **Specific line:** 215 (right boundary of `direct_pattern`)

## Related Issues

- **#15050** — Make repository selection optional for Jira and Jira DC resolvers (broader fix, recommended)
- **Linear APP-1068** — Jira missing repo information should be optional

## Testing Strategy (If We Fix the Regex)

Add unit test in `enterprise/tests/unit/integrations/test_utils.py`:

```python
def test_infer_repo_with_trailing_punctuation():
    """Repo mentions followed by ?!; should be extracted correctly."""
    assert infer_repo_from_message("work on owner/repo?") == ["owner/repo"]
    assert infer_repo_from_message("work on owner/repo!") == ["owner/repo"]
    assert infer_repo_from_message("repos: owner/repo; other/repo") == ["owner/repo", "other/repo"]
    assert infer_repo_from_message("See owner/repo.") == ["owner/repo"]  # trailing . stripped
```

title: perf: cache small auth lookup tables instead of querying on every auth check (replaces #14633)
body:
## Why

Follow-up to #14633, re-scoped per the analysis in that thread: adding indexes will **not** reduce load on `user_authorizations` and `blocked_email_domains`.

Both tables hold only ~31 rows (a single ~8 KB page). For a table that small the Postgres planner will keep choosing a sequential scan over any index — a 1-page seq scan (≈ `seq_page_cost` + 31·`cpu_tuple_cost`) is cheaper than index + heap access, so a new index would simply go unused and the `seq_scan` counts wouldn't move. The evidence confirms this: `seq_tup_read / seq_scan` ≈ 31 for both tables (each scan reads all 31 rows in ~1 page).

The cost driver is **query volume**, not per-scan cost. These tables are read on every authentication/authorization path via `UserAuthorizationStore.get_authorization_type` — millions of calls — and an index can't reduce the number of calls. The effective fix is to stop hitting the DB on the hot path: cache these small, rarely-changing tables in memory with a short TTL (and/or invalidate on write).

## Validation

Hot path to change:
- `UserAuthorizationStore.get_matching_authorizations` / `get_authorization_type` — `enterprise/storage/user_authorization_store.py:52`
- Callers: `enterprise/server/auth/saas_user_auth.py:740`, `enterprise/server/auth/user/default_user_authorizer.py:64`

Proposed approach:
- Load the full `user_authorizations` rule set (and the blocked-domain list) into process memory behind a short TTL cache (e.g. `cachetools.TTLCache` or an `@lru_cache` wrapped with a TTL) and evaluate the email/provider match in Python instead of issuing a query per request. Invalidate on the create/delete paths in the same store.
- TTL keeps a single replica's staleness window small (seconds–minutes); writes are rare so a short TTL is acceptable.

How to verify the fix:
- `seq_scan` / `calls` for both tables in `pg_stat_user_tables` drop to roughly `(replicas × table_count) / TTL` instead of tracking auth request volume.
- Existing auth tests still pass: `enterprise/tests/unit/test_saas_user_auth.py`, `enterprise/tests/unit/storage/test_user_authorization_store.py`.
- Add a test asserting a second lookup within the TTL window issues no DB query (mock the session/store) and that a create/delete invalidates the cache.

Related: #14633 (closed in favor of this).

title: Architecture: extract conversation WebSocket event interpreter
body:
## Summary
Extract conversation WebSocket event interpretation out of `frontend/src/contexts/conversation-websocket-context.tsx` into a pure, framework-free interpreter plus thin provider adapters. The public context API is already narrow; the architectural problem is that a ~1000-line React provider owns transport, event classification, cache invalidation, store mutations, planning file handling, terminal/browser side effects, optimistic cleanup, direct services, and error banners.

## Current problem
- `conversation-websocket-context.tsx` is a fat component that imports services directly and reaches into many stores: `useEventStore`, `useModelStore`, `useErrorMessageStore`, `useOptimisticUserMessageStore`, `useV1ConversationStateStore`, `useCommandStore`, `useBrowserStore`, `useConversationStore`, and `useMetricsStore`.
- Event semantics are only practically exercised through coarse provider/MSW tests such as `frontend/__tests__/conversation-websocket-handler.test.tsx`, so small behavior changes require mounting the whole provider stack.
- The most concrete duplication is the pair of near-identical message handlers, `handleMainMessage` and `handlePlanningMessage`, each doing JSON parse -> type guards -> side effects. Shared cases such as `ExecuteBashObservation` terminal output are duplicated.

## In scope
- `frontend/src/contexts/conversation-websocket-context.tsx`
- A new conversation event interpreter module and effect types
- Focused interpreter tests built from recorded event sequences
- Thin adapter code that applies interpreter effects to existing stores, QueryClient, `EventService`, and `PendingMessageService` as needed

## Out of scope / touched only as needed
- Broad refactors of the conversation, terminal, browser, metrics, or optimistic-message stores
- `frontend/src/hooks/mutation/conversation-mutation-utils.ts` beyond its existing cache-helper call sites

## Proposed direction
1. Extract a pure interpreter with a shape like `(event, context) => Effect[]`. Effects should describe intended mutations such as append-terminal-output, set-plan-content, invalidate-cache, push-error-banner, clear-optimistic-message, update-browser-observation, and related outcomes.
2. Make the provider parse WebSocket frames and call the interpreter, then apply effects through injected adapters wired to the existing stores/cache/services.
3. Parameterize the interpreter by connection role so main and planning WebSocket messages share the same logic.
4. Shrink provider/MSW tests to transport/connection smoke coverage and move event semantics into cheap interpreter unit tests.

## Expected wins
- Deletes one duplicated handler path by construction.
- Creates a fast test surface for observations and side effects without mounting the full provider.
- Keeps the public context API tiny while making the implementation behind it easier to reason about.
- Reduces blast radius for future event types and planning-agent behavior.

## Recommendation strength
Strong

title: Architecture: extract StartConversationRequestBuilder
body:
## Summary
Extract conversation startup request construction from `LiveStatusAppConversationService` into a focused `StartConversationRequestBuilder` collaborator. The builder should unify the SDK and ACP start-request paths behind one interface, while sandbox, secrets, persistence, and agent-server access remain explicit edge adapters.

## Primary file
- `openhands/app_server/app_conversation/live_status_app_conversation_service.py`

## Problem
Conversation startup is not a single undifferentiated block: it already has many well-named private helpers. The problem is that the helpers still live on a very large service that also owns conversation CRUD, export, title updates, persistence coordination, processors, and transport concerns. That keeps startup policy coupled to service state and makes request-shape behavior hard to test in isolation.

Startup also has two near-parallel request builders:
- `_build_start_conversation_request_for_user` for the SDK path
- `_build_acp_start_conversation_request` for the ACP path

Those paths solve similar problems but diverge inside the god-service, so future SDK/ACP differences are likely to spread through orchestration code.

## Proposed direction
Extract a `StartConversationRequestBuilder` module with SDK and ACP variants behind a shared interface. Feed it a small input value object containing resolved startup facts such as user identity, parent conversation configuration, sandbox info, assembled secrets, LLM configuration, tools, plugin messages, skills/hooks, and pending-message context.

Keep side-effecting dependencies at the edge behind adapters:
- sandbox lookup/readiness/version/profile seeding
- secret lookup and git-provider secret assembly
- persistence and conversation metadata reads/writes
- agent-server transport and request dispatch

Leave `LiveStatusAppConversationService` responsible for orchestration: gather facts, call the builder, dispatch the request, then coordinate persistence/processors/pending messages.

## Testing focus
Make the builder transport-free enough that unit tests can assert the produced SDK/ACP request shapes without a live sandbox or agent-server. Cover parent inheritance, sandbox selection facts, secret inclusion, LLM/tool selection, plugin message construction, skills/hooks options, and pending-message behavior through pure inputs.

## Expected wins
- Better locality for startup rules while preserving the existing helper decomposition
- Concrete unit-test leverage around SDK and ACP request shape
- Clearer boundaries between startup policy and transport/side effects
- Cheaper future changes for SDK and ACP differences because the variant logic is centralized

## Recommendation strength
Strong

title: Architecture: complete conversation mutation cache centralization
body:
## Summary
Complete the existing conversation mutation cache centralization rather than creating a new cache module. Route legacy pause/resume hooks through shared cache helpers and add a query-key factory so lifecycle hooks describe intent instead of cache mechanics.

## Files
- `frontend/src/hooks/mutation/conversation-mutation-utils.ts`
- `frontend/src/hooks/mutation/use-v1-resume-conversation.ts`
- `frontend/src/hooks/mutation/use-v1-pause-conversation.ts`
- `frontend/src/hooks/mutation/use-unified-start-conversation.ts` (exports the **resume** hook `useUnifiedResumeConversationSandbox`)
- `frontend/src/hooks/mutation/use-unified-stop-conversation.ts` (exports the **pause** hook `useUnifiedPauseConversationSandbox`)
- `frontend/src/hooks/mutation/use-update-conversation.ts`

## Problem
The helper module requested by the original framing already partially exists: `conversation-mutation-utils.ts` exports `invalidateConversationQueries()`, `updateConversationSandboxStatusInCache()`, and `updateConversationLlmModelInCache()`. The unified resume hook already delegates to that helper, but the older V1 pause/resume hooks still duplicate cache behavior inline.

The concrete duplication is snapshot/rollback boilerplate plus query-key and invalidation knowledge. `use-v1-resume-conversation.ts` duplicates the same invalidation set as `invalidateConversationQueries()`. `use-v1-pause-conversation.ts` duplicates only part of that set and omits the `sandboxes` and `unified/vscode_url` invalidations, with no documented reason.

The pause path is inconsistent in two places, not one. Beyond the V1 pause hook invalidating only a subset, the **unified** pause hook (`useUnifiedPauseConversationSandbox` in `use-unified-stop-conversation.ts`) has no `onSettled` and performs no invalidation at all — it neither routes through `invalidateConversationQueries()` nor invalidates any keys on its own. So the "unified hooks already delegate" framing holds for resume but not for pause. The invalidation decision below must cover both pause hooks: V1 pause (invalidates 3 of the 5 keys) and unified pause (invalidates none).

The optimistic-update framing should be precise: only some hooks perform real optimistic `setQueryData` updates. Pause/resume mostly snapshot for rollback, so the refactor should target shared snapshot/rollback behavior and centralized invalidation/query keys, not a generic optimistic-update abstraction.

## Proposed direction
Finish centralizing mutation cache behavior around the existing utility module:
- route `use-v1-resume-conversation.ts`, `use-v1-pause-conversation.ts`, and the unified pause hook (`use-unified-stop-conversation.ts`) through shared invalidation helpers
- explicitly decide whether pause should invalidate `sandboxes` and `unified/vscode_url`; apply that decision to **both** pause hooks (V1 and unified) and document it in code
- add a shared `onMutate`/`onError` snapshot-rollback helper for hooks that only need rollback state
- add a query-key factory so keys like `["user", "conversations"]`, `["user", "conversation", id]`, `["sandboxes"]`, and `["unified", "vscode_url"]` stop being repeated string literals

## Testing focus
Add focused tests around lifecycle transitions that assert the query keys invalidated and rollback behavior for start, stop, pause, resume, and update. Cover both pause hooks (V1 and unified) so the pause invalidation decision is enforced and future changes do not silently drop related cache refreshes.

## Expected wins
- Lower duplication across mutation hooks
- Fewer missed or inconsistent invalidations
- Better leverage from small tests over lifecycle transitions
- A contained, low-risk cleanup before larger conversation UI work

## Recommendation strength
Recommended

title: Architecture: extract settings access policy
body:
## Summary
Extract settings route access and redirect decisions into a pure policy module. The route loader should gather route/config/cache facts at the edge, pass plain data into the policy, and receive a render-or-redirect decision.

## Files
- `frontend/src/routes/settings.tsx`
- `frontend/src/utils/settings-utils.ts`
- `frontend/src/hooks/use-settings-nav-items.ts`
- `frontend/src/utils/org/permission-checks.ts`
- `frontend/src/utils/org/billing-visibility.ts`

## Problem
The settings `clientLoader` owns path classification, SaaS-only path guards, feature-flag hide redirects, ACP gating, selected-organization lookup, billing visibility, admin permission checks, and redirect selection.

Some of the decisions are already factored into helpers such as `getFirstAvailablePath`, `isBillingHidden`, `rolePermissions`, and `getActiveOrganizationUser`. The remaining problem is that orchestration and redirect selection are still procedural in the loader, and the loader directly reads query-cache data such as organizations and personal settings. That coupling makes the redirect matrix awkward to unit-test and keeps low-level organization/config imports in the route.

## Proposed direction
Introduce a pure policy function, for example:

```ts
decideSettingsAccess(facts): { kind: "render" } | { kind: "redirect"; to: string }
```

Keep `queryClient.getQueryData(...)`, selected-organization store reads, route params, and config lookup in a thin fact-gathering step at the route edge. The policy should receive plain facts such as `config`, feature flags, `pathname`, selected organization, current user, organization membership/permissions, and personal settings.

The policy should own the SaaS path guard, feature flag hide rules, ACP gating, organization permission decisions, billing visibility behavior, and fallback navigation target selection.

## Testing focus
Add unit tests for `decideSettingsAccess(...)` that cover the redirect matrix without React Router loaders, TanStack Query, or store setup. Include cases for SaaS-only paths, hidden settings sections, ACP redirects, missing/changed selected organizations, billing visibility, and admin-only pages.

## Expected wins
- Better locality for settings access rules
- Higher leverage tests over redirect behavior
- Less direct importing of low-level organization or config details from settings routes
- Cleaner separation between cache/fact gathering and access policy

## Recommendation strength
Worth exploring

title: Architecture: map enterprise organization seams before extraction
body:
## Summary
Map enterprise organization axes and churn before extracting one organization module. Early shallow-clone data points at conversations or membership as likely first seams, but the first extraction should be selected from a fuller churn map rather than file size alone.

## Files
- `enterprise/server/routes/orgs.py`
- `enterprise/storage/org_service.py`
- `enterprise/server/routes/org_models.py`
- Member, financial, git-claim, and conversation organization modules

## Problem
The organization route module contains roughly 30 endpoints across several independent axes of change: lifecycle/defaults, membership, financials, git claims, conversation listing, conversation stats, CSV export, and stop actions. Supporting organization files are also large, including `org_service.py` and `org_models.py`.

This does suggest multiple modules hiding under one interface, but splitting by file size alone would be risky. The valuable first step is to identify which axis changes often enough, and is cohesive enough, to justify a genuine extracted interface.

## Proposed direction
First produce a churn-and-axis map for the enterprise organization code:
- classify routes and storage/model changes by lifecycle/defaults, membership, financials, git claims, and conversations
- re-run churn over a longer window before committing to the first extraction
- use the deletion test: the selected seam should let the route delete a meaningful block of code, not merely relocate functions to another file

Early shallow-clone data from approximately Apr 23, 2026 to Jun 30, 2026 suggests conversations and membership have the strongest movement. If a full-year churn check does not contradict that signal, conversations are a strong first candidate because the route block is large, self-contained, and covers listing, stats, usage, CSV export, detail fetch, and stop behavior.

For the first selected axis, extract a real interface such as `OrgConversationsService` or `OrgMembershipService`, with route handlers delegating to that service rather than preserving the current route-level implementation shape.

## Testing focus
Before extraction, add or identify focused tests for the chosen axis. For a conversations-first extraction, cover listing, stats/usage behavior, CSV export, detail access, and stop action authorization. For membership, cover member listing/counts, financial views, role updates, and removal behavior.

## Expected wins
- Better locality for enterprise-only organization changes
- Clearer leverage from tests that target one organization axis
- Reduced risk from broad route-module changes
- A data-backed first seam instead of a size-driven split

## Recommendation strength
Speculative until full-year churn data selects the first seam

title: OAuth Email Verification Trap: Users Can Change to Unverified Emails
body:
# OAuth Email Verification Trap: Users Can Change to Unverified Emails

## Problem Description

When users authenticate via OAuth (GitHub/Google), their email is initially verified by the OAuth provider. However, the system allows users to change their email address to any arbitrary email in the Enterprise Server UI. When they do this:

1. The new email is set as their account email
2. `email_verified` is set to `false` 
3. A verification email is sent to the new address
4. **The user interface provides no way to resend this verification email**

If the user misses the verification email (spam folder, typo in address, etc.), they become stuck in a state where:
- Their account shows `email_verified: false`
- They cannot verify their email because there's no resend button in the UI
- Depending on the client (Agent Canvas), they may lose access to features

This creates a **permanent trap** - once a user changes their email and misses the verification, they have no self-service recovery path.

## Additional Complexity: GitHub Multiple Email Addresses

GitHub allows users to have multiple email addresses, each with independent verification status. Users can:
- Add multiple emails to their GitHub account
- Set any email as "primary" 
- Change which email is primary at any time

The primary email is what GitHub returns during OAuth, along with its verification status. This creates scenarios where:
- A user's GitHub primary email is unverified → OAuth returns `email_verified: false`
- A user changes their GitHub primary email → their OpenHands email verification status changes on next login
- A user has verified emails in GitHub that aren't being used in OpenHands

Currently, OpenHands doesn't capture or expose the user's other GitHub emails, limiting their flexibility.

## Current Behavior

**OAuth Login Flow:**
```
1. User authenticates with GitHub
2. GitHub returns user info including:
   - email: user's primary email in GitHub
   - email_verified: verification status of that primary email
3. OpenHands stores this email and verification status
4. User has access to the system
```

**Email Change Flow (via Enterprise Server UI):**
```
1. User navigates to settings and changes email
2. Backend sets email_verified = false in both:
   - Keycloak (emailVerified: false)
   - OpenHands database (email_verified: false)
3. Verification email is sent to new address
4. User must click verification link to restore email_verified = true
```

**The Problem:**
- No UI exists to resend the verification email
- User cannot recover if they miss the initial email
- Admin intervention may be required to fix stuck accounts

## Proposed Solution (High Level)

### Option 1: Capture All OAuth Provider Emails
When a user authenticates via OAuth:
1. Fetch **all** their emails from the OAuth provider (e.g., GitHub's `/user/emails` API)
2. Store all verified emails from the provider
3. Let users **switch between** their verified OAuth emails
4. Only allow switching to emails that are already verified by the provider
5. Keep manual email changes for users who want to use non-GitHub emails (with verification)

**Benefits:**
- Leverages OAuth provider's email verification
- Gives users flexibility to choose which GitHub email to use
- Prevents the unverified email trap for OAuth users
- Stays in sync with GitHub when users add/remove/verify emails there

### Option 2: Add Email Verification Recovery UI
At minimum, add UI elements to:
1. Show current email verification status clearly
2. Provide a "Resend Verification Email" button
3. Allow users to revert to a previously verified email

**Benefits:**
- Simpler implementation
- Provides escape hatch for trapped users
- Works for both OAuth and password authentication users

### Recommended: Combination Approach
- Implement Option 1 (capture OAuth emails) for OAuth users
- Add resend verification UI for manual email changes
- This provides both prevention and recovery

## Impact for Agent Canvas

Agent Canvas currently disables navigation links when `email_verified === false`. This is more strict than the Enterprise Server backend (which allows all API operations regardless of email verification status). 

The combination of:
1. No email verification recovery UI in either Enterprise Server or Agent Canvas
2. Agent Canvas blocking navigation for unverified emails
3. Users being able to change to unverified emails

Creates a situation where OAuth users can accidentally lock themselves out of Agent Canvas features by changing their email address.

## Related Code Locations

- Email change endpoint: `/workspace/OpenHands/enterprise/server/routes/email.py`
- OAuth login flow: `/workspace/OpenHands/enterprise/server/routes/auth.py` (around line 400)
- User settings model: `/workspace/OpenHands/enterprise/storage/user_settings.py`
- Token manager (fetches OAuth user info): `/workspace/OpenHands/enterprise/server/auth/token_manager.py`

## User Impact

**Current State:**
- Users who change their email and miss verification are permanently stuck
- No self-service recovery mechanism exists
- Requires manual database/Keycloak intervention to fix

**Desired State:**
- Users can choose from their verified OAuth emails without re-verification
- If users add custom emails, they have clear visibility and recovery options
- No permanent trap states exist in the system

title: [Bug]: Conversation list panel shows raw error string with no fallback UI on failed request
